questions.question: Bills of exchange drawn on London or Glasgow merchants circulated among colonial merchants as a means of paying debts across the Atlantic, while colonial assemblies issued paper currency for local use of widely varying reliability. The two instruments coexisted because colonies chronically lacked

answers.text: any form of money whatsoever before 1750
specie — gold and silver coin — which drained away to pay for imports in a persistently unfavorable balance of trade
laws permitting contracts between private parties
merchants willing to trade beyond their own colony

questions.explanation: Coin left as fast as it arrived because imports exceeded staple earnings in coin terms, so credit paper filled the gap: sterling bills for Atlantic settlement, local paper for internal trade. Contracts and intercolonial merchants were abundant; it was hard money that was scarce.

questions.question: The Quebec Act of 1774 extended Quebec's boundaries to the Ohio River, continued French civil law and seigneurial tenure, and guaranteed the Catholic Church's position, without creating an elected assembly. Continental colonists denounced it as one of the intolerable measures chiefly because they read it as

answers.text: a tax on Canadian furs payable in Boston
an order closing all Protestant churches in Canada
a model of unrepresentative, royally controlled government planted on their western border, joined to claims on lands western colonies coveted
a grant of independence to Canada effective immediately

questions.explanation: To seaboard colonists the act combined three threats: blocked western claims, a neighboring government without an assembly, and state-secured Catholicism they associated with arbitrary rule. It imposed no Boston-paid tax, closed no churches, and granted no independence.

questions.question: A brilliant red dye made from insects harvested from prickly pear cacti in Oaxaca became, after silver, among the most valuable exports of Spanish America, because European wool and silk dyers prized its colorfastness. The dye's production remained in Native community hands using pre-conquest techniques. This case shows that colonial export economies

answers.text: always replaced Native production techniques with European ones
involved only mineral extraction and no agricultural products
excluded Native producers from any earnings by law
could rest on Indigenous knowledge and community labor embedded in global markets

questions.explanation: Cochineal joined Indigenous technical knowledge to worldwide demand without displacing the community producers who mastered the harvest and processing. It was an agricultural product, not a mineral, and Native towns negotiated earnings from its sale rather than being legally excluded from them.

questions.question: After Brown, many southern districts adopted 'freedom of choice' plans under which any student could nominally transfer to any school, and years later almost no white children attended Black schools and only a fraction of Black children attended white ones. In Green v. County School Board (1968), the Supreme Court rejected such plans where they failed in practice, holding that districts bore

answers.text: no duty at all once a formal choice was offered to parents

an affirmative duty to convert to a unitary system in which racial discrimination would be eliminated root and branch, judged by whether the plan actually dismantled the dual system rather than by its neutral wording
a duty only to equalize funding between the formerly separate schools
a duty to maintain racial balance in every classroom nationwide by exact quota

questions.explanation: Green shifted the test from form to results: a plan that left the dual system intact in fact — same racially identifiable schools year after year — did not satisfy Brown, whatever it promised on paper. The duty was to desegregate the district's own system, not to equalize separate schools or to impose universal classroom quotas; effects within the formerly segregated district were the measure.

questions.question: The postwar Treaty of Detroit pattern linked autoworkers' annual wage increases to estimated productivity growth plus a cost-of-living adjustment. The formula's significance for household budgets was that it

answers.text: froze autoworker pay at 1941 levels
made rising real living standards a routine contractual expectation rather than a strike-by-strike gamble
applied only to executives
covered every American worker by law

questions.explanation: An escalator-plus-productivity formula institutionalized steady real gains for covered workers across a five-year contract. Pay rose rather than froze, the bargain was a private union contract for autoworkers, and no statute extended it to all workers.

questions.question: During the mid-2000s housing boom, many borrowers took out interest-only adjustable-rate mortgages of the kind that later figured in the 2008 financial crisis. A borrower holds a 200,000 dollar interest-only adjustable-rate mortgage. At a six percent annual rate the monthly interest payment is 1,000 dollars. If the rate resets to nine percent, the new interest-only monthly payment would be

answers.text: 1,500 dollars
1,000 dollars
1,250 dollars
2,000 dollars

questions.explanation: Two hundred thousand times nine percent is 18,000 dollars a year, divided by twelve equals 1,500 dollars a month. The payment cannot stay at 1,000 when the rate rises, 1,250 would correspond to seven and a half percent, and 2,000 would require a twelve percent rate.

umpje.quiz_title: UMPJE Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam

questions.question: A mail-order pharmacy is preparing a shipment of a medicine for which a Medication Guide must be dispensed with the drug. A packer suggests including the guide only when a patient specifically asks for one, to save postage. What is the correct handling?

answers.text: Include the guide only with the first shipment, never with later ones
Substitute a general advertising leaflet that mentions the drug by name
Provide the Medication Guide with the medication as required, rather than only on patient request
Post the guide on the pharmacy's website and print a note that patients can look it up there

questions.explanation: A required Medication Guide must be dispensed with the drug, so mail-order shipment must include it as required and not only when a patient asks, making C correct. A is wrong because the requirement attaches to dispensing the drug, not only to a first shipment. B is wrong because promotional material is not the required guide, and D is wrong because making the guide available online does not substitute for providing it with the medication.

questions.question: A patient asks to move a Schedule IV prescription with refills remaining from your pharmacy to a competitor across town. Which action is correct?

answers.text: Communicate the transfer directly, pharmacist to pharmacist, so the receiving pharmacy can continue dispensing the remaining refills
Refuse, because controlled substances may never change pharmacies
Send the patient with a photocopy and let the new pharmacy work from it
Tell the patient a new prescriber visit is legally required for any transfer

questions.explanation: Schedule IV prescriptions may be transferred, with the information communicated directly between pharmacists, so A is correct. B is wrong because the no-transfer rule applies to Schedule II, not Schedules III through V. C is wrong because a patient-carried photocopy is not the pharmacist-to-pharmacist communication required. D is wrong because no new prescriber visit is required to transfer existing refill authority.

questions.question: The pharmacy receives notice of a Class I recall for a lot of a dispensed medication because of a defect creating a reasonable probability of serious harm or death. Some tablets from the lot remain on the shelf. What must the pharmacy do?

answers.text: Quarantine the recalled stock, dispense none of it, and carry out the recall steps for affected product and patients
Keep dispensing the stock until it runs out, because the recall is voluntary
Return the stock to the regular shelf after a visual inspection shows the tablets look normal
Downgrade the response, because Class I is the least serious recall class

questions.explanation: Class I is the most serious recall category, and recalled stock must be quarantined and never dispensed while the pharmacy follows the recall process. Option B is wrong because a recall being voluntary for the firm does not permit a pharmacy to keep dispensing recalled product, option C is wrong because appearance cannot clear a recalled lot, and option D reverses the classes; Class III is the least serious.

questions.question: A patient with severe arthritis tells the pharmacist she cannot open child-resistant caps and asks for easy-open closures on her oral prescriptions. No one else has raised the issue. What may the pharmacist do?

answers.text: Refuse, because child-resistant packaging can never be waived
Agree only if the patient first obtains a court or board waiver
Honor the patient's own request and dispense her prescriptions in non-child-resistant packaging
Honor it only for over-the-counter products, never for prescriptions

questions.explanation: Most oral prescriptions must be dispensed in child-resistant containers unless the patient or the prescriber requests otherwise, and this patient's own request is enough. Option A is wrong because the requirement has a request-based exception, option B is wrong because no external waiver is needed, and option D is wrong because the exception applies to prescription dispensing, not just over-the-counter sales.

questions.question: A 17-year-old asks at the pharmacy counter to buy levonorgestrel emergency contraception from the over-the-counter shelf. A clerk says a prescription, proof of being 18, and a parent's permission are all needed first. What is the correct federal position?

answers.text: The clerk is right that all three are required before the sale
A prescription is required, but no proof of age or parental permission is needed
Proof of age is required, but no prescription or parental permission is needed
The product is available over the counter with no age restriction, so none of the clerk's three requirements applies

questions.explanation: Levonorgestrel emergency contraception is over the counter with no age restriction under the federal framework, so D is correct. A is wrong because it imposes a prescription, an age threshold, and parental permission that the federal position does not impose. B is wrong because no prescription is required for this over-the-counter product, and C is wrong because no proof of age is required either.

questions.question: Before a morning vaccination session, a pharmacist finds that the refrigerator holding the day's vaccines recorded a temperature excursion outside the labeled storage conditions overnight. The vials look normal and a full waiting room is expected. What should the pharmacist do with those vials?

answers.text: Administer them as scheduled, because appearance is the practical test of vaccine quality
Administer them only to patients who agree after being told about the excursion
Discard the documentation of the excursion so the session can proceed without delay
Set the affected vials aside and not administer them, document the excursion, and determine the product's integrity through the proper excursion process before any use

questions.explanation: D is correct because drugs must be stored at their labeled conditions and temperature excursions must be documented and resolved before the product is used; a normal appearance does not establish that an excursion left the vaccine unaffected. A is wrong because visual inspection cannot substitute for the storage and excursion requirements. B is wrong because patient agreement does not cure uncertainty about a product stored outside its labeled conditions. C is wrong because destroying the excursion record compounds the problem; excursions are to be documented, not concealed.

questions.question: A pharmacy technician's state registration lapsed last week when her renewal was not completed. She has submitted the renewal paperwork and asks to keep filling prescriptions in the meantime, since she worked at the pharmacy for six years without a problem. What should the pharmacist-in-charge do?

answers.text: Let her keep filling, because six years of experience outweighs a brief paperwork lapse
Let her fill only refills until the renewal is confirmed, since refills involve less judgment
Let her work under the pharmacist-in-charge's license number until her own registration is current again

Keep her out of technician duties and out of restricted prescription-department work until her registration or licensure is current, because performing technician duties requires that credential to be in effect

questions.explanation: D is correct because technician registration or licensure is issued under state board authority and is a precondition to performing technician duties, not a formality that can trail behind the work. A is wrong because experience does not substitute for a current credential. B is wrong because a lapsed credential is not partially cured by limiting the work to refills, and C is wrong because a pharmacist's license does not cover another person's unregistered practice.

questions.question: A pharmacist is found to have diverted controlled substances from the pharmacy's stock over several months. He argues that because he has not been convicted of any crime, neither the licensing board nor the federal drug enforcement authority can touch him — only his employer can fire him. Which statement is correct?

answers.text: Only the employer may act until a criminal conviction is entered
The board may act, but the federal authority may never act against a state-licensed pharmacist

Both tracks are available: the board can discipline the license for impairment or diversion, and the federal authority can deny or revoke the controlled-substance registration, without waiting for a criminal conviction
Discipline is barred because diversion by an employee is treated solely as a store inventory problem

questions.explanation: C is correct because board discipline reaches unprofessional conduct, impairment, and diversion, and the federal authority can separately deny or revoke a controlled-substance registration. A is wrong because neither track depends on a prior criminal conviction. B is wrong because federal registration authority operates alongside state licensure, and D is wrong because personal diversion is not reduced to a bookkeeping issue for the store.

questions.question: A prescriber faxes a Schedule II prescription for a patient receiving hospice care at home, and the pharmacy's staff ask whether they must wait for a paper original before dispensing, as they ordinarily would with a faxed Schedule II order. What is the correct treatment of this fax?

answers.text: The fax can never be used, and the hospice nurse must hand-deliver the original before any dose is prepared
The fax may be used only if the patient also brings a signed copy to the pharmacy in person
The fax must be converted to an electronic prescription by an intermediary before it can be relied on
For hospice patients the fax may serve as the original prescription, so the pharmacy may dispense from it without waiting for a separate paper original

questions.explanation: Although a fax generally does not serve as the original for a Schedule II prescription, hospice patients are one of the recognized exceptions, along with long-term care and home-infusion patients, where the fax may serve as the original. A applies the general rule while ignoring the hospice exception. B adds a patient-delivered copy that the exception does not require, and C is wrong because an intermediary-converted transmission is not a valid electronic prescription.

questions.question: A lot of a nighttime sleep-aid tablet is recalled because some tablets contain roughly double the labeled amount of active ingredient. Patients who took them reported pronounced next-day sedation that resolved fully within a day after stopping, with no lasting injury expected. How is this recall classified?

answers.text: Class I, because any error in labeled strength is automatically the most serious class
Class III, because the defect is unlikely to cause harm
Class II, because the likely harm is temporary and medically reversible
No recall class applies until a patient is hospitalized

questions.explanation: C is correct: Class II covers recalls where the likely harm is temporary and medically reversible, which fits fully resolving sedation with no lasting injury expected. A is wrong because classification turns on the probability and severity of harm, not on the mere existence of a strength error. B is wrong because Class III covers defects unlikely to cause harm, while these patients did experience an adverse effect. D is wrong because a recall is classified on the risk presented, without waiting for a hospitalization.

questions.question: A prescriber documents that a patient has a confirmed allergy to gelatin and sends a patient-specific prescription for a compounded version of a commercially available capsule product, made in a gelatin-free dosage form the patient can safely take. How should the pharmacy proceed?

answers.text: Refuse, because compounding any version of a commercially available product is always prohibited
Compound the gelatin-free preparation for this patient, because the prescriber has documented a significant clinical difference for this patient
Compound the preparation only if the patient also agrees to pay the full cash price in advance
Dispense the marketed gelatin capsules with a warning to watch for a reaction

questions.explanation: B is correct: a compounded copy of a commercially available drug is permitted where the prescriber documents a significant clinical difference for the individual patient, and a documented allergy to an ingredient of the marketed product supplies that difference. A is wrong because the prohibition on copies has this documented-difference exception. C is wrong because advance cash payment is not the condition that makes compounding a copy permissible. D is wrong because dispensing the very product the patient is allergic to ignores the documented clinical need the compounded form addresses.

questions.question: During counseling on a new prescription, a patient says they plan to keep the medicine in a glove compartment so it is always handy in the car. The pharmacist has covered the dose and route but nothing about keeping the product properly. What should the pharmacist add?

answers.text: Nothing, because where a patient keeps a medicine is a personal choice outside counseling
A note that storage may be discussed only by the prescriber who wrote the prescription
A referral to a technician, who can explain storage while the pharmacist verifies other fills
Counseling on proper storage, because storage is one of the key points counseling should cover

questions.explanation: Storage is one of the key counseling points, along with the drug's name and description, dosage form and route, duration, special directions, precautions, side effects, refill information, and missed-dose guidance, so D is correct. A is wrong because storage is part of the pharmacist's counseling content, not an excluded personal matter. B is wrong because the counseling duty on storage belongs to the pharmacist as well as the prescriber, and C is wrong because a technician may not provide this counseling.

questions.question: While the registrant was on vacation last week, a covering pharmacist with no power of attorney signed the pharmacy's Schedule II orders so stock would not run out. Today the registrant executes a power of attorney for that pharmacist and asks whether the document validates last week's signatures. What is the answer?

answers.text: Yes, because the power of attorney reaches back to the start of the pharmacist's employment
Yes, if the registrant also ratifies the earlier orders verbally in front of staff
No, because signing authority comes from a power of attorney that has been executed before the signing; a document executed today does not retroactively authorize signatures made without it
Yes, because the orders signed last week were routine restocking rather than special purchases

questions.explanation: Authority to sign controlled-substance order forms or electronic orders belongs to the registrant or to a person who has been granted an executed power of attorney, so the grant must be in place when the signing occurs and cannot cure earlier unauthorized signatures after the fact (C). A is wrong because execution today does not reach back to the start of employment. B is wrong because verbal ratification is not the executed grant the framework requires, and D is wrong because the authority requirement does not depend on whether an order was routine.

questions.question: A pharmacist resolves a board case over a dispensing incident by a consent agreement imposing probation and a fine. A patient injured in the same incident then files a malpractice suit, and the pharmacist moves to dismiss it on the ground that the board case already resolved the matter. Which position is correct?

answers.text: The consent agreement ends every other proceeding over the same act
A civil suit may proceed only if the board first found a violation after a full hearing
Malpractice and board discipline are independent tracks, so the board resolution does not bar or decide the patient's civil claim
The patient must sue the board instead, because the board handled the incident first

questions.explanation: C is correct because malpractice and board discipline are independent tracks; civil, administrative, and criminal exposure can all arise from the same act, and resolving the administrative track does not decide the civil one. A is wrong because a board consent agreement binds the licensing matter, not a patient's separate civil claim. B is wrong because the civil claim does not depend on a prior board finding after a hearing. D is wrong because the patient's malpractice claim is against the pharmacist or pharmacy in civil court, not against the board.

questions.question: At a pharmacy's receiving dock, a staff member drops a tote and a bottle of Schedule III tablets shatters, scattering tablets across the floor where they are contaminated and cannot be dispensed. The manager asks whether a theft-or-loss notice is due to the federal authority by the next business day. What is the correct handling?

answers.text: Yes, because any controlled-substance shortage, however it occurred, is reported as a theft or significant loss within one business day

No, because breakage and spillage are documented in the pharmacy's records with witness attestation and any destroyed stock is handled through the registrant disposal process, rather than reported on the theft-or-loss pathway
No record of any kind is needed, as long as a staff member can explain the shortage verbally if asked
Return the unbroken tablets gathered from the floor to stock and document only the tablets that are visibly crushed

questions.explanation: B is correct because breakage and spillage follow a different pathway from theft and loss: the incident is documented in the pharmacy's records with witness attestation, and destroyed stock goes through the registrant disposal process. A is wrong because it collapses that distinction, treating an explained, witnessed accident as if it were an unexplained theft or significant loss. C is wrong because the incident does require a record; a verbal explanation is not the documented handling the framework calls for. D is wrong because contaminated tablets scattered on a floor may not be returned to dispensing stock, and documenting only part of the loss misstates the incident.

questions.question: At the receiving dock, a pharmacist checks in a shipment whose paperwork shows ten bottles of a Schedule II medication, but the sealed tote contains only eight. The supplier confirms it shipped ten, and no dispensing or breakage record explains the two missing bottles. How must the pharmacy treat the shortage?

answers.text: As a vendor billing dispute only, to be settled on the next invoice without any outside report
As a discrepancy to hold until the biennial inventory, in case the bottles turn up in another tote
As a significant loss: notify the DEA in writing within one business day of the discovery and complete the federal theft/loss report form
As breakage and spillage, documented in the pharmacy's own records with no outside report

questions.explanation: An unexplained shortage of this kind is a significant loss, which requires written notice to the DEA within one business day of discovery and completion of the theft/loss report, Form 106 (C). A is wrong because treating it as a billing matter ignores an actual unexplained loss of controlled substances. B is wrong because the notification duty runs from discovery, not from the next inventory, and D is wrong because the breakage-and-spillage documentation route applies to stock actually broken or spilled, not to bottles that are simply gone.

questions.question: A pharmacy hires a technician who holds a current national technician certification and several years of experience, but who has not obtained the technician registration or licensure this jurisdiction's board requires. The technician asks to begin counting and labeling prescriptions on the first shift. What is the proper response?

answers.text: Allow the work, because national certification is accepted in place of state registration everywhere
Allow the work for a probationary month while the state application is prepared
Withhold technician duties requiring the state credential until the board-issued registration or licensure is in place, limiting the new hire to assignments that do not require it
Allow the work if a pharmacist checks every prescription the technician touches

questions.explanation: C is correct: technician registration or licensure is issued by the state board, and duties requiring that credential may not begin until it is held, however experienced or nationally certified the hire is. A is wrong because national certification does not replace the board's own registration or licensure. B is wrong because there is no probationary period for performing credentialed duties without the credential. D is wrong because pharmacist checking, while required for verification, does not waive the credential requirement for the technician's own work.

questions.question: During a declared public health emergency, the federal food and drug agency authorizes an unapproved antiviral product for a specific emergency use, with fact sheets that must be given to recipients and conditions that limit who may receive it. A pharmacist is asked to dispense it to a patient who falls outside those conditions, on the theory that authorization means the product is now approved for general use. What should the pharmacist do?

answers.text: Dispense only within the authorization's stated conditions and provide the required fact sheet, because emergency authorization is not general approval of the product
Dispense it freely, because emergency authorization converts the product into a fully approved drug for all uses
Refuse to dispense the product to anyone, because an unapproved product may never be dispensed under any circumstances
Dispense it outside the conditions if the patient signs a waiver releasing the pharmacy

questions.explanation: A is correct: an emergency use authorization lets the agency authorize an unapproved product or use during a declared emergency, but dispensing follows the authorization's conditions, including its fact sheets and limits on who may receive it. B is wrong because authorization for a defined emergency use is not full approval for general use. C is wrong because the authorization exists precisely so the product may be dispensed under its conditions. D is wrong because a patient waiver cannot override the conditions attached to the authorization.

questions.question: A pharmacist asks a registered pharmacy technician, working under the pharmacist's supervision, to make scripted intake calls to new patients to record demographic details, medicine lists, and allergy histories word-for-word in the profile for the pharmacist's review. During one call, a patient describes a past reaction and asks the technician whether that reaction means the new medicine is unsafe for her. How should the technician handle the call?

answers.text: Reassure the patient that most past reactions do not affect new medicines, and finish the intake
Interpret the reaction history and note in the profile whether the new medicine is safe

Record the history exactly as the patient states it and refer the safety question to the pharmacist, because gathering information verbatim is a proper technician task while judging its clinical significance is not
End the intake and tell the patient the pharmacy cannot fill for her until a prescriber clarifies the reaction

questions.explanation: C is correct: a technician working under supervision may perform the mechanical task of collecting and recording patient information exactly as given, but assessing what a reaction history means for a new medicine is clinical judgment reserved to the pharmacist. A is wrong because reassuring the patient about safety is itself a clinical judgment, however generally worded. B is wrong because interpreting the history and charting a safety conclusion performs the pharmacist's review function. D is wrong because it overcorrects: the intake may be completed and the question referred, rather than abandoning the patient to resolve the issue with the prescriber alone.

questions.question: At prescription data entry, the pharmacy system flags a serious interaction between a new order and a medicine already on the patient's profile. To keep the intake line moving, the registered technician entering the order clears the alert herself and queues the prescription for filling, planning to mention it to the pharmacist only if the pharmacist happens to ask. What is correct?

answers.text: The technician acted properly, because clearing alerts is part of data entry
The alert may be cleared by whoever sees it first, as long as the prescription is eventually filled accurately
The flagged interaction must go to the pharmacist for prospective review and judgment; a technician performs mechanical tasks under supervision and may not judge or clear a clinical alert on her own
The alert should be deleted from the profile so it does not slow down future refills

questions.explanation: C is correct: prospective drug utilization review, including screening for interactions, is the pharmacist's review before dispensing, and technicians work under pharmacist supervision on non-judgmental, mechanical tasks; deciding that an interaction alert does not matter is clinical judgment the technician may not exercise. A is wrong because data entry does not include disposing of clinical alerts. B is wrong because accurate counting and labeling do not cure the skipped pharmacist review of a flagged interaction. D is wrong because deleting the alert destroys the very screening the review depends on.

nbrc-rte.quiz_title: NBRC RTE Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam

questions.question: Which question best assesses a patient's activities of daily living as part of a respiratory assessment?

answers.text: "Do you need help with bathing, dressing, or climbing the stairs in your home because of your breathing?"
"What was your most recent FEV1 in the pulmonary function laboratory?"
"How many cigarettes did your father smoke each day?"
"What time of day do you prefer to take your inhaler?"

questions.explanation: The key is right: activities of daily living are the basic self-care and mobility tasks of everyday life, so asking whether breathlessness forces the patient to need help with bathing, dressing, or stairs directly measures functional impact. The FEV1 distractor is wrong because a laboratory value is an objective test result, not a report of daily functioning. The father's smoking distractor is wrong because it explores family history, not the patient's own daily activities. The inhaler-timing distractor is wrong because it addresses medication scheduling preference, not the ability to perform daily tasks.

questions.question: A glass blood gas ampoule breaks on the counter, scattering glass fragments mixed with blood. How should the debris be collected?

answers.text: Pick up the fragments by hand wearing procedure gloves, working quickly
Use a mechanical method — tongs, forceps, or a brush and dustpan — to collect the fragments into a rigid sharps container, then disinfect the surface
Sweep the fragments into the regular trash with a paper towel
Push the fragments into a floor drain with running water

questions.explanation: The key is right: broken contaminated glass is collected mechanically, never by hand, and goes into a rigid sharps container, followed by surface disinfection — gloves alone do not stop glass from cutting skin. The by-hand distractor is wrong because it invites a combined sharps and blood exposure. Regular trash is wrong because loose glass injures waste handlers through the bag. The floor-drain distractor is wrong because it spreads contaminated material into the plumbing and leaves fragments unaccounted for.

questions.question: An interhospital transfer has been accepted for a ventilated patient. Which steps must be completed with the receiving facility before departure?

answers.text: Confirm the accepting provider and receiving unit's readiness, send the records and imaging, agree the estimated arrival time, and report any change in the patient's condition before and during the transfer
Depart as soon as the ambulance arrives and telephone the receiving unit after arrival
Send the patient's records by post the following day, since the transport team carries a verbal summary
Confirm only the destination address; clinical details are the receiving team's responsibility to discover

questions.explanation: The key is right: a safe transfer is a continuum - acceptance, readiness, transmitted records and imaging, an agreed arrival estimate, and updates on any change - so the receiving team is prepared and no information is lost at the handover. The call-after-arrival distractor is wrong because it leaves the receiving unit unprepared for the patient's actual needs. The post-the-records distractor is wrong because decisions en route and on arrival depend on records travelling with or ahead of the patient. The address-only distractor is wrong because a destination without clinical preparation is a delivery, not a transfer of care.

questions.question: A 50-year-old man recovering from ARDS has been stable for 12 hours on FiO2 0.40 and PEEP 12 cm H2O with SpO2 96%, plateau pressure 20 cm H2O, and he is awake and comfortable. The team wants to begin reducing support. Which PEEP strategy is most appropriate?

answers.text: Drop PEEP directly from 12 to 0 cm H2O to test whether he still needs it
Increase PEEP to 16 cm H2O now that he is improving, to protect the lungs

Perform a stepwise PEEP decrement — small reductions with observation of saturation, compliance, and comfort after each step — keeping FiO2 steady so the effect of each change is interpretable, and stopping if oxygenation or mechanics worsen
Change PEEP and FiO2 simultaneously by large amounts so the trial finishes faster

questions.explanation: Recovering ARDS lungs still derecruit easily, so PEEP is weaned the way it was titrated — in small steps, one variable at a time, with saturation and compliance checked after each step and the last tolerated level restored if he worsens. Dropping straight to zero (option A) risks abrupt derecruitment and a hypoxemic setback. Raising PEEP during recovery (option B) moves against the weaning goal and adds pressure without indication. Changing two variables by large amounts at once (option D) makes the result uninterpretable — if he worsens, no one will know which change caused it.

questions.question: A term newborn delivered through thick meconium-stained fluid is limp and apneic at birth with a heart rate of 70/min. The airway is positioned and the mouth and nose are cleared of visible secretions. What should the team do next?

answers.text: Perform routine tracheal suctioning under direct vision before any ventilation attempt
Begin positive-pressure ventilation promptly, because a non-vigorous infant with apnea and a heart rate below 100/min needs ventilation, not routine tracheal suctioning
Continue drying and tactile stimulation for a full minute to see if respirations return
Give free-flow 100% oxygen and reassess the heart rate in 1 minute

questions.explanation: B is correct: a non-vigorous meconium infant who is apneic with bradycardia needs effective ventilation as the priority; meconium in the airway is managed only if obstruction is suspected after ventilation begins. Routine tracheal suctioning is wrong because it delays ventilation and is no longer recommended for non-vigorous infants. Prolonged stimulation is wrong because apnea with a heart rate below 100/min has already declared the need for PPV. Free-flow oxygen is wrong because it cannot ventilate an apneic infant.

questions.question: A therapist is measuring bedside spontaneous breathing mechanics in a cooperative postoperative patient. Which sequence correctly measures vital capacity with a bedside spirometer?

answers.text: Have the patient exhale maximally first, then measure a normal tidal inhalation
Record the volume of three quiet tidal breaths and average them
Have the patient inhale maximally, then exhale maximally into the spirometer
Ask the patient to pant rapidly for 15 seconds and multiply by four

questions.explanation: Vital capacity is the volume exhaled after a maximal inhalation, so the patient inhales fully and then exhales completely into the device — C is correct. B measures tidal volume, not vital capacity. A reverses the maneuver and captures only a tidal breath from end-expiratory level. D approximates a rate/volume product resembling minute ventilation, not vital capacity.

questions.question: A ventilator circuit includes an inline condensate water trap in the expiratory limb. Since the circuit was hung, condensate keeps reaching the flow sensor and ventilator instead of collecting in the trap, and the trap's cup stays nearly empty even though it sits at the circuit's lowest point. The cup is mounted sideways, its inlet and outlet at the same height with the collection well horizontal. Why is the trap not working?

answers.text: A water trap separates condensate by gravity into a dependent well below the gas path; mounted sideways it has no well below the flow, so condensate is carried past it - it must hang vertically at the low point
Water traps work by absorption, and this trap's absorbent is exhausted and should be replaced
The trap is in the wrong limb - traps only function in the inspiratory limb of a circuit
The ventilator's expiratory flow is too fast for any trap, so traps should be removed from adult circuits

questions.explanation: The key is right: the trap is a gravity separator - gas passes across the top while liquid falls into the cup hanging below it; rotated sideways, the cup is beside the gas path instead of beneath it, so condensate streams past toward the sensor. The absorption distractor is wrong because these traps contain no absorbent to exhaust; they are empty mechanical separators. The wrong-limb distractor is wrong because traps are correctly placed at low points in either limb, commonly the expiratory limb where condensate load is highest. The remove-traps distractor is wrong because expiratory flows are exactly what traps are designed for when oriented correctly.

questions.question: A preterm infant with respiratory distress syndrome is placed on bubble CPAP. The expiratory limb of the circuit is submerged 6 cm below the water surface in the bubble chamber. What CPAP level does this provide, and what determines it?

answers.text: About 6 cm H2O, set by the depth the expiratory limb is submerged below the water level
About 6 L/min, set by the fresh gas flow into the circuit
A level determined by the size of the nasal prongs alone
A level that rises automatically as the infant's lung compliance falls

questions.explanation: In bubble CPAP the pressure in the system equals the depth of water the expiratory gas must bubble through, so a limb submerged 6 cm delivers about 6 cm H2O, adjusted by raising or lowering the limb. Describing the level in liters per minute is wrong because that confuses the fresh gas flow, which must be sufficient to generate bubbling, with the pressure the depth creates. Prong size is wrong because prongs affect leak and fit, not the pressure set by the water column. Automatic rise with falling compliance is wrong because this simple device has no feedback mechanism; its pressure changes only when the depth or leak changes.

questions.question: A 71-year-old man with COPD is intubated and ventilated. His capnography tracing shows a prolonged, sloping expiratory upstroke with no flat alveolar plateau, giving the waveform a shark-fin appearance, while the end-tidal value itself is only modestly changed. Which interpretation best explains this tracing?

answers.text: Expiratory airflow obstruction from bronchospasm is slowing alveolar emptying, so exhaled gas reaches the sensor unevenly and late
The patient is hyperventilating, which washes carbon dioxide out too quickly to form a plateau
A large circuit leak is diluting the sampled gas
A sudden pulmonary embolism has cut off pulmonary blood flow

questions.explanation: The key is right: obstructed airways empty at different rates, so carbon dioxide arrives at the sensor progressively through exhalation, producing the sloping shark-fin upstroke and loss of plateau typical of bronchospasm in COPD and asthma. Hyperventilation is wrong because it lowers the end-tidal value but preserves a normal waveform shape. A circuit leak is wrong because leaks reduce sampled volume and value rather than reshape the upstroke this way. Pulmonary embolism is wrong because its classic capnographic signature is an abrupt fall in end-tidal carbon dioxide from lost perfusion, not a prolonged expiratory slope.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man treated for influenza pneumonia was improving, then returns to the emergency department on illness day 6 with recurrent fever 39.4°C, rigors, new purulent sputum, and a worsening right upper lobe infiltrate with a small cavitation. Which development should the therapist suspect and help evaluate first?

answers.text: Resolving viral pneumonia, requiring no further workup
A pulmonary embolism as the only plausible explanation
Dehydration from fever as the sole cause of the new infiltrate
Secondary bacterial superinfection, classically including Staphylococcus aureus — obtain sputum and blood cultures and recommend broadening antimicrobial coverage

questions.explanation: Biphasic deterioration after influenza — improvement followed by new fever, purulence, and cavitary infiltrate — is the classic pattern of secondary bacterial superinfection, with S. aureus a leading concern; cultures and broader coverage are indicated. A ignores clear deterioration. B is possible in general but does not explain purulent sputum and cavitation. C does not cause a new cavitary infiltrate.

questions.question: At a pre-operative clinic, a 60-year-old woman scheduled for major bowel surgery in 5 weeks has hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL with iron deficiency. She clearly states that her faith prohibits blood transfusion and asks what can still be done to prepare her safely. What plan best respects her wishes while optimizing her?

answers.text: Tell her surgery is impossible and discharge her from the clinic
Treat the iron deficiency, evaluate erythropoietin eligibility, document her refusal, and coordinate blood-conservation measures such as meticulous technique and cell salvage if she accepts it
Plan to transfuse her under anesthesia without telling her, since she will be asleep
Delay surgery indefinitely until she agrees to accept transfusion

questions.explanation: The key is right: patient blood management — correcting iron deficiency, considering erythropoietin, documenting an informed refusal, and using conservation techniques the patient accepts — optimizes oxygen-carrying capacity while honoring autonomy. A is wrong because surgery is often feasible with blood management. C is wrong because transfusing against a known refusal violates consent and is a serious ethical and legal breach. D is wrong because indefinite delay punishes a lawful preference instead of planning around it.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man with COPD attends clinic. During the visit he tells the respiratory therapist he still smokes half a pack a day, but asks her not to document it because he fears his insurance coverage could be affected, and an earlier note incorrectly records him as a former smoker. What should the therapist do?

answers.text: Agree to leave the smoking out of the record as he requests
Document that he quit smoking, matching the earlier note, to keep the record consistent
Document his current smoking accurately, explain honestly why an accurate record matters for his care, and offer cessation support and resources
Remove the earlier note from the chart so there is no contradiction

questions.explanation: Key C is correct: the clinical record must reflect reality — his current smoking directly affects exacerbation risk, therapy choices, and cessation support — so the therapist documents accurately, explains the reason transparently rather than deceiving him, and pairs the correction with an offer of help to quit. A is wrong because omitting a material clinical fact falsifies the record and deprives the team of information his care depends on. B is wrong because recording a false quit status compounds the earlier error instead of correcting it. D is wrong because deleting prior entries destroys record integrity; corrections are made by addendum, not removal.

questions.question: A patient with a high spinal cord injury has a maximal inspiratory pressure of -84 cm H2O (near predicted) but a maximal expiratory pressure of only 28 cm H2O (far below predicted), and the cough is visibly feeble with retained secretions. How should these strength results be evaluated?

answers.text: As global respiratory muscle failure requiring immediate full ventilatory support
As normal strength, because the inspiratory value is preserved
As diaphragmatic paralysis, because expiratory pressure is the diaphragm test
As isolated expiratory muscle weakness with preserved inspiration: breathing in is adequate, but cough and secretion clearance are impaired, so airway-clearance support is the priority problem

questions.explanation: The key is right: MIP tests the inspiratory muscles including the diaphragm and is preserved here, while MEP tests the expiratory muscles (abdominals and intercostals) that generate cough - its severe reduction explains the feeble cough and retained secretions in a high cord injury, making secretion clearance, not ventilation, the primary deficit. Global failure is wrong because inspiration is objectively near normal. Calling the set normal ignores the frankly abnormal MEP and the clinical cough failure. Diaphragmatic paralysis is backwards - the diaphragm is an inspiratory muscle and would lower the MIP, which is the preserved value.

questions.question: During an emergency airway attempt, intubation has failed, a supraglottic airway has failed, and bag-mask ventilation cannot maintain oxygen saturation, which continues to fall. What is the most appropriate next action?

answers.text: Emergency front-of-neck access (e.g., cricothyrotomy) to establish an airway
Make one more prolonged direct laryngoscopy attempt
Administer additional neuromuscular blocker and wait
Stop all airway efforts and obtain a chest radiograph

questions.explanation: A cannot-intubate/cannot-oxygenate situation is a surgical-airway emergency: front-of-neck access (cricothyrotomy) is the definitive rescue when intubation, supraglottic, and mask ventilation have all failed and saturation is falling. B wastes the remaining oxygen reserve. C deepens paralysis without an airway. D delays the lifesaving intervention.

questions.question: During a team huddle, a colleague proposes prone positioning for a patient with severe hypoxemia. The therapist knows this patient also has an unstable spinal injury documented in the chart. What should the therapist do?

answers.text: Say nothing, because positioning is the nurse's decision alone
Document a private disagreement in the chart and let the maneuver proceed
Wait until after the turn to mention the spine injury, to avoid embarrassing the colleague
Speak up in the huddle, share the documented contraindication, and invite the team to discuss alternative oxygenation strategies with the provider

questions.explanation: The key is right: a documented contraindication is safety information the team needs before acting, so the therapist raises it in the huddle and redirects the discussion toward alternatives. Silence is wrong because prone positioning with an unstable spine can cause catastrophic injury and positioning is a team decision. A private chart note is wrong because it records a concern without preventing the harm. Waiting until after the turn is wrong because the information is only useful before the maneuver happens.

questions.question: At a sleep clinic visit, a 52-year-old man with BMI 47 kg/m2 uses CPAP nightly for obstructive sleep apnea but reports unrefreshing sleep, morning headaches, and daytime sleepiness. Daytime ABG on room air: pH 7.36, PaCO2 58 mmHg, HCO3 32 mEq/L, PaO2 68 mmHg; SpO2 91%. His CPAP download shows good adherence and a low residual apnea index. What should the respiratory therapist recommend?

answers.text: Recommend evaluation for bilevel PAP titration because chronic daytime hypercapnia indicates hypoventilation that CPAP alone is not correcting
Recommend adding nocturnal supplemental oxygen alone to the CPAP circuit
Recommend discontinuing PAP therapy since his apnea index is controlled
Recommend daytime oxygen only and no change to nighttime therapy

questions.explanation: A is correct: compensated chronic hypercapnia (elevated PaCO2 with raised bicarbonate) plus obesity and sleep-disordered breathing defines obesity hypoventilation; bilevel support augments alveolar ventilation in a way CPAP, which mainly splints the airway, does not. B is wrong because oxygen alone can worsen nocturnal hypercapnia by reducing ventilatory drive and worsening V/Q matching. C is wrong because his apnea is controlled but his hypoventilation is not; stopping PAP removes needed therapy. D is wrong because the hypoventilation is predominantly nocturnal and daytime oxygen does not treat it.

questions.question: A patient's metered-dose inhaler doses seem weaker since the valved holding chamber was washed and then vigorously dried inside and out with a terry towel, as the patient proudly reports doing after every use. The inhaler itself is in date and its dose counter is advancing. What handling fault explains the reduced delivery?

answers.text: Washing a chamber always ruins it, so it must be replaced after any cleaning
The dose counter advancing proves the full dose reached the patient's lungs
The chamber's one-way valve is designed to trap medication, so weaker doses are expected
Towel-drying builds static charge on the chamber walls, which attracts and holds aerosol particles; the chamber should be washed as directed and left to air-dry without toweling

questions.explanation: The key is right: plastic chambers hold aerosol in suspension only briefly; a static charge built up by toweling pulls particles onto the walls before inhalation, reducing the respirable dose - manufacturer-directed washing and drip/air drying without toweling minimizes static. The washing-ruins-it distractor is wrong because periodic washing is recommended care; it is the toweling, not the washing, that causes this problem. The counter distractor is wrong because the counter tracks actuations leaving the canister, not the dose surviving the chamber to reach the lungs. The valve distractor is wrong because the valve's purpose is to hold the aerosol for the patient's next breath and open on inhalation, not to trap and waste it.

questions.question: A healthcare worker with a documented prior positive tuberculin skin test and completed treatment for latent infection now has a new exposure to active tuberculosis. The worker is asymptomatic with a clear chest radiograph. Which recommendation is most appropriate?

answers.text: Repeat the tuberculin skin test to see if it has become negative
Recommend symptom review and chest imaging surveillance rather than repeat skin or blood testing, because prior positive tests remain positive and retesting adds no information
Start four-drug therapy for active tuberculosis immediately
Recommend bronchoscopy to exclude active disease

questions.explanation: Key B is correct: after a documented positive test and completed latent treatment, repeat TST or IGRA remains positive and is uninformative; monitoring relies on symptom review and chest imaging. A is wrong because prior positive skin tests do not revert reliably and retesting is not recommended. C is wrong because there are no symptoms or imaging findings of active disease to justify full therapy. D is wrong because invasive bronchoscopy is not indicated in an asymptomatic person with a clear radiograph.

questions.question: A patient with advanced COPD and decision-making capacity is told that worsening respiratory failure will likely require intubation. After a clear discussion of benefits, burdens, and alternatives, the patient consistently states they do not want intubation under any circumstances, while accepting noninvasive support and comfort measures. What should the therapist recommend the team do?

answers.text: Honor the informed refusal, document a do-not-intubate plan, and continue noninvasive support and symptom-focused care consistent with the patient's wishes
Plan to intubate anyway when the patient becomes too breathless to repeat the refusal
Ask the family to override the patient's decision, because family preference outranks a capacitated patient's refusal
Withdraw all respiratory support immediately, because declining intubation means declining every form of support

questions.explanation: The key is right: a patient with decision-making capacity may refuse intubation after informed discussion, and honoring and documenting that refusal while continuing accepted supports respects autonomy and remains full, active care. Intubating once the patient cannot object is wrong because it directly violates a known, valid refusal. Family override is wrong because a capacitated patient's own decision takes precedence over family preference. Withdrawing all support is wrong because the patient accepted noninvasive support and comfort measures, so refusal of one intervention is not refusal of everything.

questions.question: A 49-year-old woman with severe pulmonary arterial hypertension and right ventricular failure is intubated after a syncopal episode. On the ventilator her ABG deteriorates to pH 7.27, PaCO2 58 mmHg, PaO2 64 mmHg on FiO2 0.70, and her systemic blood pressure falls whenever she becomes more acidemic. What respiratory decision is most appropriate?

answers.text: Tolerate the hypercapnia and acidemia without change, since permissive hypercapnia is always preferred
Adjust ventilation to correct hypercapnia and hypoxemia and recommend an inhaled pulmonary vasodilator such as inhaled nitric oxide or epoprostenol with the team
Increase sedation only and accept the current gas values
Reduce FiO2 to 0.30 to avoid oxygen toxicity as the first step

questions.explanation: B is correct: in pulmonary hypertension, hypoxemia, hypercapnia, and acidemia all raise pulmonary vascular resistance and worsen RV failure; correcting the gas abnormalities and adding a selective inhaled pulmonary vasodilator reduces RV afterload without systemic hypotension. A is wrong because permissive hypercapnia is specifically harmful in this physiology. C is wrong because deeper sedation does not fix the gas exchange problem and may drop systemic pressure further. D is wrong because lowering FiO2 in a hypoxemic patient would intensify hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction.

texas-mpje.quiz_title: Texas MPJE Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam

questions.question: A pharmacist is found working while impaired and diverting controlled substances, creating an immediate risk to patients who will be served that same day. What expedited board action is available?

answers.text: Summary suspension of the license where there is imminent danger
No action until the pharmacist is convicted of a felony
A product recall issued by the board for the diverted drugs
Transfer of the pharmacist's license to another state board for review

questions.explanation: A board may summarily suspend a license where imminent danger is present, rather than waiting for the ordinary timeline to run while patients remain at risk. A felony conviction is a separate ground and process and is not a prerequisite for this expedited action, a recall addresses products rather than a dangerous licensee, and transferring the license does not protect the public the board serves.

questions.question: An electronic controlled-substance order passes through a transmission intermediary whose software reformats and changes the directions field before the order reaches pharmacist Rachel Kim's pharmacy system. What integrity rule applies to that handling?

answers.text: The intermediary may edit any field needed to make the order process smoothly
The pharmacy's receiving system may rewrite the directions to match local defaults
The contents of the electronic prescription may not be altered by an intermediary or the receiving system
The patient may authorize the intermediary to correct the order after transmission

questions.explanation: A valid electronic prescription must be transmitted directly from the prescriber's system without an intermediary altering its content, and the receiving system likewise may not rewrite its contents. Editing for processing convenience, applying local defaults that change directions, and patient-authorized corrections after transmission all accept altered content in place of the prescriber's order.

questions.question: A prescriber confirms to pharmacist Robert Hayes by phone that the quantity and directions on a Schedule II prescription should both be revised to match a new dosing plan. What may the pharmacist do?

answers.text: Refuse both changes because no Schedule II element may ever be altered
Change only the directions and leave the quantity permanently unchanged
Change both the quantity and the directions after that prescriber consultation
Change both without documenting any prescriber contact, to save time

questions.explanation: Quantity and directions are elements a pharmacist may change on a Schedule II prescription after consulting the prescriber. Refusing all changes and changing only one of them both understate that permitted authority, while making the changes without prescriber consultation removes the condition that makes them permissible.

questions.question: A pharmacist working under a collaborative practice agreement orders a lab test and changes a therapy in a way the agreement does not authorize, reasoning that the change was clinically appropriate. How is this conduct best characterized?

answers.text: Acceptable, because a good clinical outcome cures any paperwork problem
Practicing outside the delegated authority of the agreement
A minor documentation error with no practice consequences
Permitted whenever the pharmacist documents the clinical reasoning

questions.explanation: Authority under a collaborative practice agreement ends at the agreement's boundaries, so acting beyond them is practicing outside delegated authority regardless of clinical intent. A favorable outcome or thorough documentation does not retroactively authorize functions the agreement never granted.

questions.question: An adult patient in Texas asks to consolidate refills of a dangerous drug into a single larger supply. Which set of conditions must all be met for consolidation?

answers.text: The total may exceed the authorized amount if the patient consents and is over 18
The drug must be a psychotropic, the patient must consent, and the prescriber need not be notified
The quantity may be up to a 90-day supply, the total dispensed must stay within the authorized amount, the patient must consent, the prescriber must be notified, and the patient must be 18 or older
The consolidation is allowed for any age if the prescriber required smaller fills for medical necessity

questions.explanation: Consolidation may reach a 90-day supply only when the total stays within the amount authorized, the adult patient consents, and the prescriber is notified. The total may never exceed the authorized amount. Psychotropic drugs are excluded, and consolidation is not allowed when the prescriber has required periodic smaller fills for medical necessity.

questions.question: A prescriber's written Schedule II prescription lists a drug strength that the pharmacy does not stock, though a different strength of the same drug is available. Pharmacist Emily Ross wants to dispense the available strength. What step is required first?

answers.text: Consult the prescriber, because drug strength may be changed only after prescriber consultation
Dispense the available strength and inform the prescriber next month
Ask the patient to choose the preferred strength
Change the strength only if a technician verifies the stock count

questions.explanation: Drug strength is an element a pharmacist may change on a Schedule II prescription after consulting the prescriber. Dispensing first and informing the prescriber later reverses the required sequence, the patient's preference does not supply the authority, and a technician's stock verification is not a substitute for prescriber consultation.

questions.question: A pharmacist in Longview with a poor disciplinary record applies to renew his Texas license, and the board, citing the established grounds in his file, declines to let the license continue into a new term. Which sanction is the board exercising?

answers.text: Refusal to renew the license
Restriction of the license
Reprimand
Probation

questions.explanation: Refusing to issue or renew a license is a listed sanction, and declining to continue the license into a new term at renewal is exactly how it operates. Restriction would let the pharmacist practice within limits, a reprimand is a formal rebuke that leaves the license in place, and probation allows continued practice under supervision and conditions.

questions.question: Patient Faith Mensah asks pharmacist Rob Ellison for a list showing the disclosures the pharmacy has made of her protected health information to outside parties. What must the pharmacy be able to provide her?

answers.text: An accounting of disclosures of her protected health information
A statement that disclosures are never tracked and cannot be reconstructed for any patient
Only the names of pharmacy employees who have worked during the past week
A copy of every other patient's disclosures for the same period, for comparison

questions.explanation: Patients may obtain an accounting of disclosures of their protected health information, showing disclosures the pharmacy has made. The pharmacy cannot claim disclosures are untracked and unknowable, employee schedules are not an accounting of disclosures, and another patient's disclosure information is that patient's private information, not a comparison document.

questions.question: Patient Rosa Delgado asks pharmacist Ben Carter for a copy of her own prescription records held by the pharmacy. A technician says patients may look at a summary the pharmacy prepares but may never obtain copies of their own records. Who is right?

answers.text: The technician, because pharmacy records are the pharmacy's property and patients have no access right
The technician, because only prescribers and health plans may receive copies of prescription records
Rosa, because patients have the right to access and obtain copies of their own records
Neither, because patient access is allowed only after a court order is obtained

questions.explanation: Patients have a right to access and copy their own health records, so the pharmacy may not limit a patient to a pharmacy-prepared summary or demand a court order. Prescribers and health plans are not the only parties who may receive copies, and the pharmacy's custody of the records does not extinguish the patient's access right.

questions.question: A patient files a detailed complaint alleging that a pharmacist repeatedly dispensed the wrong medication. Before deciding whether any sanction is warranted, what board power is exercised first in the ordinary course?

answers.text: The power to revoke the license summarily without gathering facts
The power to investigate the complaint and gather the relevant facts
The power to award the patient money damages for the alleged errors
The power to prosecute the pharmacist for a felony in criminal court

questions.explanation: Boards hold the power to investigate complaints, which is how the facts are gathered before any determination about sanctions is made. Investigation is distinct from imposing a summary sanction without fact-finding, boards do not award patients civil damages, and criminal prosecution belongs to prosecutors rather than the licensing board.

questions.question: Before dispensing a refill, pharmacist Lena notices the patient is already taking another drug in the same therapeutic class for the same condition, with no explanation in the profile. Which prospective review concern does this present?

answers.text: A storage-temperature excursion
A labeling error by the manufacturer
Therapeutic duplication that must be screened before dispensing
A child-resistant packaging failure

questions.explanation: Prospective drug utilization review before dispensing screens for therapeutic duplication, so two drugs duplicating therapy for the same condition require review before the refill is dispensed. A storage excursion, a manufacturer labeling error, and a packaging failure are not duplication concerns and are not identified by comparing the profile's active therapies.

questions.question: Pharmacist Victor Hale needs the issuance date of an order to judge refill timing, but the order itself, though otherwise complete and signed, bears no date at all. The patient suggests Victor simply use the pickup date. What is the correct treatment of the missing date?

answers.text: The pickup date automatically satisfies the requirement, so no action is needed
The date of issuance is a required element of a valid prescription and must be obtained rather than assumed
A signed order needs no date because the signature supplies the timing
The pharmacist may omit the date if the prescriber's address is present

questions.explanation: The date is a required element of a valid prescription, together with patient identification, drug name and strength, dosage form, quantity, directions, and prescriber identification and signature. A pickup date is not the issuance date, a signature does not supply the missing timing element, and a prescriber's address does not substitute for the date.

questions.question: To save counter time, a pharmacy posts a notice telling patients they can read the Medication Guide for their drug on the manufacturer's website or ask a kiosk to print one if they want it. Pharmacist Lydia Grant reviews the practice for a drug whose guide is required. Is the practice sufficient?

answers.text: No, the guide must be handed over with the drug itself rather than merely made available on request or online
Yes, because posting the notice shows the pharmacy offered the information
Yes, because a website version is identical in content to a printed guide
Yes, for refills, as long as the notice was posted when the drug was first dispensed

questions.explanation: A required Medication Guide must be dispensed with the drug itself, so passive availability through a website link or an on-request kiosk printout does not satisfy the requirement. Identical content and a posted notice do not change the delivery obligation, which applies at dispensing including refills.

questions.question: In Weslaco, a pharmacist first confirms a generic would cost the patient less and asks the patient, who chooses the generic. While preparing the fill, the pharmacist then notices the prescriber's handwritten brand-medically-necessary certification on the face of the prescription, which had been overlooked. What must happen next?

answers.text: The generic fill proceeds, because the patient already chose it
The generic fill proceeds, if the pharmacist notes the oversight in the record
The pharmacist must stop and dispense the certified brand instead
The prescription must be returned to the patient as unfillable

questions.explanation: A brand certification discovered late still controls: when the practitioner certifies a specific brand is medically necessary, that brand must be dispensed. A patient choice made before the certification was noticed cannot override it, noting the oversight does not cure it, and the order remains fillable with the certified brand.

questions.question: While filling an oral prescription, a technician notices the patient's intake form says no children live in the home and suggests switching to a plain snap cap for convenience. Neither the patient nor the prescriber has asked for non-child-resistant packaging. What should pharmacist Tom Becker do?

answers.text: Keep the child-resistant container, because that packaging remains the default unless the patient or the prescriber requests otherwise
Use the snap cap, because a household with no children is automatically exempt from child-resistant packaging
Use the snap cap whenever the intake form lists only adult residents, without asking anyone
Let the technician decide based on how crowded the packaging shelf is that day

questions.explanation: Child-resistant packaging is the default for most oral prescriptions, and the absence of children in the household does not by itself remove that default. The packaging changes when the patient or the prescriber requests otherwise, not when staff infer an exemption from an intake form or choose based on convenience or shelf space.

questions.question: Established patient Tom Becker tells pharmacist Ingrid Larsen that he was recently diagnosed with significant kidney disease. His profile's conditions section still lists only hypertension, and several of his long-term medications are affected by kidney function. What must Ingrid do with this information?

answers.text: Record the newly reported kidney disease in the relevant-conditions portion of Tom's profile so it informs future review and counseling
Leave the profile unchanged, because conditions may be entered only when a prescriber sends a new prescription stating them
Write the diagnosis on a sticky note kept at the dispensing counter until the profile is next printed
Remove all of Tom's kidney-affected medications from his profile so the condition no longer matters

questions.explanation: Relevant conditions are one of the profile elements maintained to support drug utilization review and counseling, and a newly reported condition that affects the patient's medications must be recorded in the profile itself. Entering it only when a prescriber happens to restate it, or keeping it on a counter note outside the record, leaves the screening tool incomplete, and deleting medication entries destroys the history review depends on rather than documenting the condition.

questions.question: In Plano, an adult patient consents to consolidating refills of a non-psychotropic dangerous drug. The prescriber will be notified and has not required smaller periodic fills. The refills that remain authorize a combined total equal to a 75-day supply, but the patient asks for a single 90-day bottle. What may pharmacist Victor dispense?

answers.text: A 90-day supply, because 90 days is always the consolidated amount
A 90-day supply, if the patient promises to obtain a new prescription before the extra days are used
A 120-day supply, because consolidation adds a bonus month to the authorized total
No more than a 75-day supply, because the consolidated total must stay within the amount already authorized

questions.explanation: Consolidation allows up to a 90-day supply only if the total dispensed stays within the authorized amount; here the remaining refills authorize only a 75-day total, so 75 days is the ceiling. Consent and prescriber notification do not create additional authorized quantity. A promise to obtain a new prescription later does not authorize dispensing the extra amount now, and consolidation adds no bonus quantity.

questions.question: Pharmacist Kenji Sato's pharmacy receives a shipment of a Schedule IV medication ordered from its wholesaler. The receiving technician checks the bottles against the supplier's invoice, marks it received, and proposes shredding the invoice at the end of the week now that the stock is on the shelf. What is correct?

answers.text: The invoice may be shredded once the stock is shelved, because invoices are shipping documents only
The invoice must be sent to the DEA with the pharmacy's next inventory
The invoice is a controlled-substance record for the Schedule III through V order and must be retained, for at least the federal two-year minimum, in the pharmacy's retrievable records
Invoices need retention only when they list Schedule II drugs

questions.explanation: Schedule III through V drugs are ordered on invoices, and those invoices form part of the pharmacy's controlled-substance records, which must be kept for at least two years under the federal floor and remain retrievable. Checking the shipment completes receiving, not the record's life, invoices are retained by the pharmacy rather than forwarded with an inventory, and the retention duty is not limited to Schedule II paperwork.

questions.question: A single review in Corpus Christi sustains three findings against one pharmacist: she failed to provide patient counseling on one fill, skipped a drug regimen review on another, and disclosed prescription-record contents without authority on a third. Using the board's penalty schedule, what is the combined scheduled amount, and what else may the board add?

answers.text: $15,000 on the schedule, because every sustained finding is scheduled at the $5,000 maximum
$3,000 on the schedule ($1,000 for each of the three findings), and the board may still combine another sanction such as probation or reprimand with the penalty
$1,000 total, because the schedule allows only the single highest finding per review
$500 total, because counseling and review failures are grouped with order violations at the lowest tier

questions.explanation: The schedule sets $1,000 each for failing to provide patient counseling, failing to conduct a drug regimen review, and failing to maintain the confidentiality of prescription records, totaling $3,000 for the three distinct findings. The $5,000 figures attach to matters such as forged prescriptions and audit shortages, the $500 figure to order or program-contract violations, and penalties may be assessed in addition to other sanctions rather than displacing them.

questions.question: An accountability audit at a Class A pharmacy in Conroe uncovers a shortage of prescription drugs, and the pharmacy's inventory records turn out to be incomplete, with purchases and disposals of regulated drugs not fully or accurately documented. The owner argues the incomplete paperwork is a side issue once the shortage itself is addressed. How should the pharmacist-in-charge view the records failure?

answers.text: As a side issue with no independent significance, since only the missing drugs matter
As excused, because a shortage automatically explains any gaps in the records
As significant only if the board first proves who took the missing drugs

As an independent problem, because failing to maintain required records, including complete and accurate records of purchases and disposals of regulated drugs, is itself a ground for discipline, separate from the shortage

questions.explanation: Texas law treats the records failure as its own violation: failing to maintain required records, or complete and accurate records of purchases or disposals of drugs regulated under the controlled-substance and dangerous-drug chapters, is itself a ground for discipline. A shortage does not excuse the gaps; it is compounded by them, because the pharmacy cannot account for its stock. The records ground does not depend on first proving who took the missing drugs.

water-treatment-class-1.quiz_title: Water Treatment Class I Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam

questions.question: How is chlorine demand defined for a treated water?

answers.text: The contact time multiplied by the chlorine residual
The chlorine dose divided by the plant flow in MGD
The chlorine dosage minus the chlorine residual that remains
The total chlorine residual minus the free chlorine residual only

questions.explanation: Chlorine demand is the portion of the dose used up reacting with substances in the water. It equals dosage minus residual, and conversely the dose needed equals demand plus the desired residual.

questions.question: What is the main effect of short-circuiting in a sedimentation basin?

answers.text: It increases the effective settling area without adding equipment
It raises the alkalinity of the water by concentrating dissolved minerals along the direct flow path to the outlet
It makes the sludge blanket easier to measure with a core sampler
It lets part of the flow reach the outlet quickly, reducing the effective detention time for that water

questions.explanation: Short-circuiting means some flow takes a direct path through a basin instead of using its full volume. That portion gets less detention and less settling, lowering overall basin performance.

questions.question: How should the SCADA network be arranged to reduce cybersecurity risk?

answers.text: Connect it directly to the public internet for convenience
Put SCADA and customer billing on one open network
Keep it separated from general office and public networks
Allow any personal device to join the control network

questions.explanation: Network separation is a basic SCADA cybersecurity measure, limiting who and what can reach the control system.

questions.question: What is the static water level in a well?

answers.text: The water level in the well when it is not being pumped
The water level measured only while the pump is running at full capacity
The depth from the pump intake to the bottom of the well
