questions.explanation: Punishment arrangements can generate escape and avoidance of the people, places, or activities linked with them, even before the target behavior occurs. This pattern is important data for the supervisor reviewing the plan.

questions.question: Since a time-out component began, a clients data show the target behavior dropping, but the client now cries when the RBT arrives and avoids session activities. The RBT should:

answers.text: Hide the avoidance so the plan is not changed
Attribute the crying to manipulation in the notes
Report the emotional and avoidance changes to the supervisor promptly along with the behavior data
End the time-out component on their own judgment

questions.explanation: Punishment can produce emotional responding and escape or avoidance, and those changes are clinical information the supervisor needs right away. The RBT reports both the gains and the side effects and leaves plan changes to the supervisor.

questions.question: At an after-school program, Omar, age 11, shouts a staff member's name repeatedly while that staff member is helping other students sign in. When the staff member walks over and talks with him, he stops shouting. Which function does this pattern most plausibly serve?

answers.text: Escape from a demand or activity
Social attention from others
Access to a tangible item or preferred activity
Automatic (sensory) reinforcement

questions.explanation: This pattern most plausibly serves social attention: shouting the staff member's name continues until the busy staff member comes over and interacts with him. The behavior changes when attention is delivered, and it is not followed by a task being removed or a withheld item being handed over.

questions.question: The plan for Iona, age 7, begins each trial only after the RBT says her name and she orients to the table. If trials started while she faced away, the most likely measurement problem would be what?

answers.text: Trials would be scored as naturalistic opportunities
Nonresponses caused by not contacting the instruction would be mistaken for lack of skill
Prompted responses would be counted as independent
Reinforcement would be delivered on an interval schedule

questions.explanation: A trial only measures the target skill if the learner actually contacts the instruction, so starting while the learner faces away confounds inattention with inability. The orienting step keeps the resulting data interpretable for the supervisor.

questions.question: One parent reports that 9-year-old Vince now ties his shoes at home, while the other says he cannot, and session data show he still needs prompts. The RBT is unsure how to record mastery. What is the best step?

answers.text: Share the conflicting reports and the session data with the supervisor for direction
Record mastery because one parent said so
Accuse one parent of lying in the session note
Average the reports and mark the goal half-mastered

questions.explanation: Conflicting information about a mastery decision goes to the supervisor along with the objective session data; mastery calls rest on defined criteria, not on picking which report to believe. The RBT contributes observations, not the final clinical judgment.

cpt.quiz_title: CPT Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam

questions.question: Regarding preanalytical quality indicators for phlebotomy, which set belongs to the collection phase that a quality program monitors?

answers.text: Analyzer calibration curves, reagent manufacturing lots, and reference laboratory staffing
Patient misidentification, hemolyzed specimens, and quantity-not-sufficient collections
Billing denial rates, appointment wait times, and parking availability
Result-report wording, provider interpretation, and treatment decisions

questions.explanation: B is correct because misidentification, hemolysis, and insufficient quantity are errors introduced during collection — the preanalytical phase the phlebotomist controls and the quality program trends. A is wrong because those are analytical-phase and manufacturing concerns outside the collection process. C is wrong because those are administrative measures, not specimen-quality indicators. D is wrong because interpretation and treatment occur after results are reported and are outside the phlebotomist's collection role.

questions.question: Regarding technique for an alcohol-based hand rub when hands are not visibly soiled, which description is correct?

answers.text: Apply a small drop, wipe it off immediately on a towel, and glove at once.
Apply rub only to the palms, because the backs of the hands do not carry organisms.
Use rub only after the draw, never before patient contact.
Apply enough product to cover all hand surfaces and rub until the hands are dry.

questions.explanation: D is correct because an alcohol-based rub must cover all hand surfaces and be rubbed in until dry to achieve its disinfecting effect. A is wrong because wiping the product off immediately ends contact before it can work. B is wrong because the backs of the hands, fingers, and thumbs also carry organisms and must be covered. C is wrong because hand hygiene is required before patient contact as well as after care.

questions.question: Regarding documentation after reporting a critical POC value, the phlebotomist has notified the ordering provider by phone. What documentation completes the process?

answers.text: No documentation is needed once the call has been made
A note in a personal notebook kept outside the patient record
Documentation only if the provider later questions the result
The value, the time of the report, and the name of the provider notified, recorded in the patient record per policy

questions.explanation: D is correct because critical-value communication is complete only when the value, time of report, and provider notified are documented in the patient record per policy. A is wrong because an undocumented report cannot be verified. B is wrong because a personal notebook is not part of the official record. C is wrong because documentation is required at the time of the report, not only if questioned later.

questions.question: Regarding chain of custody as a specimen moves through processing, which practice maintains an unbroken custody record?

answers.text: Each person who handles or transfers the specimen documents the transfer with identification, date, and time, and the specimen stays sealed and secured between transfers
Only the original collector signs the form, since later handling is routine
The specimen may be left unsecured in a shared refrigerator as long as it is labeled
Custody documentation is completed at the end of the week from memory

questions.explanation: A is correct because chain of custody requires every handler to document each transfer with who, date, and time, with the specimen kept sealed and secured throughout, creating an unbroken record. B is wrong because custody must account for every transfer, not only collection. C is wrong because an unsecured shared location breaks controlled access. D is wrong because reconstructing transfers from memory days later is unreliable and not contemporaneous documentation.

questions.question: Regarding opened control material for a waived point-of-care test, what must the phlebotomist do when a new vial of control solution is opened at a clinic station?

answers.text: Rely on the printed expiration date alone, since opening the vial does not change how long it may be used
Mark the vial with the opened date and the discard date from the manufacturer's instructions, and stop using it once either date has passed
Leave the vial unmarked and let the next operator judge by appearance whether it is still usable
Freeze the opened vial between uses to extend its usable life beyond the manufacturer's stated period

questions.explanation: B is correct because opened control material is used only within the manufacturer's stated in-use period, and marking the opened and discard dates is how the station proves that limit is honored. A is wrong because the printed expiration applies to an unopened vial and does not replace the opened-vial limit. C is wrong because appearance cannot show whether control material is still valid, and unmarked vials defeat traceability. D is wrong because storage must follow the manufacturer's instructions, and freezing is not a substitute for the stated discard date.

questions.question: In a busy waiting area, a patient says they do not want to state their full date of birth aloud where others can hear it. Regarding two-identifier verification that also protects privacy, what should the phlebotomist do?

answers.text: Skip the second identifier because the patient is uncomfortable
Ask the patient to say the date of birth louder so it can be heard clearly over the noise
Offer a private way to verify, such as showing identification or writing the date of birth, and compare it with the requisition away from the crowd
Verify the patient using their seat location and appointment time instead

questions.explanation: C is correct: identifiers can be verified through identification documents or a written response in a more private setting, completing two-identifier verification without forcing the patient to announce personal information publicly. A is wrong because discomfort does not waive the identification requirement before a collection. B is wrong because it increases the privacy exposure the patient is trying to avoid. D is wrong because seat location and appointment time are not patient identifiers.

questions.question: During a waived glucose test, the meter flags that the strip received an insufficient amount of blood after application has already begun. Regarding completing this test correctly, what should the phlebotomist do?

answers.text: Add a second drop of blood on top of the first application on the same strip
Estimate the result from the partial reading and record it with a note
Discard that strip, obtain a fresh free-flowing drop, and apply it to a new strip following the manufacturer's instructions
Shake the meter gently so the blood already on the strip spreads across the test area

questions.explanation: C is correct: a strip flagged for insufficient sample cannot produce a valid result, so the test is repeated with a new strip and an adequate, free-flowing drop as the instructions direct. A is wrong because topping up a strip after application has begun is not a validated technique and distorts the reaction. B is wrong because an estimated value is not a test result and must never be recorded as one. D is wrong because shaking the device does not correct an inadequate sample volume.

questions.question: Regarding mixing requirements by tube type, a plain red-top tube with no additive, no gel, and no clot activator has just filled completely. How should this tube be handled immediately after collection?

answers.text: Invert it 8 to 10 times, the same as an EDTA tube
Set it upright without inversions, because there is no additive in the tube to mix with the blood
Invert it 3 to 4 times, the same as a citrate tube
Shake it once vigorously to start clotting faster

questions.explanation: B is correct because inversion exists to mix an additive with blood; a plain red-top tube contains no additive, gel, or clot activator, so no inversions are required and it is simply set upright to clot. A is wrong because 8 to 10 inversions is the count for anticoagulant tubes such as EDTA and heparin, whose additives this tube does not contain. C is wrong because 3 to 4 inversions is the count for the sodium citrate tube, not for a tube with nothing to mix. D is wrong because tubes are never shaken; shaking causes hemolysis, and clotting does not need mechanical acceleration.

questions.question: In an outpatient clinic, a visibly anxious adult patient says needles make them panic and asks to lie down and take a moment before the draw. Regarding care for an anxious patient, what should the phlebotomist do?

answers.text: Tell the patient anxiety is not a medical concern and start immediately
Leave the patient alone reclined with the needle already uncapped on the tray beside them
Rush through the explanation so there is less time to worry
Honor the request to recline, explain calmly, allow a brief pause and slow breathing, and proceed only when the patient is ready within the visit

questions.explanation: D is correct: reclining, calm explanation, and a brief pause with slow breathing address anxiety and reduce syncope risk before proceeding. A is wrong because dismissing anxiety ignores a factor that affects safety and cooperation. B is wrong because leaving an uncapped needle beside a reclined patient is a sharps hazard. C is wrong because rushing the explanation usually heightens anxiety rather than reducing it.

questions.question: An ammonia specimen has been collected correctly on an inpatient unit and must be kept chilled until testing. Regarding transport handling that prevents a preanalytical error for this chilled specimen, how should it be transported?

answers.text: At room temperature in a sealed bag if it will arrive within the hour
On an ice slurry so it stays chilled without the tube freezing against a solid frozen surface
Taped directly against a dry-ice block so it becomes as cold as possible
In a warmed carrier so the plasma does not separate during transport

questions.explanation: B is correct: chilled specimens such as ammonia are transported on ice slurry, which keeps them cold while avoiding direct freezing contact that can damage the specimen. A is wrong because a specimen ordered to be kept chilled loses integrity at room temperature. C is wrong because dry-ice contact can freeze the specimen, which is not the same as chilling it. D is wrong because warming a chilled specimen defeats its special handling requirement.

questions.question: At an inpatient bedside, the vein chosen for an evacuated tube system draw lies noticeably deeper than a typical antecubital vein, though it palpates well. Regarding insertion angle for this deeper vein, which approach stays within the correct technique?

answers.text: Insert at about 45 degrees, because a deeper vein needs a steeper angle than the standard range
Insert toward the upper end of the 15- to 30-degree range, bevel up, rather than exceeding that range
Insert at less than 15 degrees, skimming just under the skin toward the vein
Insert bevel down at 30 degrees so the needle tip reaches depth faster

questions.explanation: Venipuncture insertion stays within 15 to 30 degrees with the bevel up; a deeper vein is approached at the upper end of that range, not beyond it. A 45-degree insertion exceeds the standard range and risks passing through the vein. An angle under 15 degrees suits a very shallow approach and may never reach a deeper vein. Bevel-down insertion is incorrect at any angle in this range, because the bevel is always positioned up.

questions.question: At an outpatient station the vein rolls away each time the needle approaches, and two gentle attempts produce no flow because the vein keeps shifting under the skin. Regarding this rolling vein, which adjustment gives the next attempt the best chance?

answers.text: Insert the needle more quickly with a jabbing motion to catch the vein before it moves
Remove the tourniquet so the vein lies flatter and moves less
Re-anchor firmly by pulling the skin taut below the site to hold the vein still during insertion
Press the needle hub down harder once the skin is punctured to pin the vein in place

questions.explanation: C is correct: a rolling vein is steadied by firm anchoring, pulling the skin taut below the site so the vein cannot shift during insertion. A is wrong because a jabbing motion increases tissue trauma and does not stabilize the vein. B is wrong because removing the tourniquet makes the vein less full and harder to enter. D is wrong because pressing the hub down after puncture changes the needle angle rather than anchoring the vein.

questions.question: During an infant heel collection, a trainee positions the lancet toward the middle of the back of the heel, reasoning that the spot is easy to reach. Regarding heel puncture placement, why must the phlebotomist redirect the trainee?

answers.text: The posterior curve of the heel is too close to the heel bone, so the puncture belongs on the medial or lateral plantar surface
The back of the heel has no capillaries, so no blood could be collected there
The posterior curve is acceptable as long as a shallow device is used
The trainee should move to the arch of the foot, which is the preferred infant site

questions.explanation: Redirecting to the medial or lateral plantar surface is correct because the posterior curve of the heel lies close to the calcaneus, and puncturing there risks bone injury and infection. B is wrong because the area does have blood flow; the objection is safety, not absence of capillaries. C is wrong because no device depth makes a prohibited site acceptable. D is wrong because the arch is not the approved infant site; the plantar medial and lateral surfaces are.

questions.question: Before a fasting lipid panel, a patient reports taking their usual prescribed morning medication with a small sip of water, exactly as the ordering instructions directed. Regarding testing-requirement compliance, what should the phlebotomist do?

answers.text: Proceed with the collection and document the medication taken as instructed
Cancel the draw, since any medication taken that morning voids a fasting test
Ask the patient to skip the next scheduled dose to compensate for taking this one
Draw the specimen but record the patient as non-fasting without noting the circumstances

questions.explanation: A is correct: medication taken as directed, with a small sip of water, follows the preparation instructions, so the draw proceeds with that fact documented. B is wrong because instructed medication with water does not void the fast. C is wrong because advising a patient to skip a prescribed dose is outside the phlebotomist's scope and unsafe. D is wrong because recording the patient as non-fasting misrepresents a compliant preparation.

questions.question: At an outpatient site, two levels of control are run on a waived testing device. One level falls within its acceptable range and the other falls outside it. Regarding control results, what should the phlebotomist do before reporting patient results from that device?

answers.text: Report patient results because at least one control level passed
Average the two control results and proceed if the average is in range
Withhold patient results, follow the troubleshooting steps in the procedure, repeat the failed control as directed, and escalate if it still fails
Record the passing level in the log and omit the failed level so the record looks complete

questions.explanation: C is correct: all required control levels must be acceptable before patient results are reported; a failed level triggers troubleshooting, repeat testing as directed, and escalation if unresolved. A is wrong because one passing level does not validate the device. B is wrong because control levels are judged individually against their own ranges, never averaged. D is wrong because omitting a failed control falsifies the quality record and hides a problem.

questions.question: Before a routine draw begins, a student observer is brought into the room to watch the collection for training. The patient says they are not comfortable being observed. Regarding patient rights, what should the phlebotomist do?

answers.text: Proceed with the observer present because training is part of care in a teaching setting
Tell the patient the observer will leave only if the draw becomes difficult
Honor the patient's preference and have the observer step out before proceeding
Have the observer stand behind a curtain so the patient cannot see them, and proceed

questions.explanation: C is correct: the Patient Bill of Rights supports privacy and the patient's preference about who is present during their care, so the observer should step out. A is wrong because a training benefit does not override the patient's stated preference about observation. B is wrong because it conditions a privacy right on how the draw goes rather than honoring it at the start. D is wrong because being hidden behind a curtain still means the patient is being observed against their stated wishes.

questions.question: At a rehabilitation clinic, a patient with a delicate vein needs several tubes totaling a modest volume, and the phlebotomist chooses a syringe draw. Regarding syringe selection for this collection, which choice best fits the method?

answers.text: The largest syringe on the cart, so there is spare capacity for any add-on tubes
A syringe sized close to the total volume needed, so gentle plunger control can be maintained for the whole draw
The smallest syringe available, refilled through repeat punctures if more blood is needed
A syringe chosen by its needle length alone, since barrel size does not affect the draw

questions.explanation: B is correct because matching the syringe barrel to the volume needed keeps plunger movement small and controllable, which is the whole advantage of the syringe method on a delicate vein: the phlebotomist meters the vacuum by hand instead of exposing the vein to full tube vacuum. A is wrong because an oversized barrel invites stronger, harder-to-meter pull than the fragile vein tolerates. C is wrong because planning repeat punctures for more blood adds needless sticks when one correctly sized syringe suffices. D is wrong because barrel size directly governs how the vacuum is applied, so it is central to the selection.

questions.question: One phlebotomist is responsible for two timed collections that fall due at the same moment in different areas of a facility: a 1-hour glucose tolerance draw for one patient and a peak drug level for another. Analyzing how to protect both results, what is the correct approach?

answers.text: Collect the peak level about 20 minutes early, then collect the tolerance draw on time
Collect the tolerance draw on time and collect the peak level about 20 minutes late without documenting the difference
Arrange coverage in advance, such as a second qualified collector or supervisor help, so each specimen is collected at its ordered time
Decide that one of the two timed orders can simply be treated as a routine draw and collected on the next round

questions.explanation: The key is correct because both collections are only valid at their ordered times, so arranging coverage in advance is the only approach that keeps both specimens on schedule. Collecting the peak early is wrong because a peak drawn before its protocol time does not measure the peak. Collecting the peak late without documentation is wrong because the result would be misread as a true peak and the record would be inaccurate. Treating a timed order as routine is wrong because a timed level drawn at the wrong time is a wrong result even if the draw itself is technically perfect.

questions.question: The phlebotomist arrives to collect a trough drug level and the patient reports that they did not take the medication dose the level was meant to follow, because they felt unwell. Analyzing what this means for the timed collection, what should the phlebotomist do?

answers.text: Collect the specimen anyway and label it as a trough, since the appointment time was met
Ask the patient to take the dose now and collect the trough immediately afterward
Give the patient a new trough time later that day without informing anyone
Withhold the draw as a trough, document that the dose was not taken, and notify the ordering provider or care team so the timed collection can be directed correctly

questions.explanation: D is correct: a trough level is defined by its relationship to a dosing schedule — immediately before the next dose, after prior doses — so a level drawn when the dose history has changed cannot be reported as a valid trough, and the care team must direct the next step. A is wrong because meeting the clock time does not make a specimen a trough when the dosing premise has failed. B is wrong because administering medication is outside the phlebotomist's scope, and a trough is never drawn immediately after a dose. C is wrong because rescheduling a timed therapeutic level on their own authority, without the care team knowing the dose was missed, hides information the interpretation depends on.

questions.question: The phlebotomist has just prepped a site with an alcohol-based antiseptic, and before any needle insertion the patient says that this type of prep caused blistering the last time it was used on them. Analyzing the safest next step, what should the phlebotomist do?

answers.text: Insert the needle quickly and finish the draw before any skin reaction has time to start
Wipe the antiseptic off with gauze and puncture that same site immediately, since the agent is now removed
Stop before puncture, do not use that prepped site, assess the patient, report and document the disclosure, and prepare a different site with an approved alternative antiseptic
Proceed with the draw because the chart lists no antiseptic allergy, so the patient's report can be set aside

questions.explanation: C is correct: a reported reaction to the agent already on the skin is a stop point before puncture; the phlebotomist protects the patient, escalates and documents the new information, and re-preps a different site with an alternative approved antiseptic. A is wrong because racing the reaction still exposes the patient to an agent they reported harm from. B is wrong because wiping does not undo the exposure or make that site an appropriate choice. D is wrong because a missing chart entry does not override a direct patient report of a prior reaction.

cpcta.quiz_title: CPCT/A Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam

questions.question: Regarding postoperative respiratory exercises, what does the TCDB routine include when the technician assists a patient through it?

answers.text: Turning the patient once per shift, with coughing and deep breathing only if they request it
Having the patient blow into a spirometer as fast as possible every few hours
Turning, coughing, and deep breathing performed regularly as ordered to help keep the lungs expanded and clear
Keeping the patient flat and still so the incision is never stressed by breathing exercises

questions.explanation: C is correct because TCDB stands for turn, cough, and deep breathe, done regularly as ordered after surgery to expand the lungs and help clear secretions. A is wrong because the routine is performed on the ordered schedule, not once a shift or only on request. B is wrong because fast blowing into a spirometer describes neither TCDB nor correct incentive spirometry, which uses a slow deep inhale. D is wrong because avoiding breathing exercises to protect an incision works against lung expansion; the incision can be supported during coughing instead.

questions.question: Regarding normal adult respiratory rate at rest, which range is the reference standard for the patient care technician?

answers.text: 8-12 breaths per minute
20-28 breaths per minute
12-20 breaths per minute
30-40 breaths per minute

questions.explanation: C is correct because the normal adult respiratory rate at rest is 12-20 breaths per minute. A is wrong because 8-12 is below the normal adult range. B is wrong because 20-28 is above the normal adult range. D is wrong because 30-40 is well above the normal adult range and would signal a value needing prompt reporting.

questions.question: Regarding limb electrode placement for a standard resting 12-lead, which statement is correct?

answers.text: All four limb electrodes are placed on the torso to keep them from moving
The limb electrodes are placed on the limbs, and the right leg electrode serves as the ground
The right leg electrode records the rhythm and may be placed anywhere on the torso
Only three limb electrodes are needed because the chest electrodes supply the rest

questions.explanation: Key B is correct: for a standard resting recording the limb electrodes go on the limbs, and the right leg electrode is the ground. A is wrong because torso placement is not the standard resting position and changes the recording. C is wrong because the right leg electrode is the ground, not a rhythm-recording electrode placed at convenience. D is wrong because the standard set uses all four limb electrodes plus the six precordial electrodes.

questions.question: Regarding a patient's refusal of an ordered cleansing enema, which statement describes the patient care technician's correct response?

answers.text: The technician should proceed once the patient is positioned, because a provider's order overrides a refusal at the bedside
The technician should ask a family member to persuade the patient, and proceed if the family agrees to the enema
The technician respects the refusal, does not force the procedure, notifies the nurse, and documents the refusal per policy
The technician should chart the enema as given so the ordered care appears complete for the shift

questions.explanation: C is correct: a patient may refuse a procedure, and the technician's role is to respect the refusal, avoid forcing care, notify the nurse so the care team can follow up, and document per policy. A is wrong because an order does not cancel a competent patient's right to refuse a bedside procedure. B is wrong because consent belongs to the patient, not the family, and recruiting relatives to override a refusal is coercion. D is wrong because charting care that was not given falsifies the record and hides the refusal the care team needs to address.

questions.question: Regarding a personal or religious item a patient wears, such as a bracelet they do not remove, which standard guides the technician during bathing and care?

answers.text: Keep the item in place whenever it does not interfere with care or safety, handle it respectfully if it must be moved, and involve the nurse if removal is ever required
Remove all such items at admission so they cannot be lost or damaged during care
Ask the patient to explain the item's meaning in detail before agreeing to leave it on
Cover the item with a dressing during every bath so it never gets wet, even if the patient objects

questions.explanation: A is correct because personal and religious items carry meaning for the patient, so they stay in place when care and safety allow, are handled respectfully, and any required removal goes through the nurse rather than the technician's unilateral decision. B is wrong because routine removal at admission disregards the item's significance and the patient's wishes. C is wrong because the patient does not owe an explanation of their beliefs as a condition of respectful care. D is wrong because covering the item against the patient's wishes overrides the patient for a minor concern that can usually be managed by working around it.

questions.question: A patient who requires a mechanical lift for transfers needs to get up, the unit is busy, and no second trained staff member is immediately free. Which decision best applies workplace-injury prevention?

answers.text: Move the patient alone with a gait belt to save time, since the patient is partially cooperative
Drag the patient up by the arms, which avoids lifting the full body weight
Ask the patient's family visitor to operate one side of the lift
Wait for or obtain the trained help the lift requires, use the lift as trained, and alert the nurse if the delay affects the patient's care needs

questions.explanation: D is correct because safe patient handling requires using mechanical lift equipment as trained with the required number of trained staff; escalating a delay to the nurse protects both the patient and the plan of care. A is wrong because substituting a gait belt for a required lift risks a fall and a lifting injury. B is wrong because pulling a patient up by the arms can injure the patient's shoulders and the technician. C is wrong because untrained visitors must never operate patient-handling equipment.

questions.question: At the end of a clinic session, a portable EKG machine's battery indicator shows a low charge as the patient care technician is putting it away after its last recording. Regarding putting this machine away, what should the technician do?

answers.text: Store the machine uncharged, because charging is the responsibility of whoever uses it next
Run the machine until the battery is completely empty, because a full discharge must come before any recharge
Remove the battery and store it loose in a supply drawer until the next clinic session
Connect the machine to its charger as facility policy directs and report it if it will not charge, so the machine is ready for its next use

questions.explanation: Key D is correct: routine equipment care includes leaving a portable machine charging, or reporting a charging fault, so its battery is ready when the next recording is needed. A is wrong because storing a low machine uncharged passes a foreseeable failure to the next user and patient. B is wrong because deliberately draining the battery adds no benefit and leaves the machine unusable in the meantime. C is wrong because removing and loosely storing the battery separates the machine from its power source and risks loss or damage.

questions.question: During cleanup after care, the technician removes their gloves and finds blood on an area of cracked, broken skin on one hand where a glove had torn. Regarding the exposure control plan, what should the technician do?

answers.text: Wait until the end of the shift to mention it, since the amount of blood was small
Wash the area promptly, report the exposure to the supervisor, and follow the exposure control plan for evaluation
Apply hand sanitizer, cover the area with a bandage, and continue working without reporting
Rinse the hand only if symptoms such as redness or pain develop later

questions.explanation: B is correct because blood contact with non-intact skin is an exposure: the area is washed promptly, the exposure is reported, and evaluation follows the exposure control plan without delay. A is wrong because waiting until the end of the shift delays time-sensitive evaluation and follow-up. C is wrong because sanitizer and a bandage do not replace washing, reporting, and the plan's evaluation process. D is wrong because the need to wash and report does not depend on symptoms appearing later.

questions.question: A restless patient at high fall risk keeps attempting to climb out of bed, and a coworker suggests applying restraints right away to settle the situation. Analyzing restraint use in fall prevention, which response is correct?

answers.text: Try alternatives first, such as meeting toileting and comfort needs and increasing observation, and use restraints only on a provider order with monitoring per policy
Apply the restraints because a coworker's suggestion counts as authorization
Apply restraints loosely so the patient can still move a little
Raise all four side rails fully instead, which requires no further steps

questions.explanation: A is correct: restraints are a last resort used only on a provider order with monitoring and documentation per policy, after alternatives such as toileting, comfort measures, and closer observation are tried. B is wrong because a coworker's suggestion is not an order. C is wrong because loose application does not make unauthorized restraint use acceptable and can still injure the patient. D is wrong because fully raised rails are not a risk-free substitute and do not replace assessment, alternatives, and policy steps.

questions.question: A patient requires both contact and droplet precautions, and the technician will wear a gown, a surgical mask, goggles, and gloves to provide care. Regarding the donning sequence for this set, which order is correct?

answers.text: Perform hand hygiene, then gown, mask, goggles, and finally gloves pulled over the gown cuffs
Put gloves on first, then pull the gown on over the gloved hands
Put the mask on last, adjusting it with gloved hands after touching the gown front
Put goggles on after beginning care, once splashing actually starts

questions.explanation: A is correct because donning starts with hand hygiene, proceeds from gown to mask to eye protection, and ends with gloves over the gown cuffs to seal the wrist. B is wrong because gloves donned first are contaminated by handling the gown and leave the cuff unsealed. C is wrong because the mask must be fitted with clean hands before gloves go on. D is wrong because eye protection must be in place before the splash risk begins.

questions.question: A newly admitted patient appears tense before personal care and says they are nervous because they do not know the technician who will be helping them. Which approach best supports this patient?

answers.text: Introduce themself and their role, explain each step before doing it, ask about the patient's preferences, and proceed at a pace the patient can manage
Begin the care quickly without explanation so the unfamiliar part is over sooner
Tell the patient that all technicians provide care the same way, so introductions are unnecessary
Leave the care undone and avoid mentioning the patient's nervousness to the nurse

questions.explanation: A is correct because introducing themself, explaining care in advance, and asking about preferences reduces anxiety and gives the patient a sense of control during personal care. B is wrong because unexplained care from an unfamiliar person tends to increase, not reduce, nervousness. C is wrong because it dismisses the patient's feelings instead of addressing them. D is wrong because it omits needed care and keeps the nurse unaware of the patient's anxiety.

questions.question: After breakfast, a patient vomits into an emesis basin, and the material looks dark and grainy, resembling coffee grounds, which is new for this patient. Regarding this output finding, what should the technician do?

answers.text: Discard the basin's contents and reassure the patient that vomit appearance is never significant
Measure the output, report the appearance promptly to the nurse, and document the amount and description without diagnosing a cause
Offer the patient a full meal right away to settle their stomach before reporting anything
Chart the episode as food poisoning so the nurse knows what happened

questions.explanation: B is correct because new coffee-ground-appearing emesis is an output change to measure, document by amount and description, and report promptly, while determining its cause belongs to the nurse. A is wrong because discarding the material and dismissing its appearance removes a finding that should be reported. C is wrong because feeding the patient before reporting delays communication and ignores that the patient has just vomited. D is wrong because naming food poisoning states a diagnosis, which is outside the technician's scope.

questions.question: After helping reposition a patient with MRSA, a technician keeps the same gloves on while pressing the elevator button and opening a supply-room door on the way to another task. Analyzing this against MRSA transmission and the chain of infection, what is the problem?

answers.text: There is no problem, because MRSA spreads only through direct skin contact with the patient
The only problem is wasted gloves; elevator buttons cannot carry MRSA
The gloves protect the technician, so surfaces they touch afterward stay clean
The contaminated gloves transfer MRSA to shared surfaces, making the technician's hands the vehicle that can carry the organism to the next patient or surface

questions.explanation: D is correct because MRSA on used gloves is transferred to every surface touched afterward, so gloves must be removed and hand hygiene performed at the point of care before touching shared surfaces. A is wrong because MRSA also spreads indirectly through contaminated hands, gloves, and surfaces. B is wrong because high-touch surfaces such as elevator buttons can carry MRSA and pass it to the next person's hands. C is wrong because the outside of a used glove is contaminated even though the inside protected the technician's skin.

questions.question: Two patients with the same last name are in adjacent rooms, and a technician is about to begin care for one of them using an order pulled up on a screen. Analyzing the identification risk, which step best protects against wrong-patient care?

answers.text: Rely on the room number shown on the screen to confirm the right patient
Verify the patient's full name and date of birth against the wristband and the order before starting care
Ask the roommate which patient the order belongs to
Proceed with the nearer patient and verify identifiers afterward

questions.explanation: B is correct: two identifiers — full name and date of birth — are checked against the wristband and the order before care, which is essential when names are similar. A is wrong because a room number is never a patient identifier. C is wrong because a roommate is not a reliable or appropriate source for identification. D is wrong because verification must happen before care, not after it has already been delivered to a possibly wrong patient.

questions.question: A patient who was alert and eating lunch at midday is found in the late afternoon drowsy and difficult to arouse, responding only briefly when spoken to. Regarding this change in level of consciousness, what should the patient care technician do first?

answers.text: Stay with the patient and notify the nurse immediately of the change
Let the patient sleep undisturbed and recheck them at the evening meal
Offer the patient a caffeinated drink to help them wake up before reporting
Document the finding and raise it during the next day's shift report

questions.explanation: A is correct: a drop in level of consciousness from alert to difficult to arouse is an acute condition change, so the technician stays with the patient and notifies the nurse immediately. B is wrong because unusual drowsiness of this kind cannot be assumed to be ordinary sleep and left unchecked for hours. C is wrong because giving a drink to a patient who is difficult to arouse is unsafe and delays the report. D is wrong because an acute change is reported at once, not held for the next day.

questions.question: During purposeful rounding, a patient says their call light has gone unanswered several times and they no longer trust that help will come. Regarding operational standards for responsiveness and patient experience, what should the technician do?

answers.text: Tell the patient the unit is busy and that delays are expected
Move the call light out of reach so the patient uses it less often
Document that the patient is difficult so future staff are warned
Apologize, address the immediate need, ensure the call light is in reach, and report the repeated delays to the nurse

questions.explanation: D is correct because operational standards tied to patient experience, including HCAHPS awareness, call for prompt responsiveness, meeting the immediate need, keeping the call light in reach, and reporting a repeated pattern to the nurse. A is wrong because excusing delays does not address the need or the pattern. B is wrong because removing access to the call light is unsafe and directly worsens responsiveness. C is wrong because labeling the patient is unprofessional and does not fix responsiveness.

questions.question: While completing pre-operative preparation tasks, a patient awaiting surgery becomes tearful and asks the technician to explain what could go wrong during the operation so they can decide whether to go ahead. Which response is appropriate?

answers.text: Explain the main risks of the operation in simple terms so the patient can decide quickly
Reassure the patient that operations like this almost never have complications, and finish the preparation
Stay with the patient, acknowledge their concern, and notify the nurse promptly so the patient's questions can be addressed by the appropriate team member before surgery
Tell the patient it is too late to ask questions because the preparation is already underway

questions.explanation: C is correct: the technician provides emotional support and escalates promptly — questions about operative risks and the decision to proceed belong with the nurse and provider, not the technician. A is wrong because explaining surgical risks to support a consent decision is outside technician scope. B is wrong because blanket reassurance dismisses a genuine concern and states something the technician cannot guarantee. D is wrong because a patient may raise questions or reconsider at any point; preparation tasks never override that right.

questions.question: On an inpatient unit, the patient care technician has made two unsuccessful venipuncture attempts on a delegated draw. The patient is tense and asks whether the technician will keep trying until blood is obtained. Analyzing the technician's next step, what should they do?

answers.text: Make one more attempt in the other arm, since the patient has not yet withdrawn consent
Leave the needle in place and probe gently side to side until the vein is entered
Stop attempting, care for the puncture sites, and notify the nurse so the collection can be reassessed or assigned to a more experienced collector per policy
Ask the patient to pump their fist continuously while the technician prepares a third attempt

questions.explanation: C is correct because repeated unsuccessful attempts are stopped, the sites are cared for, and the nurse is notified so the order can be reassessed or reassigned under facility policy rather than continued by persistence. A is wrong because a further attempt by the same collector after two failures exceeds appropriate attempt limits and ignores the patient's distress. B is wrong because probing with the needle in place injures tissue and must never be done. D is wrong because fist pumping does not remedy failed attempts and prolonged pumping can affect some results.

questions.question: The patient care technician collects blood specimens from two patients in neighboring rooms during one round and plans to carry both sets of tubes to the nurses' station to label them together where the printer is. Regarding bedside labeling, what should the technician do instead?

answers.text: Label at the nurses' station as planned, as long as each patient's tubes are carried in a separate bag
Pre-label both patients' tubes before starting the round so labeling is already done
Ask a coworker at the station to double-check the tubes against memory before labeling them
Label each patient's tubes at that patient's bedside, in their presence, immediately after that collection and before moving to the next patient

questions.explanation: D is correct because specimens are labeled at the bedside, in the patient's presence, immediately after collection, which ties each tube to the correct patient before the technician moves on. A is wrong because carrying unlabeled tubes away from the bedside creates a mix-up risk that separate bags do not eliminate, and labeling must occur in the patient's presence. B is wrong because pre-labeling tubes before collection risks applying a label to the wrong patient's specimen. C is wrong because a coworker's check from memory is not a substitute for labeling at the point of collection.

questions.question: A patient's chart shows 178 lb on Monday morning and 171 lb on Tuesday evening. On review, Monday's weight was taken before breakfast in a gown on the unit scale, while Tuesday's was taken after dinner with shoes and a coat on a different scale. What is the patient care technician's best conclusion and action?

answers.text: Recognize that the two weights are not comparable, and reweigh the patient on the same scale, at the same time of day, in the same amount of clothing
Report a 7 lb loss to the nurse as an urgent change in the patient's condition
Average the two weights and chart the average as the current weight
Discard the Monday weight and use the Tuesday weight as the new baseline without comment

questions.explanation: A is correct because daily weights are comparable only when taken on the same scale, at the same time of day, and in the same amount of clothing; differing scale, timing, shoes, and a coat explain the apparent change, so a standardized reweigh is needed. B is wrong because reporting a 7 lb loss as a real condition change would escalate an artifact of inconsistent technique. C is wrong because averaging two non-comparable measurements produces a weight that was never actually measured. D is wrong because quietly changing the baseline hides the inconsistency instead of correcting the measurement conditions.

excpt.quiz_title: ExCPT Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam

questions.question: During pickup, a patient becomes visibly frustrated about a long wait and raises their voice at the counter. Which technician response best handles the interaction?

answers.text: Match the patient's volume so they understand the pharmacy is busy too
Walk away without speaking until the patient calms down on their own
Listen without interrupting, acknowledge the frustration empathetically, explain the next step and expected timing, and involve the pharmacist if the concern involves their medication
Tell the patient their prescription will move to the back of the queue for complaining

questions.explanation: C is correct because listening, acknowledging the feeling, and giving clear next steps de-escalates respectfully, while medication concerns still route to the pharmacist. A is wrong because raising one's own voice escalates the conflict. B is wrong because silently abandoning the interaction leaves the patient unheard and the issue unresolved. D is wrong because punishing a complaint with a delay is unprofessional and undermines trust.

questions.question: Regarding a nonjudgmental way to confirm a patient's understanding at pickup, which technician phrase best fits teach-back practice?

answers.text: "You understood everything I said, right?"
"This is simple, so there is no need to go over it again."
"If you forget part of it, just work it out from the label."
"To be sure I explained it clearly, can you tell me in your own words how you will take this?"

questions.explanation: D is correct: teach-back asks the patient to restate the instructions in their own words while framing any gap as the explainer's responsibility, which confirms understanding without shaming the patient. A is wrong because a yes-or-no prompt invites agreement whether or not the patient understood. B is wrong because declaring the information simple discourages the patient from revealing confusion. C is wrong because telling a patient to improvise from the label leaves misunderstandings uncorrected and can lead to a dosing error.

questions.question: Regarding how a continuous quality improvement change is tested, which statement is correct?

answers.text: A change should be rolled out to every shift at once, because a small test cannot show whether it works
A change should be judged by whether staff like it, without measuring error or near-miss data
A change is tested on a small scale first, its results are measured, and the pharmacy then decides to adopt, adjust, or abandon it before wider use
A change is permanent once announced, because revisiting it would undermine staff confidence

questions.explanation: C is correct because continuous quality improvement tests a change on a limited scale, measures its effect, and uses that evidence to decide whether to adopt, adjust, or abandon it. A is wrong because an untested pharmacy-wide rollout spreads a possibly harmful change everywhere at once. B is wrong because staff preference without outcome data does not show whether errors decreased. D is wrong because improvement depends on revisiting changes that measurement shows are not working.

questions.question: Regarding opening a glass ampule during sterile compounding, which technique is correct for the technician?

answers.text: Shake the ampule vigorously after opening so any glass particles settle to the bottom
Disinfect the neck with sterile alcohol, allow it to dry, protect their fingers, and snap the top off cleanly before withdrawing the contents
Touch the open neck with a gloved finger to check that the break is smooth before inserting the needle
Snap the neck first and disinfect the opening afterward, because alcohol cannot be used on glass

questions.explanation: B is correct because the neck is disinfected and allowed to dry before the ampule is snapped open, and finger protection and a clean break reduce contamination and injury risk. A is wrong because shaking does not remove glass particles and can contaminate or spill the contents. C is wrong because touching the open neck contaminates a critical site. D is wrong because disinfection must occur before opening, not after the contents have been exposed.

questions.question: Regarding setup of the balance before weighing ingredients for a non-sterile compound, which practice is correct?

answers.text: Place the ingredient directly on the bare pan so no paper weight has to be accounted for
Zero the balance after the ingredient is already on the pan so the reading starts fresh
Keep the balance near an open door, since air movement does not affect powder weights
Set the balance on a stable, level surface away from drafts, confirm it reads zero, and use a weighing paper or vessel with its weight tared before adding the ingredient

questions.explanation: D is correct: accurate weighing requires a level, stable, draft-free placement, a confirmed zero, and a tared weighing paper or vessel so only the ingredient's weight is measured. A is wrong because weighing directly on the pan contaminates the pan and the ingredient and makes complete transfer difficult. B is wrong because zeroing with the ingredient in place hides the ingredient's actual weight rather than measuring it. C is wrong because drafts and air currents visibly disturb balance readings, especially for small powder quantities.

questions.question: A product representative offers the technician personal gift cards if the technician steers patients toward the representative's product line when patients ask about options. Regarding this offer, how should the technician respond?

answers.text: Decline the cards and report the offer to the pharmacist-in-charge or the compliance channel, because steering patients for personal payment is an improper inducement
Accept the cards if their value is small, since small gifts cannot influence anyone
Accept the cards but donate them, which removes the conflict
Accept the cards and steer only patients who were already likely to choose that product

questions.explanation: The key is correct because payment tied to steering patients' medication choices is a kickback-style inducement; the technician must decline it and report it through pharmacy leadership or compliance. B is wrong because the impropriety lies in the steering arrangement, not the size of the payment. C is wrong because donating the proceeds does not undo accepting payment for steering. D is wrong because steering for pay is improper even when it overlaps with what a patient might have chosen anyway.

questions.question: In the afternoon, the technician finds the morning refrigerator temperature reading was never recorded and the log line is blank. Regarding inventory quality assurance for refrigerated stock, what should the technician do?

answers.text: Fill in the temperature the refrigerator usually shows, from memory
Copy yesterday's morning reading onto today's line so the log has no gap
Leave the line blank and say nothing, since the afternoon reading can cover the whole day
Record the actual current reading with its true date and time, note the missed reading following policy, and notify the pharmacist so the stored stock can be assessed

questions.explanation: D is correct because temperature records must be truthful: the real reading is logged with its real time, the gap is acknowledged through policy, and the pharmacist decides whether the stock was affected. A is wrong because a remembered usual value is invented data. B is wrong because copying another day's reading falsifies the record. C is wrong because concealing a monitoring gap leaves a possible excursion unevaluated.

questions.question: Concerning injection routes identified by the tissue layer targeted, a skin test placed into the dermis, the layer of skin just below the surface, so a small wheal forms uses which route of administration?

answers.text: Intradermal route
Subcutaneous route
Intramuscular route
Intravenous route

questions.explanation: The key is correct because the intradermal route delivers a small volume into the dermis just under the skin surface, producing the wheal used in skin testing. Option B is wrong because the subcutaneous route deposits medication into the fatty tissue beneath the skin, as with most insulin injections. Option C is wrong because the intramuscular route delivers medication deep into a muscle such as the deltoid. Option D is wrong because the intravenous route delivers medication directly into a vein, bypassing skin and muscle tissue entirely.

questions.question: Regarding transfer of a Schedule IV prescription's remaining refills to another pharmacy, the patient has given the technician the new pharmacy's name and phone number. What is the technician's correct supporting role in this transfer?

answers.text: Gather the transfer information the pharmacist will need, route the request to the pharmacist for the pharmacist-to-pharmacist communication of the required prescription and refill information, and document the transfer as the pharmacist directs
Call the new pharmacy and dictate the refill history personally, completing the transfer without involving a pharmacist
Tell the patient Schedule IV prescriptions can never be transferred, so the prescriber must write a new one in every case
Fax a copy of the prescription label to the new pharmacy and consider the transfer complete

questions.explanation: The key is correct because a Schedule IV prescription with refills remaining may be transferred, but the transfer information must be communicated between pharmacists; the technician supports the process by gathering information, routing the request, and documenting as directed. B is wrong because the technician does not personally complete the pharmacist-to-pharmacist transfer communication. C is wrong because transferable refills do exist for Schedule IV prescriptions. D is wrong because sending a label copy does not communicate the full required transfer record or complete a valid transfer.

questions.question: Grouping a new omeprazole order by body system and disease state, the technician files it with the gastrointestinal medications. Which disease-state grouping justifies that filing?

answers.text: Hypothyroidism, because omeprazole replaces thyroid hormone
Hyperlipidemia, because omeprazole lowers cholesterol
Type 2 diabetes, because omeprazole lowers blood glucose
Acid-related reflux disease, because omeprazole reduces gastric acid production as a proton pump inhibitor

questions.explanation: D is correct because omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor that reduces gastric acid and treats acid-related gastrointestinal conditions such as reflux disease. A is wrong because thyroid hormone replacement for hypothyroidism is levothyroxine. B is wrong because cholesterol lowering for hyperlipidemia is the role of statins such as atorvastatin. C is wrong because blood glucose lowering for type 2 diabetes is the role of agents such as metformin, not an acid reducer.

questions.question: A compounded preparation uses several ingredients, and one ingredient expires sooner than the others while the supported BUD for the formulation is later. Analyzing how to assign the discard date, what should the technician do?

answers.text: Assign a BUD no later than the earliest limiting date and seek pharmacist direction if the limit is unclear
Use the latest ingredient expiration date so the preparation is available as long as possible
Ignore ingredient expirations and base the date only on the day the compound was made
Extend the BUD because the finished preparation will be refrigerated, without any supporting information

questions.explanation: A is correct because the BUD can never outlast the earliest limiting factor, so an ingredient that expires sooner caps the date, and uncertainty is escalated to the pharmacist. B is wrong because using the latest expiration would keep the preparation in use after one of its ingredients has expired. C is wrong because the preparation date alone, without ingredient and stability limits, does not establish a safe discard date. D is wrong because refrigeration by itself, without supporting stability information, is not a basis for extending a BUD.

questions.question: An adjudicated claim rejects because the quantity submitted exceeds the plan limit for the days supply entered. The prescription directions and quantity appear to have been entered correctly. What should the technician do?

answers.text: Split the quantity into several smaller claims on the same day so each one stays under the limit
Reduce the dispensed quantity on their own so the claim will pay, without involving anyone else
Tell the patient the plan limit does not apply to this prescription and resubmit unchanged until it pays
Reconfirm the quantity, directions, and days supply calculation, then bring the limit rejection to the pharmacist so the prescriber or a plan authorization process can be engaged as needed

questions.explanation: D is correct because after verifying the entry is accurate, a true plan-limit rejection needs pharmacist involvement and possibly prescriber contact or an authorization request rather than a workaround by the technician. A is wrong because splitting claims to evade a plan limit misrepresents the dispensing and circumvents the payer edit. B is wrong because changing the quantity to be dispensed is a dispensing decision the technician does not make alone. C is wrong because resubmitting unchanged data will keep rejecting and the technician cannot declare a plan limit inapplicable.

questions.question: In the compounding area, the technician notices cloudiness and a visible precipitate forming immediately after two parenteral solutions are combined, before any product reaches the patient. Analyzing this physical incompatibility, what should the technician do?

answers.text: Shake the mixture vigorously until the precipitate disappears and continue compounding
Label the product and dispense it because the change is only cosmetic
Filter out the precipitate and document that the incompatibility was corrected
Stop, quarantine the mixture, and notify the pharmacist that a physical incompatibility has occurred

questions.explanation: D is correct because precipitation signals a physical incompatibility, so the product must not be used and the pharmacist must direct any remake or alternative. A is wrong because shaking does not reverse an incompatibility and could mask an unsafe product. B is wrong because a visible physical change is not merely cosmetic and the product must not be dispensed. C is wrong because filtering out precipitate does not restore the intended formulation and is not a technician correction for incompatibility.

questions.question: Analyzing a records request during an announced audit, the technician realizes a dispensing record the auditors will review contains an error the technician made last month, and a coworker advises quietly correcting the original entry before the auditors arrive so it looks right. How should the technician respond?

answers.text: Correct the original entry, because an accurate-looking record is what auditors expect
Leave the original record unchanged, tell the pharmacist about the error, and let any correction be made through the pharmacy's documented correction process
Remove that record from the file so the error is not discovered
Create a replacement record dated last month and discard the original

questions.explanation: The key is correct because original dispensing records must be preserved as created; errors are disclosed to the pharmacist and addressed only through a transparent, documented correction process, never by altering the record ahead of an audit. Option A is wrong because silently rewriting history in a record under review misrepresents what was dispensed. Option C is wrong because removing a retained record compounds the error with concealment and a retention violation. Option D is wrong because backdating a replacement and destroying the original falsifies the record trail.

questions.question: During a cycle count, the technician counts 42 tablets on the shelf for an item whose inventory system shows 90. A coworker proposes adjusting the system count to 42 immediately without looking into it. Regarding inventory accuracy, what is the best course of action?

answers.text: Adjust the count to 42 right away and move on to the next item
Leave the system at 90 because cycle counts are only estimates
Recount, check for stock in other locations and for recent unrecorded transactions, document the findings, and report the unresolved discrepancy to the pharmacist or supervisor before any adjustment
Add stock from a similar product so the shelf count matches the system

questions.explanation: C is correct because a large count gap must first be rechecked and investigated for misplaced stock or unrecorded transactions, then documented and escalated, so the adjustment that follows is accurate and auditable. A is wrong because adjusting without investigation can mask theft, a dispensing error, or a receiving mistake. B is wrong because ignoring a verified discrepancy leaves inventory records unreliable for ordering and dispensing. D is wrong because substituting a different product falsifies both the count and the stock itself.

questions.question: A medication being filled carries pregnancy-related warnings and must go out with its Medication Guide and a warning auxiliary label. The technician worries the warning will alarm the patient. Regarding these warnings, what should the technician do?

answers.text: Leave the auxiliary warning label off so the patient is not frightened
Remove the Medication Guide from the bag and mention the warning only if the patient asks
Cross out the warning wording on the printed materials so it is less prominent
Apply the auxiliary label, include the Medication Guide, and alert the pharmacist so the pharmacist can address the warning with the patient

questions.explanation: D is correct because required warnings must reach the patient intact: the auxiliary label and Medication Guide are included, and the pharmacist, not the technician, discusses the pregnancy-related warning with the patient. A is wrong because omitting a required warning label withholds safety information. B is wrong because the Medication Guide must be dispensed with the medication, not held back unless asked about. C is wrong because altering printed warning materials defeats their purpose and misrepresents the labeling.

questions.question: Regarding a moisture-sensitive medication supplied by the manufacturer in sealed blister cards, the manufacturer's directions state the tablets must remain in the original blister until use. How should the technician prepare this prescription?

answers.text: Remove all the tablets from the blisters and count them into an amber vial in advance
Punch the tablets out into the patient's weekly pill organizer so they are ready to take
Keep the tablets in their sealed original blister packaging rather than repackaging them into a vial ahead of use
Cut the blister cards apart and discard the printed outer carton before dispensing

questions.explanation: C is correct because the manufacturer directs that this moisture-sensitive product stay in its sealed original blister until use, and keeping it there preserves that protection. A is wrong because removing the tablets into a vial in advance exposes them to the moisture the blister is meant to exclude. B is wrong because punching tablets out ahead of use defeats the same protection and mixes the product outside its labeled packaging. D is wrong because discarding the outer carton removes printed lot, expiration, and product information that must stay with the dispensed product.

questions.question: Processing a new combination pain prescription fires a drug utilization review alert: the new product contains acetaminophen, and the profile also lists a regularly used over-the-counter acetaminophen product, so the combined daily amount may be too high. Analyzing this alert, what should the technician do?

answers.text: Override the alert because one of the products is sold over the counter
Hold processing and refer the alert to the pharmacist for clinical review before the prescription proceeds
Advise the patient to stop the over-the-counter product and continue with the fill
Remove the over-the-counter product from the profile so the alert stops firing

questions.explanation: B is correct because a possible excessive combined acetaminophen dose is a clinical safety question; the technician pauses and routes the alert to the pharmacist, who performs the DUR judgment. A is wrong because over-the-counter status does not make a duplicate-ingredient risk safe to override. C is wrong because directing a patient to stop a therapy is counseling and clinical judgment reserved to the pharmacist. D is wrong because deleting profile information to silence an alert hides the very risk the review is meant to catch.

questions.question: In a body surface area calculation using the Mosteller formula, BSA = square root of ((height in cm x weight in kg) / 3,600), a patient is 144 cm tall and weighs 25 kg, and the ordered dose is 120 mg per square meter. What is the dose in milligrams?

answers.text: 120 mg
60 mg
240 mg

questions.explanation: A is correct: (144 x 25) / 3,600 = 3,600 / 3,600 = 1, the square root of 1 is a BSA of 1 square meter, and 1 x 120 mg = 120 mg. B is wrong because it uses a BSA of 0.5 square meter. C is wrong because it uses a BSA of 2 square meters. D is wrong because it multiplies the ordered rate by 10 instead of by the calculated BSA of 1.

questions.question: Regarding proof of delivery for durable medical equipment, a rented wheelchair is delivered to a beneficiary's home and the delivery driver returns with a delivery ticket that has no recipient signature and no delivery date recorded. What should the technician do before the equipment is billed?

answers.text: Bill the rental from the prescriber order alone, since the order documents medical need
Hold billing and obtain a completed delivery record showing the delivery date and the signature of the beneficiary or their representative
Sign the ticket on the beneficiary's behalf, since the driver confirms the delivery occurred
Bill the equipment as a purchase instead of a rental so no delivery record is needed

questions.explanation: B is correct: DME billing requires a proof-of-delivery record with the delivery date and the signature of the beneficiary or their representative, so billing is held until that record is completed. A is wrong because the prescriber order shows medical need but does not prove the beneficiary actually received the equipment. C is wrong because the technician must never sign a delivery record on the beneficiary's behalf. D is wrong because changing a rental to a purchase misstates the transaction and does not remove the delivery documentation requirement.

california-wastewater-grade-1.quiz_title: California Wastewater Grade 1 Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam

questions.question: Who is permitted to work on electrical equipment at a wastewater treatment plant?

answers.text: Any operator who is wearing dry rubber-soled shoes at the time the work is done
Only qualified personnel
A trainee working alone, provided the task is expected to take only a few minutes
A visitor who has repaired similar electrical equipment at another type of facility

questions.explanation: Only qualified personnel work on electrical equipment. Footwear, a short task, or experience elsewhere does not qualify an unqualified person, and water and electricity are kept apart.

questions.question: After the skimmer pushes scum onto the scum beach, what happens to that material?

answers.text: It is ground into small pieces and returned to the influent so it can be settled out as primary sludge
It flows over the effluent weirs with the clarified water once the beach has filled to its full capacity
It is pumped to the sludge hopper and mixed with the settled sludge at the bottom of the clarifier tank
It is held there for removal while the water that came with it drains back to the tank

questions.explanation: The skimmer pushes floatables to the scum box or beach for removal; water drains back and the grease and scum are taken away. Scum is not reground, sent over the weirs, or mixed into the hopper sludge.

questions.question: Why does anaerobic digestion take place in a closed, heated, mixed tank?

answers.text: To keep oxygen out while gas produced is contained and collected
To expose the sludge to direct sunlight for disinfection throughout the entire stabilization period
To allow algae to produce oxygen inside the tank
To keep the sludge cold during stabilization

questions.explanation: Anaerobic digestion stabilizes sludge without oxygen in a closed, heated, mixed tank, breaking down volatile solids and producing biogas. Sunlight and algae belong to pond treatment, not digestion.

questions.question: How is detention time in a stabilization pond most accurately characterized?

answers.text: It is measured in minutes, like flow through a Parshall flume
It is long — on the order of weeks — and stated in days
It equals the detention in a primary clarifier at the same flow
It is set by the chlorine contact requirement for disinfection

questions.explanation: Ponds provide long detention, on the order of weeks, and pond detention is stated in days as pond volume divided by daily flow — far longer than the hours of detention in a primary clarifier.

questions.question: Which of the following is a function of the State Water Resources Control Board in the wastewater certification program?

answers.text: Classifying wastewater treatment plants
Selling treatment chemicals to certified plants
Repairing clarifier drives at individual plants
Hiring every operator who works at a local plant

questions.explanation: The State Water Resources Control Board classifies plants, issues certificates, and administers the examinations under the wastewater program.

questions.question: A hard hat is the required protection for an operator working in an area where which hazard is present?

answers.text: Overhead hazards
High noise levels around running equipment
Chemical splashes from an open process tank
Wet, slippery floors in a covered gallery

questions.explanation: A hard hat is worn where overhead hazards exist. High noise calls for hearing protection and splash work calls for eye protection; each item of protective equipment is matched to its hazard.

questions.question: Raw wastewater pumps sit just downstream of the headworks screens. What protection do the screens give those pumps?

answers.text: They keep large objects out of the flow so the pumps are not clogged or damaged
They remove the dissolved load from the wastewater so the pumps only ever have to move clean water
They settle the grit out of the flow so the pump impellers never come in contact with sand or gravel
They measure the flow for the pumps so the pumps can be started and stopped by the flume signal alone

questions.explanation: Screens remove large objects such as rags, sticks, and plastics that would damage or clog downstream equipment, including the raw wastewater pumps. Grit removal and flow measurement are separate preliminary steps.

questions.question: A digester's pH has drifted well below near-neutral as acids accumulate. Which bacterial group is placed most at risk?

answers.text: The acid formers, which prefer a low pH
The methane formers, which are the slower, more sensitive step
The algae growing on the digester roof
No group, because pH does not affect digestion

questions.explanation: The methane formers are the slower, more sensitive step in digestion and favor near-neutral conditions, which is why a pH drop from accumulating acids threatens digester stability most through them.

questions.question: A sodium hypochlorite solution that has sat in storage for a long time will generally have what property?

answers.text: Its strength stays exactly the same no matter how long it sits in routine day-to-day plant operation
It will have gained strength as it aged in the container
It will have lost some of its strength compared with fresh solution
It becomes stronger if it is stored warm and in bright light

questions.explanation: Hypochlorite solutions lose strength with time, so an aged solution delivers less available chlorine than a fresh one at the same feed setting; storage does not make the solution stronger.

questions.question: Grass and vegetation on pond berms have grown tall and thick. What is the correct routine response?

answers.text: Keep berms and dikes mowed as part of regular pond maintenance
Let vegetation grow to shade the pond and cool the water when checked during a normal working shift
Burn the berms during the windiest day of the season
Flood the berms so the vegetation drowns in place

questions.explanation: Keeping berms and dikes mowed, and free of trees and burrowing animals, is a standing pond operating duty that protects the dike and allows inspection.

questions.question: Dissolved oxygen is needed for a process check at a specific location and moment. Which sample type should be used?

answers.text: A composite combined over the whole day
A sample composited from sludge lines
A grab sample tested without delay
A preserved sample shipped for later testing

questions.explanation: Dissolved oxygen changes quickly, so it is measured on a grab sample tested without delay rather than on a composited or preserved sample.

questions.question: Wastewater operator certification examinations in California are administered in which format?

answers.text: On paper only, at the treatment plant where the candidate works
By mail, as an open-book take-home examination
By oral interview before a panel of plant superintendents
By computer-based testing

questions.explanation: The wastewater certification examinations are administered as computer-based tests under the State Water Resources Control Board's Wastewater Operator Certification Program.

questions.question: A drained clarifier is being refilled from one end and the water surface is rising unevenly, with one side filling much faster. What should the operator do?

answers.text: Slow down and fill the tank evenly, checking the drives and scrapers before it is loaded with flow
Finish filling as fast as possible from the same end so the uneven surface is covered over more quickly
Start the sludge pump at full speed to pull the high side down to the level of the low side of the tank
