Face the patient, speak directly to them in the first person, and allow extra time for the interpreted exchange
Write every question on paper instead of using the interpreter the patient requested
Ask the patient's hearing companion to interpret so the video service is not needed

questions.explanation: The key is correct because the patient is the person being addressed; facing them, speaking directly to them, and allowing time for interpretation preserves dignity and accuracy. Option A is wrong because it treats the interpreter as the patient and excludes the patient from their own conversation. Option C is wrong because substituting writing for the interpreter the patient requested ignores their chosen communication method. Option D is wrong because a companion is not a qualified interpreter and may filter or misstate information.

questions.question: The supply cabinet's par level for packs of registration forms is 50 packs, and a count shows 17 packs on hand. Regarding the order quantity needed to restore the cabinet to par, the assistant should order:

answers.text: 33 packs
17 packs
50 packs
67 packs

questions.explanation: Ordering to par means replacing what has been used: 50 packs at par minus 17 packs on hand = 33 packs to order. B is wrong because 17 is the quantity already on hand, not the quantity needed. C is wrong because ordering the full par amount would overshoot par by the 17 packs still in the cabinet. D is wrong because it adds the on-hand count to par instead of subtracting it.

questions.question: A patient with limited English proficiency arrives for check-in, accompanied by their teenage child who offers to interpret. How should the assistant handle the language barrier for the visit's instructions and forms?

answers.text: Accept the teenager's offer, since family members know the patient's situation best
Arrange a qualified medical interpreter through the office's language services and speak to the patient through that interpreter
Speak English more loudly and slowly until the patient nods
Skip the instructions and forms that cannot easily be explained

questions.explanation: B is correct because a qualified interpreter provides accurate, impartial communication, while family members, especially minors, may omit, soften, or misunderstand medical information and compromise privacy. A is wrong because willingness and familiarity do not make a family member a reliable or appropriate interpreter. C is wrong because volume does not create comprehension and can feel demeaning. D is wrong because withholding instructions and forms denies the patient equal participation in their care.

questions.question: Regarding clarifying a message before it is relayed, a provider's note in the chart instructs the assistant to tell a patient to 'return in two' without stating days, weeks, or months. What should the assistant do first?

answers.text: Ask the provider to specify the unit of time before relaying the instruction to the patient
Tell the patient two months, since that is the most common interval
Relay the phrase exactly as written and let the patient interpret it
Schedule the patient for two days later so a visit is at least on the calendar

questions.explanation: The key is correct because an ambiguous interval must be clarified with its source, the provider, before it is relayed; guessing could book the wrong follow-up. Option B is wrong because assuming months invents clinical timing. Option C is wrong because passing along an unclear instruction transfers the confusion to the patient. Option D is wrong because the assistant would be setting a clinical interval without direction.

questions.question: During check-in for a first visit at a new practice, a patient says quietly that they almost did not come because they get very nervous in new offices and do not know anyone there. Which response best demonstrates empathy?

answers.text: There is nothing to be nervous about here; everyone at this practice is very nice.
Starting somewhere new can feel unsettling. I will walk you through each step of check-in so you know what to expect.
I know exactly how you feel; I dislike new places too, and my first day working here was awful.
Complete these forms first, and we can talk once the paperwork is finished.

questions.explanation: B is correct: it acknowledges the patient's feeling and offers concrete support, which is empathy in practice. A is wrong because it dismisses the feeling with blanket reassurance instead of acknowledging it. C is wrong because claiming to know exactly how the patient feels and shifting focus to the assistant's own experience is sympathy and self-focus, not empathy. D is wrong because it ignores the feeling entirely and treats the encounter as paperwork only.

questions.question: Analyzing the elements of negligence, a patient files a complaint alleging that a provider was careless during treatment, but the review confirms the patient suffered no injury or loss of any kind as a result. Which element of a negligence claim is missing in this situation?

answers.text: Duty, because no provider-patient relationship existed during treatment
Breach of duty, because carelessness can never breach a standard of care
Damages, because a negligence claim requires actual harm or loss resulting from the breach
Causation, because the provider's actions were unrelated to the visit

questions.explanation: C is correct: negligence requires duty, breach of duty, causation, and damages, and a claim fails without actual harm or loss, which the review confirms is absent here. A is wrong because treatment was provided, so a provider-patient relationship and its duty existed. B is wrong because careless care that departs from the accepted standard is exactly what a breach of duty describes. D is wrong because causation concerns whether the breach caused the harm; with no harm at all, the missing element is damages, not the link itself.

questions.question: A patient is scheduled for imaging after a note documents nephrolithiasis. The medical administrative assistant breaks the term into nephr/o, lith, and -iasis to confirm what the imaging will evaluate. What does nephrolithiasis mean?

answers.text: A condition of stones in the kidney
Inflammation of the kidney
Surgical removal of the kidney
Surgical repair of the kidney

questions.explanation: A is correct: nephr/o means kidney, lith means stone, and -iasis means a condition, so nephrolithiasis is a condition of kidney stones. B is wrong because kidney inflammation is nephritis, which ends in -itis. C is wrong because surgical removal is nephrectomy, which ends in -ectomy. D is wrong because surgical repair is expressed by -plasty, not by lith or -iasis.

questions.question: A service was billed at $195. The remittance shows a contracted allowed amount of $156, the payer paid $124.80, and the remaining $31.20 of the allowed amount is patient coinsurance. Regarding the contractual adjustment for this service, what amount should be posted as the adjustment?

answers.text: $39.00, the billed charge minus the allowed amount
$31.20, the patient coinsurance portion of the allowed amount
$70.20, the billed charge minus the payer payment
$124.80, the amount the payer paid

questions.explanation: A is correct because the contractual adjustment is the difference between the billed charge and the contracted allowed amount, $195 minus $156, which is $39.00; the payer payment and patient coinsurance then account for the $156 allowed amount. B is wrong because $31.20 is the patient's coinsurance share of the allowed amount, which the patient owes, not an adjustment. C is wrong because $70.20 combines the adjustment with the patient coinsurance by subtracting only the payer payment from the billed charge. D is wrong because $124.80 is a payment to post, not a reduction of the charge.

questions.question: During open enrollment, a patient describes wanting the freedom to see specialists without a referral and to receive some coverage even when using an out-of-network provider, accepting higher cost-sharing for that flexibility. Regarding commercial plan types, which plan design matches this description?

answers.text: A health maintenance organization, because it offers open specialist access and out-of-network coverage
A supplemental Medigap policy, because it functions as a standalone plan for specialist care
A preferred provider organization, because it typically allows specialist visits without a referral and provides some out-of-network coverage at higher cost
A state Medicaid plan, because it lets members choose any provider nationally without referrals

questions.explanation: C is correct because a preferred provider organization typically permits self-referral to specialists and covers out-of-network care at a higher cost-share, matching the flexibility the patient described. A is wrong because a health maintenance organization typically requires in-network care and a primary care referral, the opposite of the stated preference. B is wrong because Medigap supplements Original Medicare and is not a standalone commercial plan for specialist access. D is wrong because Medicaid is a government income-based program, not a commercial design chosen for national open access.

questions.question: During check-in at a specialty office, a returning patient reports on the intake form that their preferred pharmacy has changed and gives a new emergency contact. Regarding completion of the encounter record, what should the medical administrative assistant do with these updates?

answers.text: Leave the updates on the paper intake form only, since the EHR already has a pharmacy and a contact on file
Enter the updates after the patient's next visit so today's check-in stays fast
Ask the patient to call the pharmacy themselves to move the information over
Enter the updated pharmacy and emergency contact into the patient's EHR during intake and verify the entries back with the patient

questions.explanation: D is correct: pertinent intake information, including current pharmacy and emergency contact details, is entered into the EHR and verified with the patient so the record stays current. A is wrong because information left only on paper is unavailable to the care and billing team working in the record. B is wrong because deferring entry leaves today's visit working from outdated contact and pharmacy data. C is wrong because updating the practice's own record is the assistant's task, not the patient's errand.

questions.question: Regarding coinsurance as part of patient financial responsibility, a patient's deductible is fully met, the payer's allowed amount for today's service is $200, and the patient's plan applies 20% coinsurance. The patient asks the medical administrative assistant how much they owe for this service. What is the correct figure and explanation?

answers.text: $40, because coinsurance is the patient's percentage share of the allowed amount once the deductible is met
$200, because the patient owes the full allowed amount whenever coinsurance applies
$20, because coinsurance is a flat fee collected at each visit
$160, because the patient pays the percentage the plan does not cover at the billed-charge rate

questions.explanation: A is correct because coinsurance is a percentage of the allowed amount: 20% of $200 is $40, and with the deductible met that percentage share is the patient's responsibility for the service. B is wrong because the full allowed amount would be owed only with 100% coinsurance or no coverage, not a 20% share. C is wrong because a flat per-visit fee describes a copayment, not coinsurance, and $20 is not 20% of $200. D is wrong because it reverses the shares — the payer pays 80% ($160) — and coinsurance is calculated on the allowed amount, not billed charges.

questions.question: A manager proposes that the practice routinely waive the copayments of insured patients as a marketing draw, with no individual hardship review, and asks the medical administrative assistant to start applying the waivers at check-in. Analyzing this proposal against federal compliance expectations, what should the assistant do?

answers.text: Apply the waivers, because a practice may set any collection policy it likes
Apply the waivers but leave them off the encounter records so they attract no attention
Not apply routine waivers and raise the proposal through the practice's compliance channel, because routinely waiving amounts owed can act as an improper inducement
Apply the waivers only to patients who say a competing practice offered them the same deal

questions.explanation: C is correct: routinely forgiving insured patients' cost-sharing, without an individual financial-hardship basis, can function as an inducement to choose the practice and raises federal compliance concerns, so it should not be started at the front desk and should be routed to compliance review. A is wrong because payer agreements and federal expectations limit how cost-sharing may be waived. B is wrong because hiding the waivers from the record adds a documentation problem to the compliance problem. D is wrong because matching a competitor's offer does not cure the inducement concern.

questions.question: To finish a work file containing patient information at home, the assistant considers uploading it to a personal cloud storage account that the practice has never approved. Regarding data storage practice in this situation, the assistant should:

answers.text: Upload the file, because the personal account is protected by a password
Upload the file and delete it the next morning, because brief storage carries no risk
Not upload the file, and keep patient information only on practice-approved secure systems, following practice authorization for any remote work
Rename the file so it no longer shows a patient name, which makes the upload acceptable

questions.explanation: Patient information may be stored only on practice-approved, secure systems, so an unapproved personal cloud account must not be used regardless of convenience. A is wrong because a personal password does not make an unmanaged account an approved storage system. B is wrong because the exposure occurs at upload; later deletion does not undo the time the data sat outside practice control. D is wrong because renaming the file does not remove the patient information inside it.

cehrs.quiz_title: CEHRS Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam

questions.question: Before a replacement workstation goes live at check-out, the EHR specialist is preparing its hardware inventory entry. Regarding putting new EHR hardware into service, what should they do?

answers.text: Add the workstation to the inventory only after its first repair, when support needs the details
List the workstation under the old workstation's entry because it serves the same desk
Create its inventory record with its asset and serial identifiers, location, and in-service status before or as it goes live, and retire the replaced device's status accordingly
Skip inventory for workstations and track only printers and scanners

questions.explanation: C is correct: new hardware enters the inventory with its own identifiers, location, and status as it enters service, and the replaced device's status is updated so the inventory stays accurate. A is wrong because waiting for a failure leaves the device unaccounted for until support is already hampered. B is wrong because two distinct devices sharing one entry corrupts identification and service history. D is wrong because workstations are core EHR hardware and belong in the inventory.

questions.question: Regarding two-identifier verification before documenting in the EHR, which pair should the EHR specialist confirm against the open chart before entering a note?

answers.text: The patient's room number and bed assignment
The patient's full name and date of birth, matched to the record's medical record number
The patient's appointment time and the provider's office location
The patient's insurance carrier name and plan type

questions.explanation: B is correct: two patient identifiers, such as full name and date of birth matched to the medical record number, confirm the open chart belongs to that patient before documentation. A is wrong because room and bed locations change and do not identify a person. C is wrong because schedule details identify an encounter slot, not the patient. D is wrong because coverage information can be shared by many patients and does not verify identity.

questions.question: Regarding relative value reports in the EHR, which description best fits this standardized financial report?

answers.text: A one-time list of patients who have not scheduled a follow-up visit
A prebuilt report that compares services using the relative value assigned to each service
A report that groups unpaid balances by the person financially responsible for each account
A summary that calculates infection rates for a quality review

questions.explanation: B is correct: a relative value report is a standardized financial report that compares services by the relative value assigned to each service, and it is run as a prebuilt report. A is wrong because a one-time follow-up list is an ad hoc clinical report, not a standardized financial report. C is wrong because grouping balances by the financially responsible person describes a guarantor report. D is wrong because infection rates are a statistical quality-improvement measure, not a relative value comparison.

questions.question: Concerning the primary purpose of conducting internal EHR audits on a routine schedule, which statement is correct?

answers.text: Routine audits proactively identify documentation errors, access problems, and non-compliant patterns so they can be corrected before they cause harm or external findings
Routine audits exist mainly to rank individual staff members for discipline
An audit is needed only after an external agency has already confirmed a breach
Routine audits are a marketing activity that demonstrates the EHR to prospective patients

questions.explanation: A is correct: internal audits are a preventive control that surfaces errors and non-compliant patterns early enough for correction. B is wrong because audit findings may inform follow-up, but ranking staff for discipline is not the audit's purpose. C is wrong because waiting for a confirmed external breach abandons the preventive value of auditing. D is wrong because audits are an internal compliance activity, not a promotional demonstration.

questions.question: Regarding a complete historic medication entry, which information set gives the entry its full value in the record?

answers.text: The medication name alone, since the prescriber can be assumed
The medication name, the period during which it was taken or its start and stop information, its discontinued or historical status, and the source of the information
The medication name and the pharmacy's street address only
The medication name copied into the active list so it is easy to see

questions.explanation: B is correct: a historic medication entry is useful when it shows what was taken, over what period, that it is no longer current, and where the information came from. A is wrong because a bare name without timeframe or status can be mistaken for current therapy. C is wrong because a pharmacy address adds no clinical meaning to the history. D is wrong because placing a past medication on the active list misrepresents the patient's current treatment.

questions.question: A public health agency requires reportable visit data from the EHR for a defined reporting program. To complete that external transmission correctly, what should the specialist do?

answers.text: Send the entire EHR database so the agency can select what it wants
Withhold all data because agency reporting is never a permitted exchange
Ask patients to hand-carry printed charts to the agency office
Send the required reportable elements for the patients in scope through the approved agency interface, after verifying the submission was accepted

questions.explanation: D is correct: agency exchange sends only the required reportable elements for the in-scope patients through the approved interface, with confirmation of acceptance. A is wrong because providing the entire database vastly exceeds the defined reporting requirement. B is wrong because compiling and transmitting data for required external reporting is a recognized EHR function. C is wrong because hand-carried printed charts are insecure, incomplete as a system submission, and not the approved interface.

questions.question: Before distribution, the EHR specialist verifies a clinic's monthly report and finds it includes patients from a sister clinic whose data should not appear in this report. What should the specialist do?

answers.text: Hold distribution, correct the report criteria so only the intended clinic's patients are included, and recheck the report before releasing it
Distribute the report and tell recipients the sister clinic's staff can ignore their rows
Black out the sister clinic's rows on the printed copies and distribute those
Rename the report to name both clinics so the contents match the title

questions.explanation: A is correct: the report contains the wrong population, so verification holds distribution while the criteria are corrected and the report is rechecked, ensuring recipients get data for the intended clinic only. B is wrong because distributing another clinic's patient data to the wrong recipients is exactly the harm verification exists to prevent. C is wrong because hand-redacting printed copies leaves the stored report wrong and any electronic copy uncorrected. D is wrong because retitling the report does not change the fact that its contents do not match the request.

questions.question: While searching the code database at an outpatient clinic, the EHR specialist finds an entry whose full descriptor specifies a detail that the encounter documentation never mentions. What should they do?

answers.text: Use the entry anyway, since extra detail in a descriptor does not matter
Add the missing detail to the encounter note so the documentation supports the entry
Use a different patient's entry that worked for a similar visit last week
Hold the entry and escalate to the provider for clarification, because the descriptor must be verified against what the documentation actually states

questions.explanation: D is correct: descriptor verification means the entry can only be used when the documentation supports everything its descriptor states, so an unsupported detail is a clarification issue for the provider, not something to overlook. A is wrong because descriptor details are part of what the entry represents and cannot be ignored. B is wrong because the specialist does not author clinical detail into a provider's note. C is wrong because another patient's entry was verified against different documentation.

questions.question: A morning check shows that outbound result messages have been sitting in the EHR interface queue since the previous evening and none reached the receiving providers. Analyzing the failed exchange, what is the best response?

answers.text: Delete the queued messages so the queue looks clear and let providers request the results again
Report the stalled interface through the escalation process, preserve the queued messages for delivery once the interface is restored, and notify affected areas that exchange is delayed
Print every queued result and mail the printouts without telling anyone about the delay
Resend each result from a staff member's personal email account to clear the backlog quickly

questions.explanation: B is correct: a stalled interface is a system exchange failure, so it is escalated for repair, the queued data are preserved for delivery, and affected areas are told exchange is delayed rather than silently lost. A is wrong because deleting queued results destroys data providers are expecting for care. C is wrong because mailing printouts bypasses the record of exchange and hides a system failure that will recur. D is wrong because personal email is an insecure channel and abandons the auditable interface route.

questions.question: In building a new encounter form in the EHR for a specialty clinic, the specialist is deciding what the form must contain to work as a superbill. Which build is correct?

answers.text: A blank free-text page, since structure slows providers down
Only patient demographic fields, since charges are added later by the payer
A list of procedures with no diagnosis section, since diagnoses stay in the note
The practice's commonly provided diagnoses and procedures with their codes and descriptions, plus fields for patient and encounter identifiers, date of service, and the rendering provider

questions.explanation: D is correct: a superbill is the encounter's charge source document, so it pairs the practice's frequent diagnoses and procedures with the encounter identifiers needed to bill that visit. A is wrong because an unstructured page cannot reliably capture the charges the form exists to record. B is wrong because demographics alone carry no charge information for claims processing. C is wrong because the form must capture the diagnosis information that supports the procedures billed for the encounter.

questions.question: A staff member returns from an extended leave and, while they were away, the practice changed the workflow for a task they perform daily. Regarding ongoing training for this returning user, what should the EHR specialist do?

answers.text: Let the returning user rediscover the changed workflow through trial and error in live records
Assign the returning user to train new hires on the task as a refresher
Repeat the user's entire original new-hire training program
Provide focused update training on the changed workflow, with practice in the training environment and a check that they can perform it correctly, before they resume the task live

questions.explanation: D is correct: a returning user needs targeted training on what changed during their absence, practiced safely and verified before they perform the changed workflow in live records. A is wrong because trial and error in live records risks errors the update training exists to prevent. B is wrong because someone who has not yet learned the new workflow cannot teach it. C is wrong because repeating the full original program spends most of its time on workflows that did not change.

questions.question: A single encounter template is used by both intake staff and the clinician during the same visit, and each group scrolls past long sections the other group completes. Which design choice best improves this shared template?

answers.text: Split the encounter into two unrelated notes so each group documents in a separate record
Require every user to complete every section, regardless of their role in the visit
Present each role with the sections relevant to their part of the encounter within the one shared template, while keeping the completed sections together in a single note
Remove the intake sections, because the clinician's sections are the important ones

questions.explanation: C is correct: role-relevant presentation lets each group work in the sections they own within one shared template, reducing clutter and scrolling while the encounter remains a single, complete note. A is wrong because splitting the visit into unrelated notes fragments the encounter record. B is wrong because forcing users through sections outside their role adds burden without improving the data. D is wrong because intake data are part of the visit record and removing them loses information the encounter needs.

questions.question: After a visit was registered as self-pay, the patient provides proof that their coverage was in effect retroactively on the date of service. What should the specialist do in the EHR?

answers.text: Leave the registration as self-pay, since the registration at check-in is final
Tell the patient nothing can be changed once a visit is complete

Update the coverage record with the verified plan information, confirm eligibility for that date of service, and route the encounter for billing to the payer so the patient's balance reflects the coverage
Delete the completed encounter and create a new one dated today so the coverage applies

questions.explanation: C is correct: coverage effective on the date of service governs how the encounter is billed, so the record is corrected, eligibility for that date is confirmed, and the encounter is routed to the payer with the patient's responsibility adjusted accordingly. A is wrong because registration is correctable when verified coverage information emerges; the initial entry does not override actual coverage. B is wrong because the workflow for retroactively effective coverage exists precisely to correct such accounts. D is wrong because recreating the encounter under a false date destroys the original record and misstates when care occurred.

questions.question: A patient asks the specialist for education material on a treatment the provider has not ordered or discussed for them, saying a friend recommended it. Analyzing that request against the specialist's education role, which response is best supported?

answers.text: Refer the request to the provider, since education the specialist provides follows the clinical team's direction for that patient's care
Provide the material, since any approved library topic may be given to any patient on request
Provide the material with a note saying the specialist also recommends asking about it
Tell the patient the treatment is not worth pursuing

questions.explanation: A is correct: the specialist provides materials the clinical team directs for the patient's care, so a request for education about an unordered treatment goes to the provider, who can address it clinically. B is wrong because library approval of a topic does not make the specialist the one who decides it fits this patient. C is wrong because adding a personal recommendation turns materials support into clinical endorsement. D is wrong because judging a treatment's worth is likewise a clinical determination outside the specialist's scope.

questions.question: Midway through a clinic session the flow board shows the provider running substantially behind, and several checked-in patients face long waits beyond their appointment times. Regarding coordinating patient flow in this situation, what should the EHR specialist do?

answers.text: Leave the board and the waiting patients uninformed so the session is not disrupted further
Cancel the remaining appointments in the EHR without contacting the patients
Update the flow information, inform waiting patients of the delay and their revised expectations, and offer affected patients the option to rebook where appropriate
Move every waiting patient into exam rooms at once so the waiting area appears empty

questions.explanation: C is correct: coordinating flow during a delay means keeping flow information current, communicating honest wait expectations to patients, and offering rebooking to those who cannot wait. A is wrong because silence leaves patients uninformed while their waits grow. B is wrong because cancelling appointments without patient contact abandons their care and their scheduling needs. D is wrong because rooming everyone at once exceeds available rooms and clinical capacity and merely hides the delay rather than managing it.

questions.question: Checking coverage information recorded in the EHR against the scanned insurance card on file, the specialist notices the subscriber identifier on the card differs from the identifier on the EHR's coverage screen by two transposed characters. How should this finding be understood?

answers.text: As a data discrepancy between the EHR and its source document, to be flagged for verification of the correct identifier
As the same identifier, because transposed characters do not change what an identifier means
As a problem with the scanned image only, since a card image can never be used to check EHR data
As proof the coverage has expired, because identifiers change whenever a plan renews

questions.explanation: A is correct: comparing an EHR field with the source document it was taken from is a basic data-validation technique, and an identifier that differs — even by transposition — is a discrepancy to flag and verify. B is wrong because identifiers match character for character; a transposed identifier points to a different value. C is wrong because the scanned card is exactly the source document coverage data are validated against. D is wrong because a character mismatch shows a recording conflict, not anything about the plan's effective dates.

questions.question: While the specialist is helping a patient navigate to a newly released result in the portal, the patient asks what the result means for their health and whether they should be worried. Analyzing where portal support ends, which response stays within the specialist's role?

answers.text: Reassure the patient that the value looks fine, so they do not leave the call anxious

Help the patient locate the result and show them how to send their question to the care team through portal messaging — or connect them with the care team directly — without interpreting the result themselves
Explain which range the value falls in and what that usually indicates for patients with this condition
Advise the patient to ignore the result until the next scheduled visit

questions.explanation: B is correct: the specialist's portal role is access and navigation — getting the patient to the result and to a working route for their clinical question — while interpreting what a result means belongs to the care team. A is wrong because reassurance about a value is an interpretation, even when kindly meant. C is wrong because explaining what a result indicates for a condition is clinical interpretation outside the EHR specialist's scope. D is wrong because telling a patient to disregard a result is clinical advice, and it also leaves their question unanswered rather than routed.

questions.question: Training records show every staff member completed the facility's safeguarding e-learning, yet when the EHR specialist asks staff to walk through the steps for reporting a suspected breach, most cannot describe them. Analyzing what this gap means and what to do next, which conclusion is best supported?

answers.text: Completion records show attendance, not competence, so the specialist should provide hands-on follow-up education on the reporting steps, verify staff can perform them, and share the gap with the compliance function
The completion records prove staff know the steps, so their answers in conversation can be disregarded
The e-learning should simply be assigned a second time, unchanged, until scores improve
Reporting steps are a compliance-only topic, so front-line staff no longer need education on them

questions.explanation: A is correct: finishing a module records participation, while the inability to describe the steps shows the skill was not learned, so targeted hands-on follow-up with verification, plus sharing the pattern with compliance, addresses both education and enforcement. B is wrong because a completion record cannot override direct evidence that staff cannot perform the task. C is wrong because repeating the identical delivery that failed to produce the skill is unlikely to close the gap. D is wrong because any workforce member may be the first to suspect a breach, so front-line staff must know how to report one.

questions.question: Months after a temporary data-cleanup project ended, a review shows a staff member still holds the elevated EHR editing access that was granted only for that project, although their regular duties need view and routine entry access only. Analyzing the access allocation, which conclusion is correct?

answers.text: The elevated access is excess privilege left over from a finished assignment and should be removed so the account matches the person's current role, with periodic access reviews used to catch this pattern
The elevated access should remain, because removing it later might inconvenience the staff member
Every staff member should receive the same elevated access, so this account is no longer unusual
The finding requires no action, because access granted once never needs to be revisited

questions.explanation: A is correct: access must track the current role, so project-only elevation that outlives the project is excess privilege, and removing it plus reviewing access periodically restores least-privilege allocation. B is wrong because convenience does not justify retaining privileges a role does not need, and the excess widens the impact of any misuse or compromise. C is wrong because elevating everyone multiplies the excess instead of correcting one account. D is wrong because role changes and ended assignments are precisely why access allocations must be revisited.

questions.question: Reviewing a physical-examination template, the specialist finds that most examination elements arrive pre-filled as normal, and clinicians often sign without changing them, including for patients whose findings were not normal. Analyzing this design risk, what should the specialist recommend?

answers.text: Keep the pre-filled values because they make signing faster for busy clinicians
Pre-fill abnormal values instead so clinicians have to change them to normal
Remove the automatic normal defaults so each element is actively selected for that patient, making the signed note reflect what was actually examined and found
Lock the pre-filled values so they cannot be edited after the template opens

questions.explanation: C is correct: default values that present findings as already normal invite documentation of examinations that may not match the patient, so requiring an active selection makes the record reflect the clinician's actual findings. A is wrong because speed does not justify a design that produces inaccurate examination records. B is wrong because pre-filling abnormal findings creates the same inaccuracy in the opposite direction. D is wrong because locking unverified defaults makes the inaccurate documentation impossible to correct at the point of entry.

cbcs.quiz_title: CBCS Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam

questions.question: Regarding the federal False Claims Act, which conduct does the law primarily target?

answers.text: A payer delaying payment on a clean claim beyond its contract terms
Knowingly submitting, or causing the submission of, false or fraudulent claims for federal payment
A patient disputing a deductible amount shown on their statement
A coder selecting an unspecified code when documentation lacks detail

questions.explanation: B is correct because the False Claims Act imposes liability for knowingly presenting false or fraudulent claims to the federal government. A is wrong because slow payment by a payer is a contract or prompt-pay issue, not a false claim by the submitter. C is wrong because a patient's billing dispute is a routine revenue-cycle matter, not federal fraud liability. D is wrong because using an unspecified code when documentation is limited is a documentation and coding-accuracy issue, not by itself a knowingly false claim.

questions.question: Regarding precertification, precertification is best described as which of the following?

answers.text: The process of appealing a claim that has already been denied
The form that directs insurance payment to the provider
The notice given when Medicare will likely deny a specific service
An advance notification and approval process a payer may require before certain services to confirm that coverage requirements are met

questions.explanation: D is correct because precertification is obtained in advance for services a payer designates, confirming coverage requirements before care. A is wrong because an appeal happens after an adverse claim decision. B is wrong because directing payment to the provider describes Assignment of Benefits. C is wrong because that notice describes the Advance Beneficiary Notice.

questions.question: About the World Health Organization's role among the organizations behind the coding manuals, which statement correctly describes that role?

answers.text: WHO publishes and maintains the international classification of diseases on which the U.S. clinical modification used for diagnosis coding is based
WHO publishes the CPT procedure codes used on professional claims
WHO sets Medicare's coding requirements for U.S. providers
WHO maintains the HCPCS Level II codes for supplies and services

questions.explanation: A is correct: WHO is responsible for the international disease classification, and ICD-10-CM is the U.S. clinical modification built on it. B is wrong because CPT is published and maintained by the American Medical Association. C is wrong because Medicare coding requirements are set by CMS, not by an international body. D is wrong because CMS maintains HCPCS Level II.

questions.question: Claims for two different payers are built in the same electronic batch, and each claim must reach the payer whose coverage applies. Regarding the payer identification carried in the electronic transmission, what is its role?

answers.text: It replaces the subscriber identification on each claim in the batch
It converts a professional claim into an institutional claim during transmission
It guarantees that every claim in the batch will be paid without review
It routes each claim to the correct payer so claims in one batch are not delivered to the wrong plan

questions.explanation: D is correct because the payer identification in the transmission directs each claim to the intended payer for processing. A is wrong because payer identification does not replace the subscriber identification that identifies the covered person. C is wrong because routing information does not guarantee payment or remove payer review. B is wrong because the claim format is determined by the type of claim submitted, not changed by the payer identifier.

questions.question: Regarding electronic claim transactions for an institutional claim, which transaction does a hospital use to submit its facility claim electronically in the standard format?

answers.text: The 837I transaction, the institutional electronic claim
The 835 transaction, because it carries claims to payers
The 837P transaction, because all electronic claims use the professional format
A scanned image of a paper form sent as an email attachment

questions.explanation: The 837I is the standard electronic institutional claim used for facility billing. Option B is wrong because the 835 is the electronic remittance advice coming back from the payer, not an outbound claim. Option C is wrong because the 837P is the professional claim format. Option D is wrong because an emailed scanned image is not a standard EDI claim transaction.

questions.question: A patient calls about a statement and insists that one listed service was never received, and they are frustrated. Regarding communicating with this patient stakeholder about a disputed charge, what should the billing and coding specialist do?

answers.text: Tell the patient to pay the full balance while the dispute is considered, so the account stays current.
Promise the patient that the charge will be removed, so the call ends on a positive note.
Transfer the patient to the clinical team and close the billing inquiry without documenting it.

Listen to the concern, explain that the charge will be researched against the documentation and the claim, document the dispute and the follow-up timeframe, and pause collection activity on the disputed amount following office policy.

questions.explanation: D is correct because clear stakeholder communication on a dispute combines hearing the patient out, explaining the review process and timeframe, documenting the conversation, and holding collection on the disputed amount per policy while the facts are checked. A is incorrect because demanding payment of an amount under active dispute, before any research, undermines the review the patient is owed. B is incorrect because the specialist cannot promise removal before the documentation and claim are examined. C is incorrect because abandoning the inquiry without documentation leaves the dispute untracked and unresolved.

questions.question: At check-in, a patient presents two active insurance cards and asks the specialist to bill the plan with the lower copay first, even though COB rules make the other plan primary. How should the specialist respond within their role?

answers.text: Determine and record the COB filing order under the applicable rules and file the primary plan first, explaining that the order is not set by copay preference
Bill the lower-copay plan first as requested, since patient satisfaction controls filing order
Bill both plans as primary and note the patient's preference on each claim
Decline to file any claim until the patient withdraws the request

questions.explanation: A is correct because filing order is determined by COB rules such as the dependent and birthday rules, not by which plan has a lower copay, and the specialist records both coverages and files in that order. B is wrong because patient preference does not override COB. C is wrong because a claim cannot accurately list two different plans as primary for the same person and service. D is wrong because the correct action is to file in proper order, not to withhold filing altogether.

questions.question: For place-of-service reporting, a patient with a minor illness is treated without an appointment inside a clinic located within a large retail store, staffed to treat walk-in patients for common, non-emergency conditions. Which place-of-service category fits this setting?

answers.text: Urgent Care Facility
Office
Walk-in Retail Health Clinic
Independent Clinic

questions.explanation: C is correct because a walk-in retail health clinic is the category for a health care facility located within a retail site that treats walk-in patients for common conditions. A is wrong because an urgent care facility is a freestanding setting equipped for prompt treatment of illnesses and injuries needing immediate care beyond a retail clinic's scope. B is wrong because an office is a provider's own practice location, not a clinic operated inside a retail store. D is wrong because the independent-clinic category describes an entity independent of a hospital or other facility, not the defining retail, walk-in character of this setting.

questions.question: Regarding CPT Category II codes, a practice appends an additional alphanumeric tracking code to a claim alongside the Category I service code because the provider documented a quality performance measure. Which statement best describes these Category II codes?

answers.text: They are supplemental tracking codes used to collect performance-measurement data; they are optional and do not by themselves report a billable service for payment
They are temporary codes assigned to emerging technologies while those technologies await a permanent code
They are five-digit service codes that replace the Category I code whenever a quality measure is met
They are supply codes used to report the materials consumed while the measured service was performed

questions.explanation: A is correct because Category II codes are supplemental, alphanumeric tracking codes that collect performance-measurement data and support quality reporting; they accompany the service code and are never a substitute for reporting the service itself. B is wrong because temporary codes for emerging technology describe Category III, not Category II. C is wrong because Category II codes do not replace the Category I code that reports the billable service. D is wrong because supplies and materials are generally reported with HCPCS Level II codes, not Category II tracking codes.

questions.question: Admitted principally for surgical treatment of a traumatic fracture from a fall, a patient with documented HIV disease has no HIV-related condition treated during the stay. Regarding principal-diagnosis selection for this admission, which conclusion follows the guidelines?

answers.text: The fracture is the principal diagnosis because it occasioned the admission, and the HIV disease is reported as an additional diagnosis
HIV disease must always be sequenced first whenever it appears anywhere in the record
The HIV disease should be omitted entirely because it is unrelated to the reason for admission
The fall itself should be sequenced as principal instead of the fracture it caused

questions.explanation: A is correct: HIV is sequenced first only when the admission is for an HIV-related condition; when a patient with HIV disease is admitted for an unrelated condition, that condition is principal and HIV is reported additionally. B is wrong because HIV has no blanket first position independent of the reason for the encounter. C is wrong because a documented coexisting condition that is part of the record is still reported as an additional diagnosis. D is wrong because external cause information supplements the injury code and does not replace the treated condition as principal.

questions.question: A denial notice is dated March 10, 2026, and the payer's instructions state that a reconsideration request must be received within 90 calendar days of the notice date. Regarding the appeal deadline for this denial, by what date must the payer receive the request?

answers.text: May 10, 2026, counting two calendar months as the limit
June 30, 2026, since appeal deadlines always fall at month-end
March 10, 2027, since appeal windows run a full year
June 8, 2026, which is 90 calendar days after March 10, 2026

questions.explanation: D is correct because counting 90 calendar days from March 10, 2026 lands on June 8, 2026, and the instructions require receipt by that date. A is wrong because it substitutes a two-month approximation for the stated 90 calendar days. B is wrong because nothing in the instructions moves deadlines to month-end. C is wrong because it invents a one-year window the payer never granted.

questions.question: Two remittances in successive weeks show an identical payment for the same service line, same date of service, and same patient, and review confirms the payer paid the line twice. Analyzing what correct payment is for this line, which statement is correct?

answers.text: Both payments are correct because the payer issued them, and the practice keeps the full amount
The duplicate payment should be billed to the patient as additional responsibility
Only one payment is correct for the line; the duplicate is an overpayment to handle through the payer's notification and refund process
The duplicate payment should be posted as a contractual adjustment so the account appears balanced

questions.explanation: C is correct because a service line is payable once; a second identical payment is an overpayment that must be identified and returned or disclosed through the payer's process, not retained. A is wrong because a payer's error in issuing payment does not make the extra amount correct payment for the line. B is wrong because the patient received one service and owes only their own cost share, not the payer's duplicate. D is wrong because a contractual adjustment represents an agreed reduction in charges, and mislabeling an overpayment hides money the practice must resolve.

questions.question: A clinic begins using a newly approved supply during procedures, and the clinical team documents its use, but no charge for the supply appears on any encounter because the charge-capture tools were never updated when the service was introduced. Regarding charge capture for a newly introduced service, what is the billing and coding specialist's best action?

answers.text: Escalate the missing charge so the charge master and encounter tools are updated, and identify the affected encounters for review before they are billed.
Substitute an unrelated existing supply charge with a similar price so each encounter shows a supply line.
Leave the charges off, because clinical documentation alone guarantees the payer will add payment for the supply.
Ask the clinical team to remove the supply from their documentation so the record matches the charges.

questions.explanation: A is correct because charge capture depends on the charge master and encounter tools reflecting current services; updating them and reviewing already-affected encounters restores the link between documentation, charges, and claims. B is incorrect because billing a different supply than the one documented misstates the encounter. C is incorrect because payers pay from submitted charges supported by documentation, not from documentation alone. D is incorrect because documentation must remain an accurate record of care; the charge tools, not the clinical record, are what need correction.

questions.question: A grandparent brings a child in for a visit and offers to sign all of the forms, but the child's parent is the insurance subscriber and no paperwork shows the grandparent as legal guardian or guarantor. Regarding registration documentation for this minor, what should the specialist collect?

answers.text: The parent-subscriber's insurance and contact information and the responsible party's guarantor information, obtaining the parent or legal guardian's signature on the Assignment of Benefits
Only the grandparent's signature, since the adult who brings the child is automatically the guarantor
The child's own signature on the Assignment of Benefits
No documentation until the child turns 18

questions.explanation: A is correct: registration needs the subscriber's coverage data and an identified responsible party, and assignment for a minor is executed by the parent or legal guardian — not assumed from whoever accompanies the child. B is wrong because bringing a child to a visit does not by itself make an adult the guarantor or guardian. C is wrong because a minor does not execute the assignment. D is wrong because documentation is collected at the encounter, not deferred for years.

questions.question: Two surgeons from different specialties work together as primary surgeons on one complex procedure, each performing a distinct portion of the same operation and each documenting their own work. The specialist is preparing each surgeon's claim for that procedure. Which modifier action reports this arrangement?

answers.text: Append modifier 62, co-surgeons, to the same procedure code on each surgeon's claim
Append the team-surgery modifier, because any operation with two surgeons is a team case
Append the assistant-surgeon modifier to both claims, because neither surgeon worked alone
Append the multiple-procedures modifier to the second surgeon's claim to show two lines exist

questions.explanation: A is correct because modifier 62 reports two surgeons acting together as primary surgeons, each performing a distinct part of one procedure and reporting the same code. B is wrong because team surgery describes a larger surgical team for a highly complex procedure, not two co-surgeons sharing one procedure. C is wrong because an assistant surgeon supports a primary surgeon rather than serving as a co-primary surgeon on a distinct portion. D is wrong because the multiple-procedures modifier addresses multiple procedures in a session, not the co-surgeon relationship.

questions.question: Regarding claim-form purposes for an imaging study, a radiologist personally interprets the study and documents the interpretation, while the imaging facility supplies the equipment, technologist, and supplies used to produce the images. Which pairing correctly matches each party's billing to its claim form?

answers.text: Both parties bill on the institutional form, because the study was produced inside a facility
The radiologist's professional interpretation is billed on the professional claim form, and the facility's technical resources are billed on the institutional claim form
Both parties bill on the professional claim form, because one study can appear on only one form type
The radiologist bills the facility's technical resources as well, because the interpretation completes the study

questions.explanation: B is correct: the professional claim form (CMS-1500) reports individual clinicians' professional services such as the radiologist's interpretation, while the institutional form (CMS-1450/UB-04) reports the facility's technical resources — equipment, technologist, and supplies. A is wrong because a clinician's professional interpretation is not a facility service and does not belong on the institutional form. C is wrong because the professional and technical components of one study are routinely billed by different parties on their respective forms. D is wrong because the interpreting clinician bills only their own professional work, not resources the facility furnished.

questions.question: Laboratory results for an encounter are documented and resulted in the record, but an interface failure kept the laboratory charges from crossing into the billing queue, and the failure appears on the interface exception report. Regarding capturing those charges, how should the billing and coding specialist proceed?

answers.text: Work the exception report, enter the documented laboratory charges once from the report, and confirm they appear a single time in the queue before the claim is created
Assume the charges crossed over anyway and create the claim without checking the queue
Enter the charges twice, once for the result and once for the report, to make up for the failure
Leave the charges uncaptured, because interface failures are the laboratory's financial responsibility

questions.explanation: A is correct: exception reports exist to surface charges an interface dropped, and the specialist recovers the documented charges from the report, entering them once and verifying the queue before claim creation. B is wrong because the exception report is evidence the charges did not cross. C is wrong because one documented service is captured once; duplicating it creates an overcharge. D is wrong because documented, performed services remain the practice's charges to capture regardless of which system failed.

questions.question: Eligibility verification returns the patient as active, but under a plan administrator name the practice has never seen, and the card on file names the employer's plan with a different administrator from a prior year. A claim sent to the old administrator would be misdirected. Regarding this discrepancy, what should the billing and coding specialist do?

answers.text: Keep billing the old administrator, because the card on file is the official record
Treat the coverage as inactive because the administrator name is unfamiliar
Update the account's payer information to the administrator the current verification identifies, document the change and its source, so claims are directed to the entity now administering the plan
Send duplicate claims to both administrators to be safe

questions.explanation: C is correct: employer plans change administrators, and the current verification response identifies who now administers the coverage; updating and documenting the payer of record routes claims correctly. A is wrong because the outdated card reflects the prior administrator, and claims sent there will not reach the current payer. B is wrong because the response shows active coverage; an unfamiliar administrator name is a routing update, not a termination. D is wrong because duplicate claims to two administrators create duplicate-billing problems instead of resolving routing.

questions.question: Reviewing an anesthesia record, the specialist finds the anesthesia time and the procedure supported are documented, but the patient's physical status is nowhere stated, although the chart lists several significant conditions. A colleague suggests inferring the physical status from those conditions. Which analysis is correct?

answers.text: Infer the most severe status the listed conditions could support, to be safe
Assign the status of a healthy patient, because nothing more specific is stated
Ask the patient to describe how healthy they felt before the procedure
Query the anesthesia provider to document the physical status, because that clinical descriptor is the provider's determination and is not the specialist's to infer from diagnoses

questions.explanation: D is correct: physical status is a clinical determination made and documented by the anesthesia provider, so the specialist obtains it by query rather than deriving it. A is wrong because inferring the most severe status fabricates a clinical judgment and could overstate the record. B is wrong because defaulting to a healthy status contradicts the documented conditions just as surely as inferring severity would. C is wrong because a patient's self-impression is not the anesthesia provider's documented determination.

questions.question: A claim for a January 28 service is denied with reason code CO-26, stated on the remittance as expenses incurred prior to coverage, and eligibility records show the patient's coverage under that plan began February 1. The intake file also documents a predecessor plan that covered the patient through January 31. Regarding resolution, what should the billing and coding specialist do first?

answers.text: Write the charges off, since the billed plan has denied them
Bill the patient directly without checking any other coverage
Appeal to the billed plan insisting a January service falls within February coverage
Verify the predecessor plan's coverage for the date of service and bill that plan, supplying the denial information if that plan requires it

questions.explanation: D is correct because the service predates the billed plan's coverage but falls inside the predecessor plan's documented coverage period, so verifying and billing that plan is the productive resolution. A is wrong because another payer appears responsible, so a write-off abandons a collectible claim. B is wrong because patient billing comes only after other coverage for the date is ruled out. C is wrong because the dates are documented and not in dispute; an appeal cannot move a coverage start date.

questions.question: What event most directly triggers the UM arbitration process?

answers.text: The policy reaches its first renewal date
The insured buys a replacement vehicle after the accident the insured was driving at the time of the accident, and buying that vehicle is what opens the arbitration the policy provides
The tortfeasor files a bankruptcy petition
The insured and insurer reach a disagreement on fault or on the amount recoverable and one side demands arbitration under the policy

questions.explanation: Arbitration is demand-driven, it begins when the parties cannot agree on the core UM questions and a party invokes the clause. Buying a replacement vehicle does not start an arbitration.

questions.question: Why must notice of a conditional renewal be given before expiration rather than after the new term begins?

answers.text: So the old policy can be cancelled mid-term without grounds as soon as the insurer decides it no longer wants the insured's business
So the insured has no choice but to accept
So the insurer can raise the premium twice in one term
So the named insured can evaluate the changed terms and arrange other coverage if the terms are unacceptable

questions.explanation: Advance notice preserves the insured's choice before being bound to new terms. It is not a device to force acceptance, which is the opposite of its purpose.

questions.question: Which statement about a small contractor's BOP eligibility is most accurate?

answers.text: Eligibility is based on the value of the largest single job the contractor performs
A contractor is eligible only if every job is completed inside its own shop
The BOP insures the contractor's unfinished projects at every jobsite as its main purpose
Eligibility centers on the contractor's office or shop premises and the scale of its operations, not on insuring large jobsite projects

questions.explanation: For artisan contractors, BOP eligibility is built around a modest office or shop premises and limited operations. The policy is not designed as builders risk for large unfinished projects, which is why the jobsite-purpose option is wrong.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes a multi-year policy?

answers.text: It is written for a single policy period longer than one year, such as three years
It is a series of one-day policies sold as a package
It has no expiration date and continues until a claim occurs
It must be rewritten every month to remain in force

questions.explanation: A multi-year term is one period extending beyond twelve months, with a stated expiration. It does have an expiration date, unlike the endless arrangement described in the strongest distractor.

questions.question: After giving an examination under oath, what may the insured be required to do with the transcript?

answers.text: File it with the police instead of the insurer
Destroy the transcript after thirty days
Rewrite any answers that sound unfavorable
Sign the sworn testimony, confirming it as the insured's statement

questions.explanation: The condition can require the insured to sign the examination testimony. The insured may not rewrite unfavorable answers or destroy the record.

questions.question: A tenant alleges disease from a leaking chemical line that seeped continuously across two policy periods. Which question is central at the definition level?

answers.text: Whether the tenant's attorney prefers one insurer over another
Which period's agent earned the largest commission
During which period or periods did the continuous or repeated exposure to the harmful conditions take place
Whether the chemical line was listed as scheduled equipment

questions.explanation: For continuous exposure, identifying when the exposure occurred drives the policy-period analysis. Commission and scheduling details do not answer the definitional timing question.

questions.question: A general contractor's audit adds premium for an uninsured electrical subcontractor. The contractor objects that it never employed the electricians. Why does the charge stand?

answers.text: Because electrical work is always charged at double the manual rate
Because the contractor signed the subcontract, which transfers all payroll to it for tax purposes, including in cases where the policy was renewed on substantially the same terms for a later period
Because premium follows the benefit exposure the contractor's policy can be called on to pay for uninsured subs' workers, not only the contractor's own hiring
Because the auditor is allowed to add any payroll found on a job site

questions.explanation: The charge rests on exposure: the contractor can be responsible for benefits owed to an uninsured sub's injured workers, so that payroll belongs in its premium base. It is not an arbitrary job-site surcharge or a tax rule.

questions.question: When other insurance applies to a loss to an owned covered auto on the same basis as the Personal Auto Policy, how does the policy pay?

answers.text: It pays nothing until the other policy's limit is exhausted
It pays a share based on the number of vehicles each policy insures
It pays the entire loss and collects from the other insurer later
It pays only its share, in the proportion its limit of liability bears to the total of all applicable limits

questions.explanation: For an owned auto, the other insurance condition shares the loss pro rata by limits, in the proportion this policy's limit bears to the total of all applicable limits. Paying nothing until the other limit is exhausted describes excess coverage, not pro rata sharing.

questions.question: A storage warehouse holds customers' insured goods. What does the no benefit to bailee clause tell the warehouse about relying on customers' policies?

answers.text: It is fully protected as long as one customer carries insurance
It only needs coverage if it stores goods for more than a year
It is protected whenever it charges a storage fee
It cannot rely on them for its own protection and needs its own coverage for its liability and exposures

questions.explanation: Customers' policies insure the customers' interests, not the warehouse's, so the warehouse must arrange its own protection. Charging a fee does not convert a customer's policy into the bailee's coverage.

questions.question: A mutual insurer builds up a large surplus over many profitable years. To whom does that surplus ultimately belong?

answers.text: The individual stockholders, in proportion to their shares
The policyholders collectively, as the company's owners
The officers who managed the company during those years
The producers who sold the policies that produced it

questions.explanation: Surplus of a mutual insurer is held for its policyholder owners as a group. There are no stockholders with a proportional claim to it.

questions.question: A base form says one thing about a coverage point and an attached endorsement says the opposite on the same point. Which wording controls?

answers.text: The base form, because it was printed before the endorsement
The wording printed in the larger typeface on the page
The endorsement, because the specific change the parties attached prevails over the base form it modifies
The wording the insurer's home office prefers after a loss

questions.explanation: When an endorsement and the form it modifies truly conflict, the endorsement controls on that point — that is the purpose of attaching it. Print order and typeface size do not decide conflicts.

questions.question: A foreign insurer prefers to keep its deposit in its home state rather than deposit in Arizona. What must the director accept in place of the Arizona deposit?

answers.text: The current certificate of the supervising public official of another state showing a like deposit is maintained in public custody there in trust, in part to protect Arizona policyholders
A letter from the insurer's chief executive promising equivalent protection, without regard to the surrounding circumstances, in every case
A deposit held by the insurer's own statutory agent, with no qualification of any kind, regardless of the particular facts involved
Nothing, because out-of-state deposits are never accepted, in all circumstances covered by the rule, at every stage of the process involved

questions.explanation: For foreign insurers the director shall accept, in lieu of an Arizona deposit or part of one, the current certificate of another state's supervising official that a like deposit is maintained in public custody there in trust; a private promise or self-held deposit is not the statutory substitute.

questions.question: An insured and the UM insurer agree the other driver was uninsured but disagree about whether that driver ran a red light and caused the injuries. Which UM mechanism is designed for this dispute?

answers.text: Arbitration of fault under the UM coverage
An appraisal of the vehicle's salvage value only
Premium audit
A certificate of insurance review

questions.explanation: Fault is one of the two classic UM arbitration questions when liability is disputed. A premium audit addresses payroll or exposure, not who caused an accident.

questions.question: An additional insured is sued over an accident that the named insured's work helped cause, even though the additional insured did not personally perform that work. What kind of protection is the endorsement principally giving the additional insured?

answers.text: Protection for liability imposed on it because of the named insured's work, rather than coverage for its own independent operations
Full coverage for every operation the additional insured performs on its own, under the provision at issue, as it is written in the current policy form
A separate liability policy issued in the additional insured's own name
Protection only for damage to the additional insured's own property

questions.explanation: The endorsement principally protects the additional insured against liability arising from the named insured's work. It is not standalone coverage for the additional insured's own independent operations.

questions.question: A museum's fine arts coverage must protect a rotating collection in which individual pieces change frequently, making item-by-item scheduling impractical. Which structure fits that exposure?

answers.text: A schedule that must list every temporary piece before it enters the building or nothing is covered
Hull coverage on the museum building itself
A policy covering only pieces the museum has owned for ten years or more
Blanket fine arts coverage on the collection as a whole, subject to an overall limit

questions.explanation: Blanket coverage insures a changing collection under one overall limit when scheduling each piece is impractical. Requiring advance scheduling of every rotating piece would leave gaps the blanket structure is meant to avoid.

questions.question: An insurer pays a shopping center owner for damage negligently caused by a roofing contractor who is not insured under the owner's policy and has no connection to it. Is subrogation available here?

answers.text: Yes, because the contractor is a third party, not an insured under the paying policy
Yes, but only if the contractor also owns part of the center
No, because subrogation requires the wrongdoer to be an insured
No, because the contractor was working on the insured property

questions.explanation: The bar on subrogation protects only persons insured under the paying policy; an unrelated negligent contractor is a classic subrogation target. Working on the property does not by itself make the contractor an insured.

questions.question: An insurer adopts two successive no-cost broadenings of the same property form provision during one policy term, with the second broadening wider than the first. A loss occurs after the second adoption. Which version governs that provision?

answers.text: The original provision, because only one revision may ever apply
An average of the first and second revisions
The second, broader revision, because it is the insurer's current adopted broadening for that provision
The first revision, because later revisions need separate approval

questions.explanation: Each qualifying adoption updates the coverage, so the loss is judged under the most recent broadening in effect on the loss date. There is no rule limiting liberalization to one revision per term.

questions.question: A manufacturer's overseas plant is destroyed when a foreign government's military force seizes and shells the region during an armed conflict, and the manufacturer seeks recovery for third-party property damage claims under its general liability policy. Which exclusion is most directly implicated?

answers.text: The war exclusion
The recall exclusion
The damage to your product exclusion
The impaired property exclusion

questions.explanation: The war exclusion addresses bodily injury and property damage arising from war and warlike action by a military force. A product defect, recall, or impaired property is not described in these facts.

questions.question: A tenant's build-out was finished months ago and the space is open for business. A customer is injured because of how the contractor installed a fixture during that finished work, and the property owner is sued as an additional insured. Which edition focus is designed for this claim?

answers.text: The edition written for completed operations, because the injury arises from work that was completed and put to its intended use
The edition written for ongoing operations, because the fixture is still physically present in the space
The edition written for ongoing operations, because the owner still operates a business there
Neither edition, because additional insured coverage ends when a project opens

questions.explanation: Completed operations additional insured coverage is designed for liability arising from finished work after it is put to its intended use. Ongoing operations coverage does not become completed operations coverage merely because the work product remains in place.

questions.question: An applicant answers every question truthfully out loud, the insurer's agent records one answer incorrectly, and the applicant signs the completed form without catching the agent's error. After a loss the insurer alleges misrepresentation. Which fact most strengthens the insured's position?

answers.text: The agent was licensed, which guarantees the insurer must pay every claim
The truth was actually disclosed to the insurer's own agent, whose recording error and knowledge may be attributed to the insurer
The loss was covered, so application answers no longer matter
The applicant signed the form, which always ends any inquiry into what was said to the agent when the application was completed, regardless of what the agent actually knew when recording it

questions.explanation: When an agent acting for the insurer hears the truth and records it wrong, courts often charge the insurer with the agent's knowledge rather than treating the applicant as the deceiver. The signature matters, but it does not erase the disclosure-to-the-agent issue.

questions.question: What is the key distinction between negligence and an intentional tort?

answers.text: Negligence involves an unreasonable risk of harm without intent to cause it; an intentional tort involves acting with intent as to the contact or consequence

Negligence always involves more serious injuries than intentional torts in every case, and a plaintiff in a negligence action must always prove a more serious injury than a plaintiff in an intentional tort case
Intentional torts never require proof of any resulting harm of any kind
Negligence requires a written contract between the parties

questions.explanation: The dividing line is the actor's state of mind: negligence is careless risk creation, while intentional torts turn on intent regarding the act's consequence. Severity of injury and contracts do not draw that line.

questions.question: Which of the following is true regarding controlling producer must render accounts in Ohio?

answers.text: Accounts rendered that detail material transactions and support commissions and charges
Commission support is the producer's private business
Year-end summaries replace transaction detail
Accounts are rendered only on the insurer's demand after a loss

questions.explanation: Money follows information: the producer's accounts must expose every material transaction and justify every dollar of commission.

questions.question: How does an exclusion differ from a condition in the work each does inside a policy?

answers.text: An exclusion defines risks the insurer has not assumed, while a condition sets a requirement that governs the parties' rights
An exclusion sets requirements, while a condition removes perils
Both provisions do the same work and differ only in placement
A condition removes coverage permanently, while an exclusion is temporary and lasts only until the insurer chooses to reinstate the coverage
