Evaporating, condensing, then desuperheating
Desuperheating, condensing, then subcooling
Condensing, evaporating, then subcooling

questions.explanation: Discharge vapor first loses sensible heat in desuperheating, then condenses at its saturation temperature, then the liquid is subcooled below saturation. Option A reverses the first two steps, option B wrongly includes evaporation, which occurs in the evaporator, and option D starts with condensing even though superheated gas must be desuperheated first.

georgia-hvac.quiz_title: Georgia HVAC Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam

questions.question: What moving parts define how a scroll compressor compresses refrigerant?

answers.text: Both scrolls rotate together on two separate crankshafts at different speeds while a set of reed valves opens and closes at the discharge port
A single piston slides back and forth inside a cylinder while suction and discharge reed valves time each stroke of the compression cycle
One scroll orbits inside a fixed scroll
Two intermeshing rotors turn inside a figure-eight housing and trap a fixed volume of gas between the rotor lobes on every revolution

questions.explanation: In a scroll, one orbiting scroll traps and squeezes gas against a fixed scroll in continuous pockets with no reed valves. Two counter-rotating scrolls on separate shafts do not describe scroll operation, the piston-and-reed description fits a reciprocating compressor, and intermeshing lobes in a figure-eight housing describe a rotary blower or screw-type machine, not a scroll.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a service disconnect located within sight of an air-conditioning unit?

answers.text: To regulate refrigerant pressure during service
To let a servicing technician shut off and control power to the equipment while working on it
To serve as the unit's normal everyday on-off control in place of the thermostat, cycling the equipment on and off to maintain the indoor temperature
To increase the available voltage at the unit

questions.explanation: A nearby disconnect gives the technician a local means to isolate and control the power source during service. It has no role in refrigerant regulation. It is not a substitute thermostat for daily operation, and a disconnect cannot raise supply voltage.

questions.question: A new refrigerant line set is to be pressure tested for leaks before evacuation. Which medium and practice are correct?

answers.text: Use oxygen from a cutting torch tank
Use compressed shop air without a regulator
Use dry nitrogen with a regulator, test at the specified pressure, and use an electronic detector or bubbles to check joints
Pressurize with refrigerant alone to maximum pressure

questions.explanation: Regulated dry nitrogen is inert and standard for pressure testing, with joints checked by detector or bubble solution, so C is correct. Oxygen can cause explosive combustion with oil, unregulated shop air adds moisture and uncontrolled pressure, and refrigerant alone is not the proper test medium.

questions.question: A manufactured-home furnace needs replacement. A standard residential furnace of the same capacity is available on the truck. What must be verified before using it?

answers.text: Whether the furnace is listed and approved for manufactured-home installation, including its combustion-air and venting arrangement for that application
Whether the furnace color matches the compartment finish, because unlisted finishes are the usual reason manufactured-home installations are rejected
Whether the furnace was built in the same state as the home, because origin determines approval for manufactured housing installations nationally
Whether the furnace has a larger blower than the original, because any furnace with a larger blower is automatically acceptable in a closet install

questions.explanation: Manufactured homes require furnaces listed for that use, with the correct sealed combustion-air and venting approach for a tight closet installation. Finish color and state of origin do not establish approval, and a larger blower alone does not make an unlisted furnace acceptable.

questions.question: A technician must adjust TXV superheat on a stable, fully loaded system. Which procedure is correct?

answers.text: Turn the stem several full turns at once and read the superheat immediately, because a TXV reaches its new equilibrium within a few seconds of any adjustment
Measure the superheat at the compressor inlet after a long suction line, because pressure drop and heat gain along that line have no effect on the reading obtained
Adjust the valve while the system is pumped down and off, counting stem turns from fully closed, because superheat cannot be set under actual operating load conditions
Measure superheat at the bulb location, turn the stem in small increments, and allow the system to stabilize between adjustments

questions.explanation: Superheat is set at the evaporator outlet where the bulb sits, in small steps with stabilization time, under steady load. Large instant adjustments overshoot a slow-responding system, a compressor-inlet reading includes line pressure drop and heat gain and misrepresents evaporator superheat, and a valve cannot be meaningfully set while the system is off and pumped down.

questions.question: Refrigerant that has been reclaimed differs from refrigerant that has merely been recovered or recycled because reclaimed refrigerant:

answers.text: Is simply removed from a system and stored in a recovery cylinder

Is cleaned on site, typically with filtration and oil separation, for reuse only in the same owner's equipment, without any laboratory analysis or verification that it meets virgin-product purity specifications for general resale
Has been reprocessed off site and verified by chemical analysis to meet virgin-product purity specifications, so it can be used in any owner's equipment
Is destroyed by high-temperature incineration

questions.explanation: Reclaim means reprocessing to virgin purity specifications with verified analysis, which is a higher standard than recovery or on-site recycling. Option A is the definition of recovery, option B is the definition of recycling, and option D describes destruction, not reclaim.

questions.question: A designer specifies external insulation on a metal supply duct crossing a hot attic instead of an internally lined duct. Which pairing of benefits and cautions is correct?

answers.text: External insulation raises airflow velocity so the duct can be downsized one full size
External insulation leaves the full duct area open to airflow and keeps fibers out of the airstream, but its outer jacket must be sealed as a vapor barrier and protected where it can be damaged
External insulation needs no vapor barrier because attic air is always dry

Internal lining and external insulation perform identically in every respect, so the choice is purely cosmetic, with the same effect on duct free area, airstream cleanliness, vapor control, and long-term maintenance access whichever side of the metal the insulation is placed on

questions.explanation: Wrapping the outside preserves the duct's internal dimensions and air quality while moving the vapor-control duty to the jacket, which must then be sealed and kept intact. Option A is wrong because insulation location does not change the velocity for a given duct size and airflow enough to justify downsizing; option C is wrong because attic air in humid weather can carry heavy moisture loads, which is exactly why the jacket must be sealed; option D is wrong because lining reduces the duct's free area and puts a fiber surface in the airstream — real differences, not cosmetic ones.

questions.question: A customer expects a UV-C lamp in the supply plenum to remove cooking odors, carbon monoxide, and dust from the house air. What is the accurate correction?

answers.text: UV-C inactivates microbes on irradiated surfaces and in the airstream within its limits; it does not remove particles, gases, odors, or carbon monoxide.
UV-C does remove odors and gases, so the customer's expectation is correct and no filtration or source control is needed in the home
UV-C replaces the air filter entirely, because irradiated dust is rendered harmless and may accumulate on the coil without consequence
UV-C generates fresh oxygen that neutralizes carbon monoxide in the duct, making a separate carbon monoxide alarm unnecessary

questions.explanation: UV-C is a disinfection technology with line-of-sight and dose limits, not a filter or gas remover. Odors and gases need ventilation and source control, filters are still required for particles and coil protection, and UV-C has no effect that substitutes for a carbon monoxide alarm.

questions.question: A customer asks the technician to 'just keep adding R-22' to a leaking system instead of replacing it. Which fact most changes that conversation?

answers.text: R-22 is still manufactured domestically in unlimited quantities, so its price is expected to fall steadily every year
Virgin R-22 production and import ended in the United States, so supply is reclaimed stock at rising and uncertain cost
Adding refrigerant to a leaking system is prohibited in all cases, including small appliances with no leak-repair options
R-22 can be freely mixed with newer refrigerants in the same system to stretch the remaining supply at lower cost

questions.explanation: New R-22 supply ended, leaving reclaimed material whose price and availability drive replacement economics. It is not still produced without limit, leak and service rules are more nuanced than a blanket ban on charging, and refrigerants must never be mixed in a system.

questions.question: Before a subcontractor starts work, why does a contractor typically collect a current certificate of insurance?

answers.text: To verify the subcontractor carries the coverage the subcontract requires
To transfer the contractor's own license obligations to the subcontractor for every project currently under contract
To guarantee the subcontractor's work will need no inspection, because insured work is exempt from code review
To set the subcontractor's labor rates for the project, since insurance certificates include a schedule of wage charges

questions.explanation: A is correct because the certificate provides evidence the subcontractor carries the insurance the subcontract requires before work begins. B is incorrect because an insurance certificate does not transfer licensing duties between businesses. C is incorrect because insured work remains subject to inspection and code requirements. D is incorrect because certificates evidence coverage limits and dates, not labor pricing.

questions.question: During a Georgia furnace installation, a Type B gas vent is roughed through a framed chase and the installer can slip only a fingertip — well under an inch — between the vent and a wood stud. The inspector has not yet been called. What should happen?

answers.text: Leave it, because Type B vent is double-wall and its outer skin stays cool enough that contact with framing is permitted anywhere along the run
Wrap the stud in gypsum board where it passes, because surface protection of the wood substitutes for the vent's listed air-space clearance
Rework the run so the vent's listed clearance to combustibles — 1 inch for Type B gas vent — is maintained for the full length
Leave it until inspection and let the inspector decide, because clearance corrections made before inspection are treated as unpermitted alterations

questions.explanation: C is correct: Type B gas vent is listed with a 1-inch minimum clearance to combustibles, and that air space is integral to its temperature performance; the run is corrected during installation, not deferred. A is wrong because double-wall construction reduces, but does not eliminate, the required clearance. B is wrong because covering the combustible does not create the listed air space. D is wrong because installers are responsible for code-compliant work before inspection; inspection verifies the work, it does not design it.

questions.question: A larger replacement furnace is set on the existing small duct system. Static pressure is very high and rise is excessive. What principle did the install violate?

answers.text: A furnace may be matched to any existing ductwork as long as the gas pipe and vent are sized correctly for the new input rating
Duct capacity increases automatically when a stronger blower is installed, because higher pressure forces proportionally more air through
Temperature rise does not need checking when equipment is replaced, because the factory blower setting fits every duct system made
Replacement equipment must be verified against duct capacity

questions.explanation: The replacement must be checked against what the existing ducts can actually deliver; a bigger furnace and blower on undersized ducts produce high static, high rise, noise, and limit problems. Option A ignores airflow compatibility, option B ignores that friction rises steeply and delivered air falls short, and option C skips a required commissioning verification.

questions.question: A system has correct refrigerant readings for its metering type but a temperature split of only 11°F across the evaporator on a humid day with a heavy latent load confirmed normal. Static pressure is low and the blower is set one tap higher than specified for the installed coil. Which explanation best fits a persistently low sensible split after the latent load is accounted for?

answers.text: Excessive airflow moving air across the coil too fast for full sensible heat exchange per cubic foot
A refrigerant undercharge, which always lowers the temperature split first, before any other measurement is taken on the system
A clogged condensate drain raising the coil temperature
A TXV sensing bulb that has completely lost its charge

questions.explanation: Too much airflow reduces the temperature change of each unit of air passing over the coil, shrinking the measured split even when the refrigeration circuit is healthy. Option B is contradicted by the correct refrigerant readings given in the scenario. Option C affects drainage, not the air temperature change across the coil, and option D would starve the evaporator and disturb the superheat readings, which are stated to be correct.

questions.question: A long suction run was undersized, creating a large suction pressure drop between evaporator and compressor. Even if evaporator temperature looks right, system capacity and efficiency suffer because:

answers.text: The compressor must work against a higher compression ratio from its lower inlet pressure, moving less refrigerant per revolution

The condenser receives more heat than it was designed for from the pipe itself, because the long, undersized suction run absorbs enough mechanical-room heat along its length to overload the outdoor condensing coil at the roof
The expansion valve gains pressure difference and overfeeds
Oil viscosity increases in the warmer evaporator

questions.explanation: Pressure drop lowers the density and pressure of vapor actually entering the compressor, raising its compression ratio and cutting mass flow and efficiency. Option B blames pipe heat that is not the mechanism, option C is wrong because suction drop does not add feed pressure at the valve, and option D misstates both where the oil problem arises and its cause.

questions.question: A compressor has suffered repeated slugging and oil foaming at start-up after long off cycles in a cool machine room. The crankcase is cold to the touch at start, oil level foams violently in the sight glass, the crankcase heater measures open circuit, and pressures and charge are normal during running. What is the most likely cause?

answers.text: A TXV stuck open, which floods during running and would collapse superheat while the system operates, which is not observed here
A failed crankcase heater
Low machine-room temperature alone, which systems tolerate routinely when the crankcase heater is working to keep refrigerant out of the oil
An overcharge flooding the compressor continuously, which would show abnormal running pressures and floodback during operation, not only at start-up

questions.explanation: Refrigerant migrating to a cold crankcase during off cycles and boiling out of the oil at start-up — with an open-circuit heater proven — explains start-only slugging and foaming. Overcharge and a stuck-open TXV flood during running and distort operating readings, and cool rooms are normal service when the heater works.

questions.question: A Georgia installer must run underground gas piping below grade through a building's foundation wall. A coworker cites the base code's heading and says such penetrations are prohibited outright. What does Georgia actually require?

answers.text: Georgia replaces the base-code prohibition: underground piping through the foundation or basement wall must be encased in a protective pipe sleeve, and the annular space between the gas piping and the sleeve must be sealed

Georgia keeps the outright prohibition and adds that sleeved penetrations are allowed only through an above-grade portion of the foundation wall, never below grade, and sleeved penetrations remain limited to walls that are not part of a rated fire assembly
Georgia allows the penetration with no sleeve or sealing at all, provided the piping material itself is approved for direct underground burial elsewhere on the job
Georgia allows the penetration only where the pipe is wrapped in coal-tar coating and the wall opening is packed with mortar instead of a sleeve and sealant

questions.explanation: Georgia substitutes the base code's 'underground penetrations prohibited' section: below-grade piping through a foundation or basement wall must be encased in a protective pipe sleeve with the annular space between pipe and sleeve sealed. B keeps the prohibition Georgia replaced, C drops both the sleeve and the seal, and D substitutes coating and mortar for the required sleeve-and-seal detail.

questions.question: A gas furnace lights reliably but shuts down 3 to 5 seconds after ignition on every cycle. Manifold pressure and flame appearance are normal. Cleaning the flame sensor restores operation. The fault was:

answers.text: Low inducer draft on the pressure switch
Oxide coating on the flame rod reducing flame-rectification current below the control's minimum, so proven flame was lost
A condensate trap losing its prime during the off cycle, allowing air to be drawn through the drain line so the pressure switch drops out before the next ignition attempt begins
Excessive flame current shorting the igniter

questions.explanation: Shutdown seconds after a good light-off is the classic weak flame-signal pattern: an insulated, oxidized rod passes too little microamp current and the board closes the gas valve. Option A would prevent ignition from being attempted at all. Option C causes draft-proving trips before ignition. Option D reverses the problem, because the failure is too little, not too much, flame current.

questions.question: A propane furnace has a nameplate input of 183,000 Btu per hour. At about 91,500 Btu per gallon, about how much propane does it burn at full input?

answers.text: About 0.5 gallon per hour, because dividing the input by four times the heat content of a gallon is the shortcut used for full-fire estimates
About 1.0 gallon per hour, because each gallon is assumed to supply the entire 183,000 Btu input regardless of its actual rated heat content
About 4.0 gallons per hour, because the input in thousands is divided by the number of burners rather than by the heat content per gallon
About 2.0 gallons per hour

questions.explanation: Dividing 183,000 Btu per hour by 91,500 Btu per gallon gives about 2.0 gallons per hour. The other answers do not perform that division with the stated heat content, and burner count does not change the total fuel rate implied by the nameplate input.

questions.question: A completed system delivers only 950 CFM against a 1,200 CFM design. Static readings show the duct system itself is within its budget, but total external static is well above the blower's rating point because the installed wet coil and filter drops are much higher than the values used in design. What went wrong at the design stage?

answers.text: The ducts shrank after installation, which raised the total static
The blower lost capacity because the thermostat was set to cooling
Nothing went wrong; blowers deliver design CFM at any external static

The static budget was built on optimistic component values instead of the actual selected coil's wet-coil drop and the real filter drop at design airflow, so the blower was asked to work beyond the point where it can deliver design CFM

questions.explanation: A blower delivers its rated airflow only up to its rated external static; if real component drops push the total past that point, airflow falls — and the budget is only as honest as the component data in it. Option A is wrong because installed sheet metal does not shrink; the discrepancy was in the design inputs, not the duct dimensions; option B is wrong because thermostat mode does not change a blower's pressure capability; option C is wrong because blower tables show airflow falling as static rises beyond the rating point — that relationship is the whole basis of the budget.

questions.question: A Georgia gas design uses the longest-length method. The longest run from the meter to the farthest appliance is 82 ft, so the sizing table's 90-ft row governs. That row lists capacities of 88,000 Btu/h for 1/2-inch pipe, 197,000 Btu/h for 3/4-inch, and 360,000 Btu/h for 1-inch. One piping section carries a total load of 162,000 Btu/h. What size must that section be?

answers.text: 1/2 inch, because the section's load is below the capacity the 80-ft row would have shown for that pipe size
1 inch, because every section of a system designed by the longest-length method is sized one step above its calculated need

1/2 inch, because the longest-length method sizes each section only by the single largest appliance connected downstream of it, which is the same shortcut used when a section serves only one large appliance at the end of the run
3/4 inch, because the section must be sized from the governing 90-ft row, and 3/4-inch pipe at 197,000 Btu/h is the smallest listed size that covers the 162,000 Btu/h section load

questions.explanation: D is correct: the longest-length method uses the table length equal to or longer than the longest run - the 90-ft row for an 82-ft run - and each section is sized for the total load it carries. At that row, 1/2-inch carries only 88,000 Btu/h, while 3/4-inch carries 197,000, which covers the 162,000 Btu/h section load. A uses a shorter row the method does not permit. B adds an arbitrary one-size margin. C sizes by a single appliance instead of the section's total carried load.

maryland-hvac.quiz_title: Maryland HVAC Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam

questions.question: What does the float inside a typical discharge-line oil separator do when collected oil reaches its level?

answers.text: It closes the discharge line to the condenser so gas pressure builds in the separator shell and forces the collected oil out through the suction line
It opens a return line so oil flows back to the compressor crankcase
It energizes the crankcase heater so the returned oil is warmed before it is allowed to re-enter the compressor through the suction service valve
It opens a drain to a waste oil container so separated oil is removed from the refrigeration system permanently after each operating cycle

questions.explanation: The separator float rises with collected oil and ports it back to the crankcase, where it is reused. It does not block the main discharge flow to the condenser, it does not control the crankcase heater, and separated oil is returned for reuse rather than drained away as waste.

questions.question: A single-phase compressor nameplate lists RLA and LRA. The locked-rotor value describes current drawn when:

answers.text: The rotor is held stationary while full rated voltage is applied
The motor runs unloaded with the suction service valve closed and the discharge valve open to the condenser
The run capacitor has failed open during normal operation
The compressor pumps down against a closed liquid solenoid

questions.explanation: Locked-rotor amps is the current drawn with the rotor unable to turn at rated voltage; it is several times the running value and explains the voltage dip and protection demands at startup.

questions.question: A large refrigerant leak into a small, closed mechanical room is dangerous primarily because the vapor:

answers.text: Raises the room's oxygen concentration sharply
Displaces oxygen and can asphyxiate occupants
Turns instantly into a flammable liquid pool
Makes the room air strongly acidic on contact

questions.explanation: Refrigerant vapor is heavier than air and pools low, pushing oxygen out of the breathing zone, so ventilation and prompt evacuation protect occupants.

questions.question: How is the nine-member State Board of HVACR Contractors composed?

answers.text: Five master HVACR contractors, two master electricians, one master plumber, and one consumer member
Five master HVACR contractors, one master electrician, one master plumber, and two consumer members
Four master HVACR contractors, one master electrician, one master plumber, and three consumer members
Six master HVACR contractors, one master electrician, one master plumber, and one consumer member

questions.explanation: The Board has nine members: five master HVACR contractors, one master electrician, one master plumber, and two consumer members. Members serve three-year terms, for no more than two consecutive terms.

questions.question: Which description best fits a Category I gas appliance?

answers.text: Positive vent pressure with flue gas temperature low enough to condense continuously inside a sealed plastic vent that drains back to the furnace
Negative vent pressure with flue gas temperature high enough to avoid sustained condensation in the vent
A sealed-combustion appliance that draws all combustion air through a pipe from outdoors
An unvented appliance that discharges products into the room

questions.explanation: Category I appliances operate with negative vent pressure and flue temperatures that avoid sustained condensation, which is option B. Positive pressure with condensing temperatures (A) describes Category IV, sealed combustion-air piping (C) may apply to several categories and is not the defining test, and unvented operation (D) is not Category I venting at all.

questions.question: What happens to refrigerant that a technician knowingly releases while disconnecting hoses beyond the small de minimis amount trapped in the hoses?

answers.text: It is permitted for A2L refrigerants specifically, because their mild flammability places them outside the federal prohibition on knowing venting
It counts as prohibited venting of a regulated refrigerant
It is permitted whenever the release happens outdoors, because outdoor air dilutes the refrigerant quickly enough to satisfy the handling rules
It is permitted if the technician recovers an equal weight later that day, because the rules track a daily net balance rather than individual releases

questions.explanation: A2L refrigerants are fully subject to the prohibition on knowingly venting regulated refrigerants during service. Mild flammability does not exempt them, outdoor dilution does not legalize a release, and there is no netting arrangement that offsets one release with later recovery.

questions.question: The same supply-to-return bypass on a zoned furnace causes repeated high-limit trips when one small zone calls for heat alone. What is the mechanism?

answers.text: The bypass returns room-temperature air that bypasses the heat exchanger entirely, so the limit trips because the blower cannot move enough air through the furnace cabinet
The bypass cools the discharge air below the furnace minimum, and the limit switch opens in response to cold air rather than to the heat built up in the exchanger
The bypass raises static pressure in the return drop, which spins the blower backward between cycles and overheats the heat exchanger during the next call
Already-heated supply air re-enters the return and passes over the exchanger again, pushing discharge temperature up to the limit

questions.explanation: In heating, bypassed supply air is already hot, and sending it back through the heat exchanger raises discharge temperature until the limit control intervenes. The bypassed air does pass through the furnace rather than around the exchanger, and the limit responds to excessive heat, not cold air or blower rotation.

questions.question: A high-MERV filter is installed in a residential air handler that was struggling with airflow, and static pressure climbs while comfort falls. What is the balanced guidance?

answers.text: Higher-efficiency filtration adds resistance, so the filter area, blower capability, and measured static pressure must be verified rather than assuming any high-MERV filter fits any system.
Static pressure always falls with a finer filter, so the reading must be a gauge error and the filter can remain without any further checks
The correct fix is to remove filtration entirely, because clean indoor air matters less than airflow in every residential application
A high-MERV filter cleans air only when it is dirty, so the system should be run until the filter loads up before static is measured again

questions.explanation: Filtration and airflow trade off: finer media need more area or blower capacity, verified by measurement. Finer filters raise, not lower, resistance, removing filtration sacrifices air quality unnecessarily, and a loading filter's resistance only grows with time.

questions.question: In general terms, an employer's duties under occupational safety rules include which of the following?

answers.text: Requiring employees to purchase all of their own protective equipment with no guidance about its proper use
Reporting only those injuries that result in a customer complaint, and keeping all other incidents unrecorded
Delegating all safety responsibility to the newest employee, because that person is closest to the daily hazards
Providing a workplace free of recognized hazards and training employees on hazards of their work

questions.explanation: D is correct because employers must address recognized hazards and train employees about the hazards and protections of their work. A is incorrect because the employer is responsible for providing required protective equipment and instruction. B is incorrect because injury reporting and recording duties do not depend on customer complaints. C is incorrect because safety responsibility rests with the employer and cannot be handed to the newest hire.

questions.question: Scaling a plan with a ruler gives one dimension, but the printed dimension string on that same duct run gives a different, larger figure. Which value should the fabricator use?

answers.text: The scaled ruler value, because measurements taken directly off the paper always override the designer's written dimensions on contract drawings
The average of the two values, because splitting the difference between a scaled measurement and a written dimension is standard fabrication practice
The printed dimension string governs over a scaled measurement
Neither value, because any disagreement between a scale and a dimension means the entire sheet must be discarded and the duct laid out by guesswork

questions.explanation: Written dimensions govern because prints can shrink, stretch, or be reproduced off scale. Scaled values are a check only, averaging invents a third wrong dimension, and a discrepancy calls for using the figure or asking for clarification rather than discarding the sheet.

questions.question: Why must insulation on a cold suction line have a continuous, sealed vapor retarder on its outer surface?

answers.text: To raise the line's pressure rating high enough for the standing pressure test done after installation
To keep the insulation bright enough to inspect for leaks
To reflect radiant heat from nearby hot-water piping runs
To stop water vapor from migrating in and condensing inside the insulation

questions.explanation: Room air vapor is driven toward the cold pipe; if it reaches a surface below the dew point it condenses inside the insulation, soaking it, destroying its insulating value, and corroding the pipe, so every joint and seam of the vapor retarder is sealed.

questions.question: An ECM blower does not run. Line power is present at the motor, but no control signal arrives at the motor connector. The correct conclusion is:

answers.text: Replace the motor and module as a set, because an ECM motor that has power but does not run is always internally failed regardless of its input signal
Do not condemn the motor; find why the control signal is missing
Replace the module only, because the module generates its own control signal internally and does not depend on a signal from the furnace control board
Install a PSC motor in its place without changing the controls, because an ECM motor and a PSC motor respond to the same inputs at the motor leads

questions.explanation: Do not condemn the motor; find why the control signal is missing. Power alone does not prove a motor failed, the module depends on the board signal, and a PSC motor is not a drop-in substitute for ECM control inputs.

questions.question: After a repair in which the system was opened and evacuated only briefly, a unit runs with head 472 psig, suction 146 psig, subcooling 23°F, superheat 12°F, discharge temperature 225°F, and poor cooling. The refrigerant charge was weighed in exactly to nameplate. What is the most likely cause?

answers.text: A TXV stuck closed, which would starve the evaporator and show low suction pressure with very high superheat instead of these values
A condenser fan running backwards after motor replacement, which would raise head pressure but was verified correct rotation and full airflow on this call
Noncondensables in the system
A simple overcharge, which is unlikely because the charge was weighed to nameplate and overcharge alone rarely drives discharge temperature this high

questions.explanation: Very high head pressure and subcooling with a weighed-in charge and a history of a rushed evacuation point to air trapped in the condenser, where it adds its partial pressure and blankets condensing surface. Overcharge is contradicted by the weighed charge, fan rotation and airflow were verified, and a stuck-closed TXV would starve the low side rather than inflate the high side.

questions.question: Evacuation of a large piped system is extremely slow through long, small charging hoses connected through valve-core ports. The most effective speed-up is to:

answers.text: Use short, large-diameter evacuation hoses connected directly to large system ports with valve cores removed, and measure vacuum at the system
Heat the vacuum pump oil with a torch

Charge a pound of refrigerant to sweep air out faster, opening the liquid service valve while the pump continues to run and relying on the added refrigerant pressure to push the remaining air and moisture out through the charging hoses
Run two micron gauges in series on the same hose

questions.explanation: Evacuation is limited by hose conductance, so large, short, core-free connections to the system itself remove the bottleneck. Option B is unsafe and does not change conductance, option C charges refrigerant into a system still full of air instead of removing it, and option D adds gauges without enlarging the flow path.

questions.question: An existing line set passes a visual check but the installer cannot confirm what is inside a long concealed section. Which test sequence best supports a reuse decision?

answers.text: Pressure test with dry nitrogen, then evacuate and confirm the vacuum holds before charging
Charge a small amount of the new refrigerant and watch head pressure for an hour to see whether the lines are clean inside
Blow the lines out with shop air and judge cleanliness by the color of whatever exits the far end of the run
Connect the new unit and rely on its high-pressure switch to reveal any blockage during the first startup run

questions.explanation: A nitrogen pressure test plus a standing vacuum check verifies tightness and dryness before refrigerant is committed. A trial charge wastes refrigerant on an unverified run, shop air adds moisture and is not a cleanliness test, and protective switches are not diagnostic substitutes.

questions.question: An electric air handler calls for both heat stages, supply air is only mildly warm, and amp draw equals roughly one stage alone. What is the best next check?

answers.text: Confirm the cooling charge first, because low refrigerant in the heat pump coil always limits electric strip output to one stage
Assume the thermostat is satisfied and leave, because mild supply air proves both stages must be operating as designed together
Check whether the second stage is energized and intact
Replace the blower motor, because low amp draw on the heat circuit is a direct measure of circulating motor performance instead

questions.explanation: Mild air with single-stage amp draw on a two-stage call means verifying control power to the second stage, its sequencer or relay, fusible link, and element continuity. Option A imports a refrigeration cause for a resistance-heat shortfall, option B accepts a clear output deficit, and option D measures the wrong circuit for a heating-stage fault.

questions.question: Another EEV system shows high superheat, low suction pressure, and a starved coil, and the controller's step count changes normally on the display. What should be checked before replacing the valve body?

answers.text: Only the refrigerant charge, because a changing step count on the display proves the physical valve has moved to the commanded position in every case
Only the indoor filter, because a starved coil with high superheat on an electronic-valve system cannot involve the valve or its drive at all
Stepper coil condition, harness continuity, and actual valve movement, because a displayed step count proves commands, not motion
Only the thermostat calibration, because a thermostat offset reproduces this exact pressure and superheat pattern without any refrigeration-side fault

questions.explanation: A displayed step count shows commands were issued, not that the coil, wiring, or rotor actually moved the pin, so the electrical drive path is tested first. Charge and airflow remain possible contributors but do not excuse skipping the valve drive, and a thermostat offset cannot create high superheat with a starved coil.

questions.question: Intermittent no-heat. A furnace runs reliably on calm days but locks out on pressure-switch faults during gusty wind. Its vent terminates on a wall near an outside corner where gusts sweep past. Measured inducer vacuum hovers at about 1.15 in. w.c. against a switch rating of 0.95 in. w.c., dipping to 0.7 in. w.c. during gusts; with the vent temporarily disconnected at the furnace for testing, vacuum holds a steady 1.4 in. w.c. Drains and trap are clear and the inducer is strong. What is the most likely cause?

answers.text: A marginal inducer that weakens in cold wind, ruled out because the same inducer holds a steady 1.4 in. w.c. once the termination's wind exposure is removed from the test
A condensate trap that plugs only on windy days, which has no mechanism tying drain blockage to gusts and is verified clear during these windy-day failures
Wind at the vent termination disturbing inducer vacuum enough to trip the switch
A pressure switch whose contacts bounce in vibration, which would fault on calm days with blower vibration as well rather than correlate tightly with outdoor gusts

questions.explanation: Vacuum is marginal to begin with and gusts at the poorly placed termination push it from 1.15 down through the 0.95 in. w.c. trip point to 0.7, while the inducer proves strong and steady at 1.4 in. w.c. without the termination's influence. The inducer, trap, and switch each fail to explain the strict correlation with wind that the termination location explains directly.

questions.question: A zoned system's smallest zone has ducts designed for 350 CFM. The two-stage air conditioner delivers 800 CFM on low stage. With only the small zone calling and its damper fully open while the others are closed, low-stage airflow still tries to force roughly 800 CFM toward a 350-CFM path. Which design correction addresses the root cause?

answers.text: Ensure the combination of equipment turndown, modulating dampers, and zone sizing keeps delivered airflow within what the smallest calling zone combination can accept at acceptable static pressure — for example by using variable-speed equipment with deeper turndown or enlarging the minimum zone grouping
Install a higher-pressure blower so it can force the full 800 CFM through the small zone
Close the small zone's damper partway so the excess air has somewhere to go
Remove the small zone's thermostat so it can never call by itself

questions.explanation: The root cause is a capacity-to-zone mismatch at minimum call; the fix is at the design level — turndown, modulation, and zone grouping — not forcing more pressure into an undersized path. Option B is wrong because more pressure means more noise, more leakage, and possible equipment trips — it intensifies every symptom; option C is wrong because throttling the only open damper raises static further and gives the excess air no destination at all; option D is wrong because defeating the zone's thermostat abandons the zoning the owner paid for instead of designing the match correctly.

questions.question: No-cool call on a 95-degree day. An R-410A condenser shows head pressure of 465 psig with near-normal superheat, its coil is clean, and the condenser fan is visibly turning slowly, drawing below its rated amps. The dual capacitor's compressor section tests in tolerance, but its fan section measures 2.3 microfarads against a 5-microfarad rating. Compressor amps are modestly high. What is the most likely cause?

answers.text: An overcharge raising head pressure, which would show elevated subcooling as its signature and would not slow the condenser fan or pull its amps below rating
A weak fan section of the dual run capacitor
A dirty condenser coil throttling heat rejection, ruled out because the coil was inspected clean and the fan itself is turning slowly on this call
A compressor with worn valves losing pumping capacity, which would lower head pressure rather than drive it to 465 psig on a hot afternoon

questions.explanation: The fan section at 2.3 of 5 microfarads starves the fan motor of torque, condenser airflow falls, and head pressure climbs to 465 psig while refrigerant-side readings stay near normal. Overcharge would raise subcooling without slowing the fan, the coil is clean, and worn compressor valves cannot build this head pressure at all.

arkansas-hvac.quiz_title: Arkansas HVAC Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam

questions.question: A liquid-line solenoid valve in a refrigeration system is used to:

answers.text: Stop or allow liquid refrigerant flow in response to a control signal, such as for pumpdown or zone control
Sense evaporator superheat and modulate flow continuously in response to changes in load, bulb temperature, and external equalizer pressure at the evaporator outlet
Relieve excessive discharge pressure to the suction side
Separate oil from discharge gas

questions.explanation: A solenoid is an electrically operated on-off valve for liquid flow, commonly used for pumpdown and zoning. Option B describes a thermostatic expansion valve, option C describes a relief or bypass valve, and option D describes an oil separator.

questions.question: On a spring-return zone damper, what happens when panel power to the damper motor is removed?

answers.text: The blade locks at whatever angle it held when power stopped, because the gear train cannot move in either direction without motor torque applied to the shaft
The blade drives fully closed at motor speed, because removing power reverses the motor through a capacitor stored in the damper actuator housing
A spring drives the blade back to its rest position, open or closed by design
The blade floats freely and follows duct pressure, swinging to whichever position the airflow in that branch happens to push it during the equipment cycle

questions.explanation: A spring-return actuator is motor driven in one direction and spring driven back to its designed rest position when power is removed, which is how its fail position is chosen. It does not lock in place, reverse electrically on stored charge, or float freely with duct pressure.

questions.question: Two draft-hood appliances are added to a common vent. How is the common-vent capacity determined?

answers.text: From the input of the largest appliance only, because the smaller appliances add heat but are assumed not to add flue-gas volume
From the combined input of all appliances sharing the vent
From the average input of the connected appliances, reduced further whenever the two appliances are not expected to fire at the same time
From the vent height alone, without adding the appliance inputs, because height is treated as the only limit on common-vent capacity

questions.explanation: From the combined input of all appliances sharing the vent. Sizing from only the largest appliance or from an average ignores the flue-gas volume of the others, and height alone does not set capacity without total input.

questions.question: Outdoor refrigerant access ports on a system in a public area are uncapped and show signs of tampering. What protection applies?

answers.text: Remove the access ports entirely and braze the stubs closed, because service access is optional once a system has been charged
Paint the ports a bright color and post a warning sign, which together are accepted as equivalent to a physical locking device
Move the ports inside the condenser coil compartment behind the fan, where no technician can reach them during normal service
Fit approved tamper-resistant locking caps where access ports are exposed to unauthorized access.

questions.explanation: Locking caps are the recognized protection against refrigerant theft and huffing at exposed ports. Brazing ports shut destroys serviceability, paint and signs do not physically prevent access, and relocating ports out of reach defeats their purpose.

questions.question: A punch list is best described as which of the following?

answers.text: A list of every employee assigned to the project and the classification used for their payroll reporting
A pricing sheet showing unit rates for additional work that the owner may order after the contract is signed
A list of incomplete or deficient items to correct before final acceptance
A schedule of submittal due dates organized by the order in which equipment must be released for fabrication

questions.explanation: C is correct because a punch list documents remaining incomplete or deficient items that must be corrected before final acceptance. A is incorrect because crew assignments and payroll classifications are administrative records, not a punch list. B is incorrect because unit rates for extras belong in the contract's pricing terms, not the punch list. D is incorrect because submittal schedules track approvals, while the punch list tracks work corrections.

questions.question: A technician plans to braze a replacement filter drier into an R-32 system that still holds a partial charge. What must happen before the torch is lit?

answers.text: Nothing beyond normal brazing practice, because a partial charge of a mildly flammable refrigerant cannot reach a flammable concentration at a joint
Only a nitrogen purge during brazing, because flowing nitrogen inside the pipe makes it safe to braze a system that still contains refrigerant under pressure
Recover the charge and verify the area is clear
Only a fire watch posted at the door, because having a second person observe is a complete substitute for removing refrigerant from the work area

questions.explanation: Refrigerant must be recovered and the work area checked clear before any torch work on an A2L system. A partial charge can still leak at flammable concentration near a joint, nitrogen purging does not make brazing a charged system acceptable, and a fire watch supplements safe preparation rather than replacing recovery.

questions.question: A PVC vent joint was dry-fitted, marked, and then assembled without primer or cement on one socket. It separates during the first heating season. What practice failure caused this?

answers.text: The installer used Schedule 40 pipe instead of a thinner-wall pipe that would have expanded more and locked the joint tightly
The joint was never solvent-welded
The installer failed to pressure-test the vent with high-pressure shop air, which is what normally fuses PVC joints together in place
The pipe was cut square instead of at an angle, so the cement had no wedge surface to grip as the fitting was pushed home fully

questions.explanation: PVC vent joints seal and hold only when they are properly primed and solvent-cemented; a dry-fitted socket has no bond and can pull apart. Option A is wrong because wall thickness does not create the joint, option C invents air-pressure fusing, and option D misstates cutting practice, since square cuts with full insertion are desired.

questions.question: An EEV stepper's four coil windings are measured: three match the specified resistance and one reads open. The valve body moves freely in a known-good test. What is the correct repair?

answers.text: Replace the stepper motor/coil assembly or repair the harness fault, since the valve body itself has been shown to move freely
Replace the entire valve body and coil together in every case, because coil faults cannot be separated from the valve they drive on any design
Replace the outdoor control board, because an open coil winding is generated inside the board's driver chip rather than in the coil or its wiring
Add refrigerant until the valve opens further, because an open coil reading is a normal response to a system that is low on charge

questions.explanation: An open coil with a free valve body localizes the fault to the motor coil or its harness, which is serviced without discarding a sound valve body. Coil and body are separable on serviceable designs, the driver chip does not create an open winding in an external coil, and charge level has no relationship to a coil continuity reading.

questions.question: During a basement furnace replacement, a technician notices an open sump pit and cracked slab joints. Why mention soil gas to the owner?

answers.text: An open sump proves the house has a carbon monoxide problem, because sumps are the primary source of combustion gases in basements
The sump should be connected to the furnace return so soil gas is diluted continuously by the air distribution system each cycle
Cracks should be widened so soil gas can enter freely and be detected sooner by a monitor placed across the basement room
Open sumps and slab cracks are entry routes for soil gases such as radon and moisture, and sealing or covering them as directed helps limit entry.

questions.explanation: Soil-gas entry points matter to indoor air quality, and an open sump is a direct pathway from below the slab. A sump is not a combustion-gas source, returning soil gas through the ducts would distribute it, and widening entry routes increases rather than controls entry.

questions.question: A wall has U-value 0.05, area 200 sq ft, and design delta T of 40 degrees F. Using Q = U x A x delta T, what is its heating load contribution?

answers.text: 40 Btuh
100 Btuh
400 Btuh
4,000 Btuh

questions.explanation: Q = 0.05 x 200 x 40 = 400 Btuh, so C is correct. A and B result from dropping factors in the product, and D is ten times too high from a decimal error in the U-value.

questions.question: A designer raises a hydronic loop's glycol concentration well above what the design freeze point requires, 'for extra safety.' What penalty should the designer expect?

answers.text: No penalty at all, because glycol solutions transfer heat better than water and become thinner as concentration increases
Lower heat-transfer capacity, higher viscosity and pump head, and reduced chiller or heat-pump capacity that must be derated
The loop will freeze sooner, because adding glycol always lowers the temperature at which a solution begins to form ice crystals
The pump will use less energy, because a more concentrated solution is easier to move through coils, valves, and fittings

questions.explanation: Beyond the needed concentration, glycol only hurts: it carries less heat per gallon, thickens the fluid, and forces capacity and pump derates. Option A states the opposite of glycol's actual properties, option C reverses the freeze-protection effect that glycol does provide, and option D ignores the viscosity increase that raises pumping energy.

questions.question: A replacement furnace is classified as a Category III appliance. Which statement correctly describes how its vent system behaves and must be built?

answers.text: It works at a negative vent pressure and produces condensate in the vent, so ordinary single-wall pipe with loose joints is the accepted vent material for it
It works at a positive vent pressure and does not condense, so the vent must be gas-tight with sealed joints so flue products cannot leak into the building
It works at a positive vent pressure and produces condensate in the vent, so it shares the corrosion-resistant sealed venting used by condensing appliances
It works at a negative vent pressure and does not condense, so it vents by natural draft exactly like a Category I appliance with a standard draft hood fitted

questions.explanation: B is correct: Category III appliances operate with positive vent pressure and a vent-gas temperature that avoids excessive condensation, and because the vent is pressurized its joints and seams must be sealed against leakage. A is wrong because it pairs a negative pressure with condensation, which describes neither Category III trait. C is wrong because sustained vent condensation is the Category IV characteristic. D is wrong because negative-pressure natural-draft venting is Category I behavior.

questions.question: A TXV system in cooling mode has normal evaporator superheat, both pressures somewhat high, and subcooling of 24°F against a manufacturer target of 10°F. Cooling capacity is slightly reduced. What condition best fits these readings?

answers.text: Overcharge, with excess liquid backing up in the condenser
Undercharge, with the condenser only partly filled with liquid
A restricted liquid-line filter drier starving the TXV
Low indoor airflow across the evaporator coil

questions.explanation: With a TXV holding superheat steady, excess charge collects in the condenser and shows up as abnormally high subcooling with elevated pressures. Option B is the opposite condition and would produce low subcooling, while option C starves the valve and raises superheat rather than holding it normal. Option D lowers suction pressure and superheat, which does not match the normal superheat reading here.

questions.question: A two-zone system with a single-stage blower serves a small zone calling alone. Airflow noise rises sharply. What is the most likely cause?

answers.text: The thermostat is set too low
Return ducts are oversized
Full blower airflow is forced through only the open zone ducts, raising velocity and static
Zone dampers always reduce total static pressure, even when only one small zone is calling and the other damper is fully closed

questions.explanation: With one zone closed, full airflow through half the duct system raises velocity and static, causing noise, so C is correct. Thermostat setting and oversized returns do not explain it, and D is false because closing dampers raises, not lowers, static unless airflow is reduced or bypassed properly.

questions.question: A standing nitrogen pressure test loses several psi overnight while the building also cooled noticeably overnight. Before condemning the piping as leaking, the technician should:

answers.text: Add refrigerant and put the system into service immediately, charging by sight glass alone without repeating the standing test, correcting for temperature change, or leak-checking any joint in the new piping run
Tighten every flare and braze joint blindly
Consider that gas pressure falls as its temperature falls, correct for or repeat the test at a comparable temperature, and leak-check joints if a true loss remains
Vent the nitrogen and skip the test

questions.explanation: At a fixed volume, nitrogen pressure varies with absolute temperature, so a cold night can mimic a small leak; temperature must be accounted for before declaring a failure. Option A puts an unverified system into service, option B can damage good joints without finding a leak, and option D abandons the test that protects the charge and the equipment.

questions.question: A medium-temperature walk-in on electric defrost finishes defrost with the coil clear, but the fans blow warm, moist air into the box for several minutes and the panels sweat. Which missing or mis-set function best explains this?

answers.text: A crankcase pressure regulator set too low
An evaporator pressure regulator that opens too early at the end of defrost, allowing warm suction vapor from the other cases on the common header to flood back into this coil for several minutes
A head-pressure control valve stuck open
A fan-delay control that should keep fans off until the coil has pulled back down after defrost

questions.explanation: Fan delay keeps evaporator fans off after defrost until the coil is cold again, preventing a blast of warm, moist air into the box. Options A and B are refrigerant-pressure controls that do not time fan restart, and option C affects condenser pressure in low ambient, not post-defrost fan behavior.

questions.question: A supplier delivers a factory-assembled, air-cooled, self-contained refrigeration unit rated at 1.5 horsepower, with all refrigerant lines contained within the cabinet. Does the licensing chapter apply to that equipment?

answers.text: The chapter does not apply to that equipment, because factory-assembled air-cooled self-contained refrigeration equipment of 1.5 horsepower or less with no refrigerant lines beyond the cabinet is exempt.
The chapter applies in full, because the exemption for self-contained refrigeration equipment ends at 1 horsepower and this unit's rating exceeds that ceiling by half a horsepower.
The chapter does not apply only if the unit is installed in a residence, because the self-contained refrigeration exemption is written as part of the household-appliance exemption for homes.

The chapter applies unless the unit is also unvented, because self-contained refrigeration equipment is exempt only when it is combined with an AGA-approved unvented space heater installation. and is combined with an AGA-approved unvented space heater installation performed as part of a single equipment package.

questions.explanation: A is correct: the equipment exemptions include factory-assembled air-cooled self-contained refrigeration equipment of 1.5 horsepower or less with no refrigerant lines beyond the cabinet, which matches this unit exactly. B is wrong because the exemption ceiling is 1.5 horsepower, not 1 horsepower. C is wrong because this equipment exemption is not limited to residences. D is wrong because the unvented-space-heater exemption is a separate listed item and is not a condition of the refrigeration exemption.

questions.question: During a furnace inspection, supply-air CO measures 8 ppm before the blower starts and climbs to 42 ppm within a minute of blower start, the flames visibly waver and lift each time the blower energizes, and a mirror inspection shows a crack along a heat exchanger cell seam. Manifold pressure and temperature rise are in spec. What is the required action?

answers.text: Clean the burners and continue running the furnace while monitoring CO weekly, leaving a known cracked exchanger in service against safety practice
Shut down the furnace for a cracked heat exchanger
Adjust the manifold pressure downward slightly, which cannot seal a physical crack that is leaking combustion products into the airstream
Replace the blower motor for running too fast, since flame disturbance alone without the CO rise and visible crack would not justify condemnation

questions.explanation: CO that climbs precisely when the blower pressurizes the exchanger, flames disturbed at blower start, and a visible seam crack together confirm combustion products entering the supply air. No pressure adjustment seals a crack, blower speed does not create CO, and a confirmed cracked exchanger is a shut-down condition, not a monitor-and-run condition.

questions.question: An attic air handler is draw-through, with the coil on the negative-pressure side of the blower, and its drain is piped straight out with no trap. Water stands in the pan and occasionally overflows even though the drain line is clear. Why is a trap needed here?

answers.text: The trap filters pollen from the condensate
The trap stores water to humidify the attic
Negative air pressure in the cabinet can hold water in the pan and draw air up the drain; a properly sized trap lets condensate drain against that pressure
The trap is only needed on gas piping, not condensate

questions.explanation: In a draw-through unit the cabinet is under negative pressure that can prevent drainage and pull air up an untrapped drain, so a trap of proper depth allows the pan to drain, option C. The trap does not filter air (A) or humidify anything (B), and condensate trapping (D) is a drainage requirement entirely separate from gas-piping practice.

questions.question: At startup a technician records supply voltage at the disconnect and then again at the compressor terminals while the unit is running under load. The running voltage is notably lower than the standing voltage. What does that difference most directly indicate?

answers.text: A correctly sized conductor with no further check needed, since the standing voltage at the disconnect was acceptable when it was measured before the compressor was started under load
An overcharge of refrigerant raising the voltage
A thermostat calling on two stages at once
A high-resistance connection or undersized wiring causing voltage drop under load, which must be corrected before final commissioning

questions.explanation: Voltage that sags only under load points to resistance in conductors or connections, and the drop must be found and corrected so the compressor is not run on low voltage. Option A is contradicted by the sag itself, option B confuses refrigerant charge with an electrical measurement, and option C may change staging but does not create a load-dependent voltage difference at the terminals.

arizona-hvac.quiz_title: Arizona HVAC Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam

questions.question: What is the purpose of a liquid receiver in a system that has one?

answers.text: To store liquid refrigerant leaving the condenser and supply a steady liquid seal to the liquid line as load and charge requirements vary
To prevent liquid from reaching the compressor on the suction side by trapping it in a large accumulator vessel installed immediately before the compressor inlet
To remove moisture and acid from the refrigerant
To measure refrigerant flow to the evaporator

questions.explanation: The receiver is a high-side storage vessel that holds condensed liquid and keeps liquid, not vapor, feeding the expansion device across varying conditions. Option B describes a suction accumulator, option C describes a filter drier, and option D describes the metering device or a flow measurement, not storage.

questions.question: Compared with air, propane vapor has a specific gravity of about 1.5. What does that mean in practice?

answers.text: It is heavier than air and tends to sink
It is much lighter than air and rises quickly to a ceiling, where it disperses through high openings before it can collect anywhere in a room
It has essentially the same weight as air, so leaked vapor mixes evenly at every height and never forms a distinct layer near a floor
It is heavier than liquid water, so leaked vapor falls as a liquid and can be mopped up rather than ventilated from a low space

questions.explanation: Propane vapor is about one and one-half times as heavy as air, so it sinks and collects at low points. It does not rise to ceilings like natural gas vapor tends to do, it does not mix evenly without forming low pockets, and its vapor specific gravity is not a comparison with liquid water.

questions.question: Three control loads draw 12 VA, 18 VA, and 15 VA at the same time. A 40 VA transformer is proposed. The proposal is:

answers.text: Undersized; the simultaneous load is 45 VA, so select at least the next adequate size
Correct, because simultaneous control loads are added only after dividing by the number of devices, which reduces the total to 15 VA in this case
Oversized, because the largest single load of 18 VA is the only figure ever used when a control transformer is selected for a system
Correct if the thermostat is electronic, because electronic thermostats return enough power over the common wire to make up a VA shortfall

questions.explanation: Undersized; the simultaneous load is 45 VA, so select at least the next adequate size. Loads are not averaged or reduced to the largest one, and a thermostat does not generate power to cover a transformer shortfall.

questions.question: Which set lists major heating load components in a Manual J calculation?

answers.text: Only window glass area
Only duct color and filter type
Transmission through envelope, infiltration, and duct losses
Refrigerant type and line-set length only, with no envelope or infiltration terms

questions.explanation: Heating load is driven mainly by heat transmission through walls, ceilings, floors and glass, plus infiltration and duct losses, so C is correct. A and D each name only one minor or unrelated factor, and B names items that do not drive the load.

questions.question: On a typical chilled-water air handler, how is coil capacity normally controlled as the zone load falls?

answers.text: By draining the coil partway so only the lower half of the finned surface ever sees chilled water flow, using a graduated sight glass on the coil return riser to hold the water level at its marked midpoint
A modulating control valve varies chilled-water flow through the coil in response to the discharge or zone temperature signal
By reversing the water flow direction through the coil every time the thermostat approaches its setpoint
By shutting down the supply fan and letting the coil cool the space by natural convection alone

questions.explanation: A two-way or three-way modulating valve meters water through the coil to match load while the fan handles airflow. Option A would maldistribute water and is never a control strategy, option C confuses piping arrangement with control, and option D abandons forced-air delivery and humidity control.

questions.question: A two-cylinder reciprocating compressor with cylinder unloaders is running but the space is already near setpoint and the system needs roughly half capacity. What should the unloader do?

answers.text: Close the discharge service valve on one cylinder head so that cylinder dead-heads against a closed outlet while the other cylinder continues to pump normally
Shut off the oil pump to the unloaded cylinder so friction slows that piston and reduces the total displacement of the machine by about one half
Open a bypass from the liquid receiver directly into the suction header so extra refrigerant flow makes up for the cylinder that has been taken offline
Hold one cylinder's suction valve open so that cylinder stops pumping

questions.explanation: A suction-valve unloader holds the valve off its seat, so the cylinder moves gas in and out without compressing it and capacity steps down. Dead-heading a cylinder against a closed discharge is dangerous and is not unloading, stopping oil flow would destroy the cylinder rather than unload it, and bypassing receiver liquid into suction risks floodback instead of reducing capacity.

questions.question: During a normal oil burner shutdown, a few drops of oil drip from the nozzle and burn smokily in the hot chamber. This after-drip is most often caused by:

answers.text: Heat expansion of oil trapped between a leaking pump cutoff or solenoid and the nozzle, pushing oil out after shutdown
The cad cell continuing to sense light after flame-out
Excess draft in the chimney during the off cycle
A high-limit control set too low

questions.explanation: Oil sealed in the line expands as it absorbs chamber heat; if the pump's internal cutoff or solenoid leaks, that expansion expels drops at the nozzle. Option B is a sensing symptom, not a source of oil movement. Option C moves air, not trapped oil, through the nozzle. Option D ends burner runs early but does not push oil from the line after shutdown.

questions.question: A tester needs leakage to outside only, not total leakage, on a house where many ducts run inside the conditioned space. Which test setup isolates leakage to outside?

answers.text: Equalize house and duct pressure
Pressurize the ducts alone with the house left open to outdoors, then subtract the supply-register airflow from the return-register airflow measured with a flow hood
Run the air handler on high speed and compare its blower-table airflow with the sum of all supply registers, treating any shortfall as leakage to outside specifically
Seal every register, pressurize the ducts to 50 Pa instead of 25 Pa, and report that higher-pressure reading because doubling test pressure cancels leaks to the inside

questions.explanation: With a blower door holding the house at the same pressure as the duct tester, no air flows through leaks to the inside, so the duct tester measures only leaks to outside. Ducts alone measure total leakage, a flow-hood shortfall cannot separate inside from outside leaks, and raising test pressure changes the reading's magnitude without cancelling inside leakage.

questions.question: In snow country, a sidewall direct-vent terminus is installed only a few inches above grade on the drift side of the house. The failure mode to prevent is:

answers.text: Snow cooling the plastic vent pipe until it becomes brittle and collapses inward even when the intake opening remains completely clear
Snow melting into the gas pipe through the vent terminus and traveling back through the heat exchanger into the gas valve body
Snow burial blocking intake and exhaust
Snow reflecting sunlight into the intake screen, which overheats the pressure-switch tubing and causes a nuisance lockout in winter

questions.explanation: Snow burial blocking intake and exhaust. Burial, not pipe brittleness, water traveling to the gas valve, or sunlight on switch tubing, is the grade-clearance concern for a low terminus.

questions.question: A portable air cleaner's clean-air delivery rate is far below the room's volume needs, and the owner expects hospital-grade air. What limit must be explained?

answers.text: Portable cleaners treat the whole house equally from any location, because cleaned air displaces dirty air in every room within a few minutes
Doubling the fan speed on an undersized unit multiplies its clean-air delivery by ten, closing any sizing gap the room presents
A portable unit can only clean the air that passes through it, so an undersized unit cannot achieve the room air changes needed for a large reduction in airborne particles.
Particle removal does not depend on airflow through the unit at all, since the cleaner's field effect treats air in rooms behind closed doors

questions.explanation: Air cleaning is a rate problem: room volume times desired air changes sets the delivery rate the device must meet. One small unit does not serve a whole house uniformly, fan speed cannot multiply capacity tenfold, and air behind closed doors never reaches the device.

questions.question: A designer raises a hydronic loop's glycol concentration well above what the design freeze point requires, 'for extra safety.' What penalty should the designer expect?

answers.text: No penalty at all, because glycol solutions transfer heat better than water and become thinner as concentration increases
Lower heat-transfer capacity, higher viscosity and pump head, and reduced chiller or heat-pump capacity that must be derated
The loop will freeze sooner, because adding glycol always lowers the temperature at which a solution begins to form ice crystals
The pump will use less energy, because a more concentrated solution is easier to move through coils, valves, and fittings

questions.explanation: Beyond the needed concentration, glycol only hurts: it carries less heat per gallon, thickens the fluid, and forces capacity and pump derates. Option A states the opposite of glycol's actual properties, option C reverses the freeze-protection effect that glycol does provide, and option D ignores the viscosity increase that raises pumping energy.

questions.question: A license expires while a disciplinary proceeding based on conduct during the license term is still pending. What is the effect of the expiration on that proceeding?

answers.text: The proceeding is dismissed automatically, because an expired license leaves nothing for the Registrar to suspend or revoke
The Registrar keeps jurisdiction to proceed and to render a decision, including denying renewal, despite the expiration
The proceeding pauses indefinitely and may resume only if the former licensee voluntarily applies for a brand new license
Jurisdiction transfers to the courts, because after expiration only a judge may make findings about a former licensee's conduct

questions.explanation: B is correct: expiration does not deprive the Registrar of jurisdiction to investigate, proceed with disciplinary action, or render a decision suspending or revoking or denying renewal, so the pending proceeding continues. A is wrong because the rule expressly preserves the proceeding rather than dismissing it on expiration. C is wrong because resumption is not conditioned on a voluntary new application. D is wrong because no transfer of the Registrar's disciplinary jurisdiction to a court is stated.

questions.question: A system with an A2L leak sensor repeatedly shuts down cooling and runs the blower, but no leak is found at the coil with a rated detector and pressures hold steady. What is the soundest next step?

answers.text: Replace the full refrigerant charge, because repeated mitigation trips with steady pressures are treated as proof that the charge itself has become contaminated
Disable the sensor permanently, because repeated trips without a confirmed leak establish that the mitigation system is unnecessary on that installation
Condemn the blower motor, because a blower that runs during a shutdown event is by definition the failed component in a mitigation sequence
Check the sensor itself, its placement relative to chemical sources, and its wiring, after a genuine leak has been ruled out

questions.explanation: Repeated false mitigation points to the sensing chain itself — sensor condition, location near a chemical source, or wiring — after a real leak is ruled out. Steady pressures do not indict the charge, disabling a safety mitigation is not an acceptable repair, and the blower running is the designed response, not evidence of blower failure.

questions.question: An oil burner consistently ignites with a loud puff several seconds after the motor starts, then runs cleanly. Spark is strong and present on time. The delay most likely comes from:

answers.text: A cad cell with low resistance in darkness, caused by a cracked cell housing that admits room light into the burner compartment even when the access panel is closed and the flame is completely out
Slow oil delivery to the nozzle — for example air in the line, a clogged nozzle strainer, or a weak delayed-opening solenoid — so fuel arrives after the trial has begun
Excessive stack draft pulling the flame off the head
A thermostat calling on both W1 and W2 together

questions.explanation: If ignition energy is on time but fuel arrives late, oil sprays into a hot chamber and lights with a puff when it finally reaches the arc. Option A would make the control think flame exists before startup and cause a different lockout fault. Option C destabilizes an established flame rather than delaying fuel. Option D is a gas-furnace staging concept that does not apply to this oil burner sequence.

questions.question: A long liquid line is one size too small for the load. The most likely operating symptom is:

answers.text: No symptom, because liquid lines cannot have pressure drop no matter how small the tubing, how long the run, or how many elbows, valves, and vertical lifts are installed between the receiver and the expansion device
Oil logging in the liquid line riser
Excessive pressure drop that consumes subcooling and can flash liquid to vapor before the expansion valve, reducing its capacity
A suction line that sweats heavily indoors

questions.explanation: Undersized liquid piping creates friction pressure drop; if drop plus lift consumes the available subcooling, flash gas forms ahead of the valve and starves it. Option A denies basic friction loss, option B misplaces oil logging, which is a low-velocity suction problem, and option D describes suction-line condensation, not a liquid-line sizing effect.

questions.question: A technician fixes the same no-cooling symptom three times by replacing a capacitor, yet the unit keeps failing each heat wave. What does callback analysis say about this pattern?

answers.text: The capacitor is likely a victim rather than the root cause, so the investigation should look for what is stressing it, such as low voltage, heat, or a struggling compressor

Replacing the same capacitor repeatedly on every callback is the correct long-term strategy, and the technician should keep installing identical parts until one finally holds through an entire summer season
The customer is at fault because heat waves coincide with the failures
Warranty requires installing the same part a fourth time before deeper diagnosis

questions.explanation: Repeated failure of the same component signals an upstream cause that must be found. Continuing identical replacements wastes visits and leaves the fault. Heat waves expose the weakness but blaming the customer or the weather does not fix it, and no warranty rule forbids proper diagnosis.

questions.question: A contractor wins nearly every bid but finishes most jobs with little or no profit. What estimating problem is most likely?

answers.text: The overhead rate is set too high, causing the company to win work it should have declined at those prices
Prices are too low because costs such as burden or overhead are being understated
The quantity takeoffs are too detailed, giving the estimator an unrealistically precise view of material needs
