questions.explanation: Low heat rise with a lazy flame and adequate inlet pressure points to underfiring, confirmed by manifold pressure against the rating plate. Blower locked-rotor amps, damper angle, and trap depth do not meter gas to the burner.

questions.question: With the air handler running, a large supply trunk joint in the attic is found disconnected. The house measures slightly negative with respect to outdoors while the system runs. Why?

answers.text: The return grille is oversized, so the blower moves extra outdoor air into the house and the attic joint is merely venting that surplus air back outside
Supply air lost in the attic is replaced by air the return side no longer gets back, which would pressurize the house because the blower is still delivering its full rated flow

The house goes negative relative to outdoors, because supply air dumped into the attic never comes back through the return side, so the blower pulls replacement air in through leaks in the building shell
The disconnected joint acts like a second return that draws attic air into the supply stream and pushes the house positive whenever the blower runs

questions.explanation: Supply air dumped outside the envelope never returns, so the house loses air and drifts negative while the system runs. An oversized return grille does not import outdoor air, the lost supply cannot pressurize a house it is leaving, and a supply-side opening blows air out rather than drawing attic air in as a return would.

questions.question: A variable-air-volume box is described as pressure dependent. Without a flow sensor, what determines its delivered airflow at a given damper position?

answers.text: The programmed maximum airflow stored in the zone thermostat
The duct static pressure at that moment, so flow rises and falls as system pressure changes
The outdoor-air temperature measured at the economizer
The number of other zones in the building that happen to be calling at that moment, regardless of the duct pressure available at the terminal

questions.explanation: With no flow measurement, a set damper position passes whatever the available pressure pushes through it. A stored setpoint cannot enforce flow without a sensor, outdoor temperature does not set terminal flow, and other zones matter only through their effect on system pressure.

questions.question: A TXV system runs with a sweating, frost-covered suction line to the compressor. Readings: suction 156 psig, superheat 2°F, subcooling 6°F, compressor amps 112% of rated, discharge superheat low, airflow and charge weight both verified correct, and the frost persists after the bulb is re-secured and insulated. What is the most likely cause?

answers.text: A dirty condenser coil restricting heat rejection, which raises head pressure sharply while leaving evaporator superheat near its setpoint
A restricted liquid-line drier, which would starve the valve, raise superheat, and show a temperature drop across the drier body
A TXV stuck open
A low refrigerant charge, which starves the evaporator and produces high superheat with low suction pressure, the reverse of this pattern

questions.explanation: Near-zero superheat with high suction pressure and frost reaching the compressor is liquid floodback from a valve feeding far beyond the load, confirmed when re-securing the bulb changes nothing. A low charge and a drier restriction both starve the evaporator and raise superheat, and a dirty condenser attacks the high side while the TXV still holds superheat.

questions.question: A condensing furnace's condensate drain has a long flat section that sags, and the furnace intermittently locks out with water backing up into the collector box. What correction best addresses the cause?

answers.text: Raise the gas manifold pressure well above the manufacturer's specification so the furnace runs hotter and dries itself out from the inside during every cycle
Plug the secondary drain port so water cannot back up
Re-pitch the drain so it slopes continuously downhill to its termination, support it so it cannot sag, and keep required traps in place
Connect the condensate line directly into a gas vent

questions.explanation: Condensate must flow by gravity through a continuously sloped, supported drain with its required trap, option C; a sagging flat run pools water that eventually backs up and trips the furnace. Manifold pressure (A) has nothing to do with drainage, plugging a drain port (B) worsens backup, and tying condensate into a gas vent (D) mixes drainage with combustion venting and is prohibited practice.

questions.question: A variable-speed drive slows a chilled-water pump to 90% of full speed. Using the pump affinity laws, about how much pump power is saved?

answers.text: About 3%, because pump power falls only in direct one-to-one proportion to the drop in pump rotational speed
About 10%, because pump power falls in proportion to the square of the speed ratio at reduced flow conditions
About 19%, because pump head and pump power always change by exactly the same percentage as each other
About 27%, because power varies with the cube of speed: 0.9 cubed is about 0.73 of full power

questions.explanation: Power follows the cube law: 0.9^3 = 0.729, so roughly 27% of the power is saved. Option A uses the flow relationship, option B uses the head (square) relationship, and option C wrongly equates head and power changes, which follow different exponents.

questions.question: A heat pump's auxiliary strip heat will not energize during a defrost-plus-heating call, though the blower and compressor run normally and line voltage is present at the heater rack. Control voltage is absent at the sequencer coil. Where does the evidence point?

answers.text: To the compressor contactor, because loss of sequencer coil voltage is produced by a pitted main contactor in the outdoor unit section.
To the strip elements themselves, because open elements would remove control voltage from the sequencer coil that switches them on.
To the control circuit feeding the sequencer — thermostat staging, wiring, or board output — since line power is present but the coil signal is not.
To the outdoor thermostat alone with certainty, because no other control-circuit component can interrupt voltage to a heater sequencer coil.

questions.explanation: C is correct: line voltage present with no control voltage at the sequencer coil points upstream in the control circuit — staging thermostat, wiring, or control board output — not at the elements. A is wrong because the compressor runs normally, separating its contactor from the heater-control fault. B is wrong because open elements do not remove coil voltage. D is wrong because the evidence narrows to the control path generally, not to one component with certainty.

questions.question: A condensate pump serving an indoor unit in a finished space cycles but the reservoir keeps filling and water spills. The pump runs when lifted by hand in a test bucket. What should be checked first on site?

answers.text: The refrigerant charge, because low charge fills the reservoir
The thermostat batteries, because they control the pump float
The pump discharge line and check valve for a clog, kink, or excessive lift, and the safety switch wiring that should stop the unit if the reservoir stays high
The suction-line insulation, because sweating fills the pump reservoir, especially where the cold suction line runs uninsulated above the finished space and drips steadily into the reservoir below

questions.explanation: A pump that runs in a bucket but cannot clear its installed reservoir is usually fighting a blocked or kinked discharge, a failed check valve, or too much lift, and its overflow switch should be verified. Option A confuses condensate volume with charge, option B names a control that does not run the pump float, and option D produces drips at the line, not a reservoir the pump cannot empty.

questions.question: Noise complaint in heating season only: a high-pitched whine starts with the prepurge, continues while the furnace fires, and has grown louder over several weeks. The indoor blower, tested alone in fan-only mode, sounds normal. The inducer motor draws 1.9 A against a 1.2 A rating with some fluctuation, and its shaft feels rough and gritty when spun by hand with power off. Draft and ignition are still normal. What is the most likely cause?

answers.text: Worn indoor blower bearings, ruled out because the blower sounds normal when run alone in fan-only mode while the whine belongs to the heating sequence
Worn inducer motor bearings that drag and whine whenever the inducer runs, drawing fluctuating current above the motor rating and leaving the shaft feeling rough when turned by hand with power off
A whistling gas regulator at high fire, which would begin at burner ignition rather than at prepurge before any gas flows through the valve
Air leaking at a loose vent joint near the inducer, which would hiss at a steady pitch related to draft rather than grow over weeks with a gritty shaft feel

questions.explanation: The whine is locked to inducer operation from prepurge onward, the motor overdraws with fluctuation, and the shaft feels gritty by hand, all pointing to its bearings wearing out. The indoor blower is exonerated in fan-only mode, regulator noise cannot precede gas flow at prepurge, and a vent leak would not rough up the shaft or raise motor amps.

questions.question: Underground refrigerant and condensate piping requires a trench in soil that is crumbling at the walls, and no protective system has been installed. A helper is told to jump in briefly to guide a pipe section. What should happen instead?

answers.text: The helper may enter if another worker watches from the edge, because a spotter can pull a worker free quickly if the trench wall gives way
The helper should enter crouched near the pipe, since staying low keeps most of the body below the level where falling soil causes serious injury
No one enters until the trench is protected against cave-in
The crew should wet the trench walls with a hose to make the soil stick together, after which the unprotected trench is safe for short entries

questions.explanation: Crumbling walls signal cave-in risk, and workers stay out until sloping, shoring, or shielding protects them. A spotter cannot out-pull collapsing soil, crouching does not prevent burial, and wetting walls can make soil heavier and less stable rather than safe.

questions.question: A heat pump blows warm air on a cooling call on an 88-degree day. The compressor and both fans run, the reversing valve solenoid measures 24 V and its coil pulls a screwdriver magnetically, yet tube temperatures at the valve match the heating position: the line to the indoor coil is hot and the house keeps warming. Refrigerant charge was verified by weight earlier in the visit. What is the most likely cause?

answers.text: A reversing valve spool stuck in the heating position despite an energized solenoid, its internal slide remaining in the heating position and routing hot discharge gas to the indoor coil throughout the cooling call
A dead reversing valve solenoid coil, ruled out because the coil is energized at 24 V and demonstrably magnetizes, pulling on a screwdriver held to it

A thermostat wired to energize the valve in the wrong mode, which would leave the solenoid de-energized on this cooling call for this unit's energize-in-cooling configuration rather than powered and magnetic
A low refrigerant charge making cooling feel like heating, which cannot deliver genuinely hot air to the indoor coil and is ruled out by the weighed-in verified charge

questions.explanation: The electrical side of the valve works (24 V, magnetic coil) but the refrigerant side never shifts: tube temperatures show the valve still routing hot gas to the indoor coil in the heating position, so the spool itself is stuck. The solenoid is proven live and magnetic, the thermostat is delivering the correct energized state for cooling on this configuration, and low charge cannot produce hot supply air.

hawaii-c52-hvac.quiz_title: Hawaii C-52 HVAC Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam

questions.question: Where should a suction-line filter be used, and what caution applies to leaving it in place permanently?

answers.text: It is required permanently on every new installation, because suction filtration is the only protection a compressor has against moisture in the refrigerant charge
It is mainly a temporary cleanup device after a burnout or contamination event, and a permanent one can cause excessive suction pressure drop
It belongs in the liquid line ahead of the drier, because suction filters and liquid driers perform the same job and are installed in the same location interchangeably
It should never be used after a burnout, because the acid and debris from a burnout can only be removed by replacing the compressor and the evaporator coil

questions.explanation: Suction filters excel at catching burnout debris and acid before the new compressor, but their pressure drop penalizes capacity, so they are monitored and often removed after cleanup. They are not a universal permanent requirement on clean new systems, they are suction-side devices distinct from liquid driers, and burnout cleanup is a primary use for them rather than a prohibited one.

questions.question: Three control loads draw 12 VA, 18 VA, and 15 VA at the same time. A 40 VA transformer is proposed. The proposal is:

answers.text: Undersized; the simultaneous load is 45 VA, so select at least the next adequate size
Correct, because simultaneous control loads are added only after dividing by the number of devices, which reduces the total to 15 VA in this case
Oversized, because the largest single load of 18 VA is the only figure ever used when a control transformer is selected for a system
Correct if the thermostat is electronic, because electronic thermostats return enough power over the common wire to make up a VA shortfall

questions.explanation: Undersized; the simultaneous load is 45 VA, so select at least the next adequate size. Loads are not averaged or reduced to the largest one, and a thermostat does not generate power to cover a transformer shortfall.

questions.question: A new refrigerant line set is to be pressure tested for leaks before evacuation. Which medium and practice are correct?

answers.text: Use oxygen from a cutting torch tank
Use compressed shop air without a regulator
Use dry nitrogen with a regulator, test at the specified pressure, and use an electronic detector or bubbles to check joints
Pressurize with refrigerant alone to maximum pressure

questions.explanation: Regulated dry nitrogen is inert and standard for pressure testing, with joints checked by detector or bubble solution, so C is correct. Oxygen can cause explosive combustion with oil, unregulated shop air adds moisture and uncontrolled pressure, and refrigerant alone is not the proper test medium.

questions.question: Why does the condition of skirting and ground moisture control under a manufactured home matter to HVAC performance, even though both are outside the duct system itself?

answers.text: Because skirting color determines solar gain on the crossover duct, which is the main factor in summer supply temperature at the far registers
Because a dry, enclosed under-home space protects ducts and the belly from moisture damage, freezing exposure, and the extra load that wet, open conditions impose
Because skirting is the combustion air source for the furnace, and any gap in the skirting changes burner air enough to alter manifold pressure readings
Because ground moisture raises refrigerant head pressure directly, since the condenser coil senses soil humidity through the home's floor assembly

questions.explanation: An enclosed, drier under-home space shields ducts and belly material from moisture, animals, and freezing air, preserving delivered capacity. Skirting color is not the main supply-temperature factor, skirting is not the furnace's combustion-air source, and soil humidity does not directly set condenser head pressure.

questions.question: Why must the outside termination of a PVC vent be supported and secured rather than left to cantilever freely from the wall?

answers.text: An unsupported termination cannot affect the vent because PVC becomes completely rigid once solvent cement has cured fully
Support is only cosmetic, required so the termination lines up evenly with siding and trim for a finished appearance outside
A free cantilever improves drainage by flexing downward under the weight of condensate until water runs out of the end quickly
Wind and weight can stress joints and shift alignment

questions.explanation: An unsupported termination acts as a lever on the last joint and penetration; wind load and its own weight can crack joints, shift slope, and open leaks. Option A overstates PVC rigidity, option B reduces a structural need to appearance, and option C treats sagging as a drainage feature when sagging actually traps condensate inside the vent.

questions.question: What distinguishes self-contained (active) recovery equipment from system-dependent (passive) recovery equipment?

answers.text: Self-contained equipment has its own compressor or pump to draw refrigerant out of a system
Self-contained equipment relies entirely on the appliance compressor and pressure differences to move refrigerant
Self-contained equipment can only be used on appliances holding less than five pounds of refrigerant
Self-contained equipment recovers refrigerant as a liquid on every job regardless of system condition

questions.explanation: Self-contained equipment carries its own compressor or pump, so it can pull refrigerant from a system that is dead or leaking. Option B describes system-dependent equipment, which needs the appliance compressor or pressure differential to work. Option C is wrong because charge size does not define the equipment class, and option D is wrong because recovered phase depends on method and conditions, not on the machine alone.

questions.question: Instead of bypassing to the return, a designer relieves excess air into a hallway and basement area that tolerate extra conditioning. What is this strategy called, and what is its main trade-off?

answers.text: A dump zone; the relieved area may be overconditioned while it absorbs excess air
A dead zone; the relieved area receives no air at all, and the trade-off is that the excess blower airflow is absorbed by raising static pressure in the trunk instead
A purge zone; the relieved area is ventilated outdoors, and the trade-off is the energy cost of discarding conditioned air through an exterior wall opening on every cycle
A staging zone; the relieved area is heated by a separate appliance, and the trade-off is the fuel cost of running two heat sources whenever only one thermostat is calling

questions.explanation: A dump zone gives excess supply air a harmless destination instead of short-circuiting it into the return, at the cost of overconditioning that tolerant area. The other descriptions send the air nowhere, outdoors, or to a second appliance, none of which describes relieving air into a non-critical conditioned area.

questions.question: A balanced ventilation system is preferred over exhaust-only ventilation in a very cold climate home with natural-draft combustion equipment mainly because it:

answers.text: Supplies about as much air as it exhausts, limiting house depressurization
Heats all of the incoming outdoor air fully up to room temperature without any heat loss or energy use of any kind during cold weather operation
Eliminates the need for local bathroom exhaust
Allows the combustion appliance to share the ventilation duct

questions.explanation: Matching supply and exhaust keeps pressures near neutral, protecting natural-draft appliances from backdrafting. Incoming air is tempered by heat recovery at best, not heated for free to room temperature. Balanced systems do not replace local exhaust, and combustion vents must never be combined with ventilation ducts.

questions.question: Why do many manufacturers require product registration within a set window after installation for extended parts coverage?

answers.text: Registration is purely a marketing enrollment that has no effect on the duration or terms of the equipment's parts coverage
Registration links the serial number to the install date and owner, activating the longer registered warranty term
The unregistered warranty is longer, so registration is offered mainly to shorten coverage in exchange for email promotions
Registration transfers the warranty to the installing company, so the homeowner no longer owns the coverage on their equipment

questions.explanation: For many brands the longer parts term applies only when the product is registered on time with its installation details. It is a coverage condition rather than mere marketing, registration extends rather than shortens the term, and coverage stays with the equipment owner rather than transferring to the installer.

questions.question: A complete bid for a rooftop unit replacement should include which set of cost elements?

answers.text: Direct labor, materials, equipment, permits, overhead, and profit
Only the purchase price of the rooftop unit and the sales tax charged on that equipment purchase
Direct labor and materials only, because overhead and profit are handled separately after the job is awarded
Materials, advertising expense for the season, and office rent, with field labor treated as an owner draw

questions.explanation: A is correct because a complete bid recovers direct job costs plus permits, overhead, and profit. B is incorrect because it omits labor, overhead, and profit needed to perform the work. C is incorrect because excluding overhead and profit from the bid understates the selling price. D is incorrect because it mixes period marketing costs into job cost while misclassifying field labor.

questions.question: After a hermetic compressor burnout, a replacement compressor is installed. Beyond changing the liquid-line drier, what contamination follow-up protects the new compressor?

answers.text: Test the oil/system for acid and fit suction-side filtration, then recheck and remove it as cleanup is confirmed
Do nothing further, because a single liquid-line drier change always removes all acid and debris left in the system by a hermetic motor burnout
Flush the new compressor itself with solvent before startup, because flushing a hermetic unit internally is the standard way to remove burnout contamination
Raise the operating superheat substantially for the first month, because running hot is an accepted substitute for removing acid from a contaminated system

questions.explanation: Burnout leaves acid and debris throughout the system, so acid testing plus temporary suction filtration with follow-up checks is the accepted cleanup approach. One drier change rarely completes a burnout cleanup, flushing inside a new hermetic compressor is not a service procedure, and running hot does not neutralize or remove acid and can harm the new machine.

questions.question: On a call for heat, the first electric stage starts promptly, but the second and third stages come on roughly 30 to 75 seconds apart. What does this show?

answers.text: A faulty thermostat that is closing its contacts slowly, one pole at a time, over more than a minute on every heat call made
Normal sequencer staging delays
Loose wire nuts heating and cooling in sequence, which randomly connects each strip as the connections expand with load current
A failing utility supply that restores one phase leg at a time after each brief sag caused by the previous strip starting up

questions.explanation: Sequencers are built with staggered thermal delays so stages energize in sequence, limiting inrush and letting the blower establish airflow, so 30-to-75-second spacing is normal. Option A misdescribes thermostat action, option C invents a thermal wiring effect, and option D describes a supply fault that would show other symptoms.

questions.question: A TXV system runs with a sweating, frost-covered suction line to the compressor. Readings: suction 156 psig, superheat 2°F, subcooling 6°F, compressor amps 112% of rated, discharge superheat low, airflow and charge weight both verified correct, and the frost persists after the bulb is re-secured and insulated. What is the most likely cause?

answers.text: A dirty condenser coil restricting heat rejection, which raises head pressure sharply while leaving evaporator superheat near its setpoint
A restricted liquid-line drier, which would starve the valve, raise superheat, and show a temperature drop across the drier body
A TXV stuck open
A low refrigerant charge, which starves the evaporator and produces high superheat with low suction pressure, the reverse of this pattern

questions.explanation: Near-zero superheat with high suction pressure and frost reaching the compressor is liquid floodback from a valve feeding far beyond the load, confirmed when re-securing the bulb changes nothing. A low charge and a drier restriction both starve the evaporator and raise superheat, and a dirty condenser attacks the high side while the TXV still holds superheat.

questions.question: A compressor is located below its air-cooled condenser, so discharge gas must rise through a vertical discharge riser before reaching the condenser. Oil management on this discharge riser should include:

answers.text: No provisions, because hot gas always carries oil at any velocity, including at the low mass flow of a lightly loaded system on a cold night when discharge velocity in the riser falls to its minimum
A liquid receiver installed in the discharge line
An EPR valve at the top of the riser
A trap at the base of the discharge riser and correct sizing so oil is carried upward rather than falling back toward the compressor at low flow

questions.explanation: Discharge risers face the same oil-lift physics as suction risers, so base trapping and adequate velocity keep oil moving toward the condenser and separator instead of slugging back. Option A ignores low-load velocity loss, option B puts a liquid vessel in a hot-gas line, and option C places a suction-side regulator where it cannot manage oil.

questions.question: A walk-in cooler holds product temperature except after busy delivery periods, when box temperature rises for hours. The coil, fans, and refrigerant readings check normal, but a door sweep is torn and the gasket pulls away at one corner. What is the most likely explanation?

answers.text: Warm, moist outside air infiltrating through the door leaks, adding latent and sensible load and frosting the coil
A failed evaporator pressure regulator that is holding suction pressure too high at all hours, including overnight periods when the doors remain closed and no warm product is loaded
An oversized compressor that short-cycles too often to dehumidify the box
A liquid-line sight glass that has become too clear during operation

questions.explanation: Infiltration through a torn sweep and leaking gasket admits warm, moist air, which loads the box and frosts the coil, especially after frequent door use. A regulator fault in option B would show in suction-pressure readings, an oversized compressor in option C would short-cycle even without delivery periods, and option D describes a normal clear glass, not an air leak.

questions.question: An applicant's papers are complete, but the file leaves the Board unsatisfied that the applicant has the financial integrity to operate as a contractor. Which Board responses does the denial rule support?

answers.text: The Board must approve the license anyway, since financial integrity cannot be tested once the experience proof is accepted
The Board may only suggest voluntary limits, since denial is reserved for applicants who fail the written examination parts
The Board must deny unless the applicant passes a new financial examination administered by the testing service each cycle
The Board shall deny for failure to prove the qualifications, and as proof of financial integrity it may require a surety bond as a condition

questions.explanation: D is correct: the Board shall deny a license when the applicant has failed to provide satisfactory proof of the qualifications, including the financial integrity to operate as a contractor, and as proof of financial integrity the Board may require the applicant to post a surety bond as a condition for licensure. A is wrong because financial integrity is itself one of the qualifications that must be satisfactorily proven. B is wrong because denial grounds reach well beyond examination failure. C is wrong because no testing-service financial examination is part of the rule; the bond is the stated financial-integrity instrument.

questions.question: Attic air temperature measures 105°F, but an uninsulated supply duct in that attic gains heat faster than attic air temperature alone predicts. The roof deck above it measures 145°F. What additional transfer path is at work?

answers.text: Convection currents from the attic floor insulation are rising through the duct wall and carrying stored heat from the ceiling below into the airstream
The duct metal is generating heat by friction as air moves through it, an effect that grows stronger directly under the hottest part of the roof deck
Ultraviolet light passing through the roof deck is heating the duct directly, because shingles and decking transmit most solar radiation into the attic
Radiant gain from hot roof deck

questions.explanation: A 145°F roof deck radiates heat directly to the duct surface, adding a radiant load on top of conduction from 105°F attic air. Floor insulation does not convect stored ceiling heat into a duct, friction heating at duct velocities is negligible, and roof assemblies block rather than transmit most solar radiation as light.

questions.question: A legacy mercury thermostat short-cycles a gas furnace: burners run about seven minutes, shut off with the room still roughly 2 degrees below setpoint, and restart soon after. The gas valve circuit measures 0.78 A. The thermostat's heat anticipator dial is set at 0.25 A. Furnace temperature rise and limit operation test normal. What is the correct adjustment?

answers.text: Set the anticipator near 0.1 A to add more anticipator heat so the burners run longer and finally bring the room fully up to setpoint before shutting off
Replace the thermostat because anticipator settings do not affect cycle length on gas equipment, and the short cycles must come from the furnace limit circuit instead
Set the anticipator to about 0.8 A to match the measured circuit current
Remove the anticipator from the circuit so the thermostat responds only to room air, accepting the wide temperature swings that follow on this type of control

questions.explanation: The anticipator is set at 0.25 A while the circuit actually draws 0.78 A, so the anticipator heater produces too much heat, satisfies the thermostat early, and short-cycles the furnace short of setpoint; matching the dial to the measured 0.8 A corrects it. Setting it lower adds still more anticipator heat and worsens the early shutoff, the limit circuit tests normal so the thermostat setting is the fault, and removing the anticipator trades short cycles for overshoot swings.

questions.question: A ventilation design uses the rate formula: CFM = 0.03 x floor area + 7.5 x (bedrooms + 1). For a 1,600 sq ft house with 3 bedrooms, what is the required continuous ventilation rate?

answers.text: 55.5 CFM, because only the floor-area term applies to houses
70.5 CFM, because the bedroom term uses bedrooms minus 1
78 CFM, because 0.03 x 1,600 = 48 and 7.5 x 4 = 30, totaling 78
108 CFM, because the floor-area coefficient is 0.05 for houses over 1,500 sq ft

questions.explanation: Both terms of the given formula count: the area term contributes 48 CFM and the occupant term, using bedrooms + 1 = 4, contributes 30 CFM. Option A is wrong because dropping the occupant term understates the rate — people, not just floor area, generate the contaminants ventilation dilutes; option B is wrong because the formula as given adds 1 to the bedroom count to represent the primary suite's two occupants; option D is wrong because the coefficient in the stated formula is 0.03; substituting 0.05 changes the given method rather than applying it.

questions.question: A blower is rated to deliver design airflow at 0.50 inches of water column total external static pressure. Measured component drops are: filter 0.12, wet cooling coil 0.28, supply duct system 0.20, and return duct system 0.10 inches. What does the budget show, and what follows?

answers.text: The system totals 0.50 inches exactly, so the blower delivers its full rated airflow as designed
Only the largest single drop matters, so the effective static is 0.28 inches and airflow will be high
The filter drop should be subtracted, giving 0.46 inches, since filters unload steadily as they collect dust over a full season of service in a dusty building
The system totals 0.70 inches, so airflow will fall short until resistance is reduced or the blower is reset

questions.explanation: D is correct: 0.12 + 0.28 + 0.20 + 0.10 = 0.70 inches, which exceeds the 0.50-inch rating point, so the blower operates higher on its curve and delivers less air. A is wrong because the four drops add to 0.70, not 0.50, so the rating point is exceeded by 0.20 inches. B is wrong because component drops in the same airstream add together; the blower works against their sum, not the largest one. C is wrong because a filter drop is a real resistance the blower must overcome, and loading raises rather than lowers it.

kentucky-hvac.quiz_title: Kentucky HVAC Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam

questions.question: On a pressure-enthalpy diagram for a vapor-compression cycle, what do the two axes represent?

answers.text: Temperature on the vertical axis and entropy on the horizontal axis, so every heat transfer process in the cycle is read as a change in entropy alone
Pressure on the horizontal axis and volume on the vertical axis, with enthalpy calculated afterward from a separate table for each plotted state point
Suction pressure on one axis and discharge pressure on the other, so compressor ratio can be read directly without knowing any heat content values at all
Pressure vertically and enthalpy horizontally

questions.explanation: A pressure-enthalpy chart plots pressure on the vertical axis against enthalpy on the horizontal axis, letting cycle work and refrigeration effect be read as enthalpy differences. Temperature-entropy and pressure-volume diagrams are different charts, and the two pressures alone do not define the cycle states.

questions.question: A VFD is applied to a supply fan that runs at half airflow for much of the day. The main energy advantage is:

answers.text: The drive converts the motor into a higher-voltage machine, so the same airflow is produced with proportionally less current at full speed
The drive eliminates the need for airflow measurement, because fan speed alone guarantees that design airflow is delivered at every condition
Fan power falls sharply as speed is reduced
The drive lets the fan run above its rated speed continuously, which is where the greatest energy savings are found in variable-air-volume work

questions.explanation: Fan power falls sharply as speed is reduced. Savings do not come from raising voltage, from assuming airflow without measuring it, or from continuous overspeed operation.

questions.question: A float switch in an auxiliary condensate pan keeps tripping. What is the correct service response?

answers.text: Clear the primary drain problem and restore normal drainage before returning the unit to service.
Bypass the switch permanently, because repeated tripping proves the switch itself is oversensitive and unreliable in humid attics
Raise the switch in the pan with a block of foam so a higher water level is required before it can interrupt equipment operation
Reset the switch repeatedly without inspection, since nuisance trips are normal whenever outdoor humidity stays high for several days

questions.explanation: Repeated trips mean primary drainage has failed and the pan is filling, so the cause must be corrected. Bypassing or raising the switch removes the protection, and resetting without inspection lets overflow damage continue.

questions.question: How does a person become a Kentucky apprentice HVAC mechanic, and what follows from registration?

answers.text: Pass the apprentice examination, pay the registration examination fee, and renew the license each birth month

Complete two years of trade employment first, then apply for an apprentice license on the master application form on the schedule and terms the licensing regulation establishes through the channel the department designates for this purpose.
Register with the department and pay the apprentice certificate fee stated in the licensing regulation schedule
Register with the department to receive a certificate with no fee, be credited in the apprentice register for supervised hours, and report address or employer changes in writing

questions.explanation: D is correct: The department issues an apprentice certificate to a person who registers as an apprentice, with no fee to obtain or renew the registration; the department keeps an apprentice register crediting supervised hours, and the apprentice must notify the department in writing of address or employer changes. A is wrong because there is no apprentice examination or apprentice fee in the current scheme. B is wrong because the certificate is by registration and is a certificate, not a license earned after two years of employment. C is wrong because apprentices are expressly not required to pay a fee for the certificate of registration.

questions.question: What instrument placed over a supply register measures delivered CFM directly?

answers.text: A manifold gauge set
A capture hood (flow hood / balometer)
A clamp ammeter
A combustion analyzer fitted with a long flue-gas sampling probe

questions.explanation: A capture hood fits over the outlet and reads volumetric flow in CFM directly, so B is correct. Manifold gauges measure refrigerant pressure, a clamp meter measures current, and a combustion analyzer measures flue gases, none of which measure register airflow.

questions.question: What distinguishes self-contained (active) recovery equipment from system-dependent (passive) recovery equipment?

answers.text: Self-contained equipment has its own compressor or pump to draw refrigerant out of a system
Self-contained equipment relies entirely on the appliance compressor and pressure differences to move refrigerant
Self-contained equipment can only be used on appliances holding less than five pounds of refrigerant
Self-contained equipment recovers refrigerant as a liquid on every job regardless of system condition

questions.explanation: Self-contained equipment carries its own compressor or pump, so it can pull refrigerant from a system that is dead or leaking. Option B describes system-dependent equipment, which needs the appliance compressor or pressure differential to work. Option C is wrong because charge size does not define the equipment class, and option D is wrong because recovered phase depends on method and conditions, not on the machine alone.

questions.question: A panel that stages equipment by zone demand has three of four zones calling on a mild day. One small zone calls alone on a colder day. How does demand-based staging treat the two cases differently?

answers.text: It runs the highest stage in both cases, because any zone call is treated as a whole-house call once at least one thermostat in the system is asking for heat
It runs the lowest stage whenever more zones call, because a larger combined duct area requires less equipment capacity to satisfy all of the calling thermostats together
It brings on more capacity when a larger share of zones calls, and holds lower stage for the single small call
It alternates stages on a timer in both cases, selecting capacity by elapsed run time rather than by how much of the house is asking for conditioning at the moment

questions.explanation: Demand-weighted panels match equipment stage to the proportion of the system calling, so most zones calling justifies higher stage while one small zone is served on low stage. Treating every call as a whole-house call defeats the staging logic, more open duct area accompanies more load rather than less, and the selection is by demand share rather than a timer.

questions.question: A clinic asks why its ultrasonic humidifier leaves white dust and why steam is often preferred in healthcare settings. What is the correct explanation?

answers.text: White dust is harmless metal flake from the ductwork, and humidifier type has no relationship to what is carried into the airstream
Steam units aerosolize more minerals than ultrasonic units, because boiling concentrates minerals and then ejects them as a fine white powder
The dust comes from the air filter shedding fibers, which happens only when an ultrasonic humidifier is installed in the same building
Ultrasonic units aerosolize the minerals and microbes in their water, while steam humidification boils water and does not carry those contents into the air the same way.

questions.explanation: Mist-type humidifiers put their water's dissolved minerals and any microbes into the air as droplets that dry to dust; boiling separates water vapor from those contents. The dust is humidifier-borne, not duct metal or filter fiber, and steam carries fewer, not more, mineral particles.

questions.question: A customer asks the technician to 'just keep adding R-22' to a leaking system instead of replacing it. Which fact most changes that conversation?

answers.text: R-22 is still manufactured domestically in unlimited quantities, so its price is expected to fall steadily every year
Virgin R-22 production and import ended in the United States, so supply is reclaimed stock at rising and uncertain cost
Adding refrigerant to a leaking system is prohibited in all cases, including small appliances with no leak-repair options
R-22 can be freely mixed with newer refrigerants in the same system to stretch the remaining supply at lower cost

questions.explanation: New R-22 supply ended, leaving reclaimed material whose price and availability drive replacement economics. It is not still produced without limit, leak and service rules are more nuanced than a blanket ban on charging, and refrigerants must never be mixed in a system.

questions.question: Why do contracting businesses retain job, payroll, and tax records for a set period after a project ends?

answers.text: So the supplier can reuse the customer's equipment selections as a template for quoting unrelated future customers
To support audits, warranty questions, tax filings, and dispute resolution
Only to fill archive space required by the office lease, with no business or legal purpose served by keeping them
To allow employees to revise their recorded hours after final pay whenever they disagree with the original timesheets

questions.explanation: B is correct because retained records substantiate taxes, payroll, warranty history, and the facts if a dispute or audit arises. A is incorrect because a customer's project records are not a supplier quoting template. C is incorrect because retention serves compliance and business purposes, not lease space requirements. D is incorrect because records are kept to preserve an accurate history, not to permit after-the-fact timesheet changes.

questions.question: An electric furnace delivers very hot air for a few minutes, trips its limit, then delivers lukewarm air. Only the first strip seems to cycle. What staging fault fits best?

answers.text: All strips are energized together with no staging delay
The thermostat anticipator is set for gas heat, causing the strips to short-cycle in a pattern unrelated to the limit trips seen
The blower is running at cooling speed, which cools the strips so fast that the limit opens from rapid temperature change
The sequencer for the later stages is holding every strip on continuously, so the limit never has a reason to open at all

questions.explanation: If all strips come on at once instead of staging, discharge temperature overshoots, the limit trips, and heat output collapses until reset, matching the hot-then-lukewarm pattern. Option B concerns cycle timing, not a single overshoot and trip, option C would lower rather than spike air temperature, and option D contradicts the observed cycling off.

questions.question: Tank pressure on a warm afternoon is well over 100 psi, yet the appliances need gas at inches of water column. What does the first-stage regulator in a typical two-stage system do?

answers.text: It cuts tank pressure to about 10 psi for the yard line
It raises tank pressure before the second stage, because appliance regulators need a boosted inlet pressure whenever outdoor temperature climbs in the afternoon
It delivers the final appliance manifold pressure directly, so no second regulation stage is needed anywhere between an outdoor tank and the indoor burners
It vents excess tank pressure to the atmosphere continuously, holding the yard line at appliance pressure by releasing whatever vapor the tank produces above demand

questions.explanation: The first-stage regulator reduces variable tank pressure to an intermediate pressure, commonly around 10 psi, for the line to the building. Final reduction to inches of water column is left to the second stage, and regulators reduce and control pressure rather than boosting it or venting vapor continuously.

questions.question: A system with verified correct charge, airflow at the air handler, and clean coils cannot hold setpoint on hot afternoons. Supply registers deliver noticeably less air than the blower produces, and the attic shows a disconnected supply duct joint blowing cooled air into the attic. What conclusion is best supported?

answers.text: Delivered capacity is being lost through duct leakage, so repairing and sealing the duct restores cooling without changing the equipment
The equipment is undersized and must be replaced with a larger system
The charge verification must be wrong, because correct charge guarantees setpoint is held, since charge alone determines whether the setpoint can be held
The thermostat is miscalibrated, because duct condition cannot affect room temperature

questions.explanation: Air produced but never delivered is lost capacity, and a disconnected joint dumping supply air into the attic fully explains a shortfall despite a healthy refrigeration circuit. Option B condemns equipment before accounting for air that is measured missing from the registers. Option C overclaims what charge verification proves, since it says nothing about the distribution system, and option D ignores a physically observed leak path.

questions.question: A masonry chimney is relined for a mid-efficiency furnace. A liner much larger than the vent connector is proposed to 'give the gases room.' The main risk is:

answers.text: Excessive draft that pulls too much dilution air through the draft hood and raises the appliance firing rate above its nameplate input
Flue gases moving so fast in the large liner that they cannot transfer heat and instead melt the liner joints within one heating season
A pressure increase inside the chimney that forces the furnace pressure switch to stay closed after the inducer has shut down
Slow, cool flue gases with weak draft and condensation

questions.explanation: Slow, cool flue gases with weak draft and condensation. A large liner does not raise firing rate or flue-gas speed, and it does not create pressure that holds a pressure switch closed.

questions.question: A reach-in cooler runs constantly at 44°F. The condenser coil in the machine compartment is blanketed with grease and lint, head pressure is well above normal for the room temperature, discharge temperature is high, superheat and charge indicators are otherwise unremarkable, and the compressor shell is very hot. What is the most likely cause?

answers.text: An undercharge, which would show low head pressure, low subcooling, and a bubbling sight glass rather than this high-pressure pattern
A TXV overfeeding the evaporator, which lowers superheat sharply and cannot explain the blanket of grease found on the condenser
A worn door gasket adding infiltration load, which lengthens runtimes but does not by itself drive head pressure and discharge temperature this high
A fouled condenser coil

questions.explanation: High head and discharge temperatures with a visibly blanketed condenser are a heat-rejection failure. An undercharge lowers the high side, a gasket adds load without this pressure signature, and TXV overfeeding shows up as collapsed superheat on the low side.

questions.question: Before replacing an indoor blower motor, a technician opens the unit disconnect. The motor circuit includes a run capacitor, and a co-worker mentions the unit has a second feed for its electric heat section on a separate breaker. Which sequence makes the work safe?

answers.text: Trust the open disconnect, since a single disconnect is required to remove every source of power from an air handler
Wait ten minutes after opening the disconnect, since capacitors and second feeds de-energize themselves in that time
Open and lock out both feeds, prove the meter on a known live source, test the unit dead, re-prove the meter, and discharge the capacitor through a resistor before handling it
Short the capacitor terminals with an insulated screwdriver as the first step, then check for voltage once the motor is out of the housing and the replacement motor is ready to wire in

questions.explanation: C is correct: Safe service requires isolating every energy source — here both the blower feed and the separate heat-section feed — locking them out, verifying absence of voltage with a meter proven live before and after the test (live-dead-live), and bleeding the run capacitor's stored charge through a resistor rather than a dead short. A is wrong because the stem states there is a second feed the single disconnect does not control. B is wrong because a charged capacitor and an unopened second breaker do not become safe with time. D is wrong because shorting a capacitor with a screwdriver can damage it and arc, and it is never a substitute for verifying the circuit is dead first.

questions.question: A building is losing its slight positive pressure whenever exhaust fans run, and doors stand ajar with wind noise at entrances. The relief and exhaust controls are not tracking supply airflow. What is the control goal that fixes this?

answers.text: Seal the relief path completely shut so building pressure rises without any limit whenever the supply fan runs at full speed on a windy day
Modulate relief or exhaust in step with supply and outdoor airflow to hold a small, steady positive building pressure
Drive building pressure strongly negative so entrance doors pull themselves closed
Control pressure from a sensor placed in the supply duct instead of in the building space

questions.explanation: Tracking relief to airflow holds the intended slight positive pressure across operating conditions. Sealing relief invites over-pressurization, strong negative pressure causes infiltration and can affect combustion appliances, and duct pressure is a different variable from space pressure.

questions.question: No-heat call. A furnace completes prepurge, proves its pressure switch, and glows its igniter on every trial, but the burners never light and no gas smell is present. A meter shows 24 V delivered to the gas valve terminals during the trial, manifold pressure reads zero, and the gas valve coil measures open circuit against a specified resistance in the tens of ohms. Inlet gas pressure is normal. What is the most likely cause?

answers.text: An open gas valve coil
A failed igniter that never reaches lighting temperature, ruled out because the igniter glows visibly on every trial and the failure includes zero manifold pressure with full valve voltage
A control board that never calls for gas, ruled out because 24 V is measured at the gas valve terminals during the ignition trial window
A closed manual gas cock starving the valve, ruled out because inlet pressure at the valve measures normal while the manifold side stays at zero

questions.explanation: Voltage arrives, inlet pressure is normal, and the coil is electrically open, so the valve can never open and manifold pressure stays at zero despite a glowing igniter. The igniter performs, the board delivers its call, and gas reaches the valve inlet, leaving the open coil as the single failed link in the sequence.

questions.question: A designer's worksheet shows: blower maximum external static 0.70 in. w.g.; available for ducts listed as 0.70; friction rate computed from 0.70 over a TEL of 200 feet, giving 0.35 in. per 100 feet. The selected coil drops 0.30 and the filter 0.15. Identify the design error and its consequence.

answers.text: The designer spent the blower's whole budget on the ducts without subtracting the coil and filter; only 0.25 in. is truly available, so the correct friction rate is 0.125 in. per 100 feet and the ducts as sized will be far too small, producing high static and low delivered airflow
There is no error, because coil and filter drops are paid from a separate budget
The only error is arithmetic: 0.70 over 200 feet gives 0.70 per 100 feet
The consequence will be oversized ducts and excessive airflow at the registers

questions.explanation: Available static for ducts is what remains after non-duct components are subtracted: 0.70 - 0.30 - 0.15 = 0.25 in., and 0.25 x 100 / 200 = 0.125 in. per 100 feet — the as-designed rate is nearly three times too high. Option B is wrong because coil and filter are external components drawing on the same single blower budget — there is no second budget; option C is wrong because the arithmetic (0.70 x 100 / 200 = 0.35) is internally consistent; the flaw is the 0.70 input, not the division; option D is wrong because an inflated friction rate sizes ducts too small, which restricts airflow rather than increasing it.

questions.question: A compressor shows discharge temperatures climbing over a season, oil that is dark and acidic at a sample, and valve wear at teardown. Suction pressure has been low and the compression ratio high because of a dirty evaporator and low airflow. What is the underlying mechanism linking these findings?

answers.text: The low suction pressure cooled the discharge gas so effectively that the oil thickened, and the thick oil is what scored the valves and darkened over time
The dirty evaporator added refrigerant to the system, and the resulting overcharge is the only condition that can raise a compressor discharge temperature
Sustained high compression ratio overheated the discharge gas, breaking down the oil
Acid formed first from a factory defect in the oil, and that acid is what raised the suction superheat and lowered the airflow through the evaporator coil

questions.explanation: Low suction pressure with maintained head pressure raises the compression ratio, which raises discharge temperature enough to degrade oil into acids and varnish that wear valves. Low suction pressure raises rather than lowers discharge temperature in this condition, an airflow fault does not add charge to the system, and the sequence runs from operating conditions to oil breakdown, not from defective oil to an airflow problem.

kentucky-hvac-journeyman.quiz_title: Kentucky HVAC Journeyman Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam

questions.question: What does the balance point of an air-source heat pump installation represent?

answers.text: The outdoor temperature at which the refrigerant charge is weighed in during the initial system start-up
The indoor temperature at which the thermostat switches the system from heating mode to cooling mode
The suction pressure at which the compressor's internal overload protector first opens on a hot afternoon
The outdoor temperature at which the heat pump's heating capacity exactly equals the building's heat loss

questions.explanation: D is correct: The balance point is the outdoor temperature where heat pump output matches the structure's heat loss; below it, supplemental heat is needed to hold indoor temperature. A is wrong because charging is done by measured methods, not at a balance point temperature. B is wrong because mode changeover is a thermostat setting, unrelated to capacity balance. C is wrong because overload operation is a fault condition, not a design balance concept.

questions.question: What is the maximum length of the flexible transition duct that connects a clothes dryer to its exhaust duct system?

answers.text: 4 feet, and the transition duct must be concealed inside the wall cavity behind the dryer for protection
12 feet, provided the transition duct is supported at every 2 feet along its concealed horizontal run
8 feet, in a single length, listed and labeled, and not concealed within construction
No limit applies, because transition duct is appliance equipment rather than part of the building duct system

questions.explanation: C is correct: Transition ducts must be a single length not exceeding 8 feet, listed and labeled for the purpose, and must not be concealed within construction. A is wrong on both the length and because concealment is prohibited, not required. B is wrong because 12 feet exceeds the limit and concealment is not allowed at any length. D is wrong because a definite 8-foot limit applies.

questions.question: A journeyman must pressure-test a newly installed refrigerant piping run with the system empty. Which gas and method are acceptable for the test?

answers.text: Shop compressed air, because its moisture content does not matter in a system that will be evacuated afterward anyway
Oxygen from a welding cylinder, because its high available pressure lets one cylinder fill even the largest piping run
Refrigerant mixed with air, because a trace of refrigerant is the only way an electronic detector can find a test leak
Dry nitrogen regulated to the test pressure, held and checked for leaks — nitrogen is inert and moisture-free

questions.explanation: D is correct: Refrigerant piping is pressure-tested with dry nitrogen through a regulator; nitrogen is inert and dry, and the standing test shows leaks safely. A is wrong because shop air introduces moisture and oil contamination and is not the accepted test medium. B is wrong because oxygen in a refrigerant system is an explosion hazard and must never be used for pressure testing. C is wrong because air is never intentionally mixed into a system for a pressure test; trace-gas methods use nitrogen as the carrier pressure.

questions.question: A journeyman is laying out a new supply duct system for a dwelling addition. What method must be used to size the ducts?

answers.text: Equal friction by eye, matching each new run to the size of the nearest existing run in the original house
A fixed velocity of 900 feet per minute applied to every trunk and branch regardless of available static pressure, checked afterward with a static pressure reading at the plenum
An approved duct sizing method such as ACCA Manual D, based on the room loads and the blower's available static pressure
One square inch of duct area per 100 Btu per hour of furnace input, applied uniformly to trunks and branches alike

questions.explanation: C is correct: Residential duct systems must be sized by an approved method — ACCA Manual D — using room-by-room loads, total external static pressure, and friction rate. A is wrong because copying existing sizes ignores the addition's loads and static budget. B is wrong because a single velocity ignores friction rate and blower capability. D is wrong because no such Btu-per-square-inch sizing rule exists for duct design.

questions.question: A journeyman has opened the disconnect and applied a lock and tag before replacing a blower motor. What must be done before the motor terminals are touched?

answers.text: Assume the circuit is dead, since an open disconnect with a lock applied removes all voltage downstream
Ask the homeowner to watch the panel and shout if anyone approaches while the motor is being changed
Verify the absence of voltage at the equipment with a meter before touching the terminals or conductors
Close and reopen the disconnect once to confirm the blades move freely, then begin work on the motor

questions.explanation: C is correct: Lockout must be followed by verification: test for absence of voltage at the point of work with a meter before touching conductors, since a wrong disconnect, backfeed, or stored charge can leave parts energized. A is wrong because an open disconnect alone is not proof of a de-energized state. B is wrong because a bystander warning does not verify the electrical state. D is wrong because operating the disconnect says nothing about voltage at the motor terminals.

questions.question: A furnace delivers 72,000 Btu per hour of output with a measured temperature rise of 45 degrees across the heat exchanger. Using CFM = output / (1.08 x rise), what airflow is moving through the furnace?

answers.text: 720 cfm, found by dividing the output by 100, a shortcut that ignores the measured temperature rise value
2,400 cfm, found by dividing the output by 30, using the minimum rise instead of the measured 45 degrees
About 1,480 cfm, found by dividing 72,000 by the product of 1.08 and the 45-degree measured rise
3,500 cfm, found by dividing the output by the rise and then multiplying the result by a duct loss factor

questions.explanation: C is correct: CFM = 72,000 / (1.08 x 45) = 72,000 / 48.6 = 1,481 cfm, about 1,480 cfm. A is wrong because dividing by 100 discards both the 1.08 air constant and the measured rise. B is wrong because it substitutes a 30-degree rise that was not measured. D is wrong because no duct-loss multiplier belongs in the temperature-rise airflow formula.

questions.question: A combustion air opening must provide 50 square inches of net free area and will be covered by a wood louver. Wood louvers may be assumed to have 25 percent free area. What gross louver area is required?

answers.text: 200 square inches of gross louver area to deliver the required 50 square inches of net free area
100 square inches of gross louver area, figured by doubling the required net free area once
67 square inches of gross louver area, figured with the free-area percentage used for metal louvers
50 square inches of gross louver area, treating the louver face area as fully open to airflow

questions.explanation: A is correct: Gross area = net free area / free-area fraction = 50 / 0.25 = 200 sq in. B is wrong because doubling assumes 50 percent free area, which is not the wood louver assumption. C is wrong because about 67 sq in. uses the 75 percent metal louver figure for a wood louver. D is wrong because a louvered opening is not 100 percent free area.

questions.question: A thermostat calls for cooling but the contactor coil measures 0 volts while 24 volts is present leaving the air handler control board. The thermostat cable run is long. What is the most likely fault?

answers.text: An oversized control transformer, which pushes so much voltage down the cable that the contactor coil burns open instantly
A failed compressor overload, which interrupts the line-voltage circuit and therefore also removes voltage from the coil circuit
An open in the low-voltage conductor or a failed contact in the circuit between the board and the contactor coil terminals
Low refrigerant charge, which opens the low-voltage circuit through the thermostat anticipator whenever superheat rises

questions.explanation: C is correct: Voltage present at the board but absent at the coil points to an open in the interconnecting low-voltage path: a broken conductor, failed safety/contact, or bad connection between the two points. A is wrong because an oversized transformer does not produce the stated pattern of voltage at one end and zero at the other. B is wrong because the compressor overload is in the line-voltage/load circuit, not the 24-volt coil feed. D is wrong because refrigerant charge does not open the thermostat circuit through an anticipator.

questions.question: A licensed journeyman prints business cards for weekend work that read 'Master HVAC Contractor' above the journeyman's name, reasoning that the journeyman passed the same trade coursework. What is the correct position?

answers.text: It is a title violation, since a person may use a title suggesting master status only while holding a valid master license
It is permitted, since any licensed HVAC mechanic may use the master title when working without an apprentice on small jobs
It is permitted if the cards also print the journeyman license number in small type at the bottom edge
It is a violation only if a customer signs a contract in reliance on the cards during the same calendar year

questions.explanation: A is correct: A person must not claim to be, advertise as, or use any title or designation likely to create the impression of being a master contractor unless the holder of the corresponding valid license. B is wrong because working alone does not confer the master title. C is wrong because printing a journeyman number does not cure a master title claim. D is wrong because the violation lies in holding out, not in whether a contract results.

questions.question: A 15 kW electric strip heater in a residential air handler operates on 240 volts single-phase. What current does the heater draw?

answers.text: 62.5 amperes, found by dividing the heater wattage by the supply voltage applied to the strip heater bank
36.1 amperes, found by dividing the heater wattage by 415 volts as a combined three-phase line value
125 amperes, found by multiplying the correct single-phase current by two for the two ungrounded conductors
31.3 amperes, found by dividing the heater wattage by 480 volts, the next standard voltage above the supply

questions.explanation: A is correct: Current = watts / volts = 15,000 W / 240 V = 62.5 A. B is wrong because 415 V is not the supply voltage; 15,000 / 415 = 36.1 A answers a different circuit. C is wrong because current is not doubled for two conductors — the same 62.5 A flows in each leg. D is wrong because 480 V was not the applied voltage; 15,000 / 480 = 31.3 A understates the actual draw.

questions.question: An electric duct heater rated 10 kW is connected to a 240-volt single-phase circuit. Ignoring power factor for this resistive load, what current does the heater draw?

answers.text: About 42 amps, found by dividing 10,000 watts by 240 volts, giving 41.7 amps for the resistive heater load
About 24 amps, found by dividing 10,000 watts by 415 volts, using a three-phase voltage the circuit does not have
About 83 amps, found by dividing 10,000 watts by 120 volts, using only half the voltage actually supplied to it
About 417 amps, found by dividing 10,000 watts by 24 volts, mistaking the control voltage for the heater supply

questions.explanation: A is correct: For a resistive load, I = P / V = 10,000 / 240 = 41.7 amps, about 42 amps. B is wrong because 415 volts is not the stated supply voltage. C is wrong because the heater is supplied at 240 volts, not 120 volts. D is wrong because 24 volts is the control-circuit voltage, not the heater power supply.

questions.question: One applicant worked two years under a Kentucky master contractor. Another worked two years doing HVAC work in another state and has verifiable documentation of it. How do the two experience paths compare?

answers.text: Only the first applicant qualifies, because experience gained outside Kentucky can never count toward this license at all, and documented out-of-state work may be used only as a character reference, never as qualifying experience toward any Kentucky license class
Only the second applicant qualifies, because supervised Kentucky employment must run four years before it satisfies the rule
Neither qualifies yet, because every journeyman applicant must complete four years of experience under the current statute

Both qualify — each of the two journeyman experience routes requires two years: supervised employment under a master, or HVAC work in Kentucky or another jurisdiction shown by verifiable documentation

questions.explanation: D is correct: The journeyman experience requirement offers two routes, each of two years: regular and principal employment under the direction and supervision of a master HVAC contractor, or two years performing HVAC work in Kentucky or another jurisdiction demonstrated by verifiable documentation. A is wrong because documented out-of-state HVAC work is the second route. B is wrong because the four-year figure is superseded; the supervised route is two years. C is wrong for the same reason: no route requires four years under the current statute.

questions.question: A homeowner wants an atmospherically vented furnace installed in a closet that opens into a bedroom. What installation arrangement satisfies the combustion-air requirement for this location?

answers.text: A direct-vent, sealed-combustion furnace, or a closet installation that draws all combustion air from outdoors
A standard atmospheric furnace drawing all of its combustion air through a louvered bedroom closet door with a note placed in the job file documenting the arrangement
A standard atmospheric furnace with one combustion-air opening cut into the closet ceiling from the attic
Any furnace, provided a carbon monoxide alarm is installed on the wall outside the bedroom door

questions.explanation: A is correct: Fuel-burning appliances serving sleeping-room areas must not draw combustion air from the sleeping space; a direct-vent sealed-combustion appliance, or an enclosed closet supplied entirely with outdoor combustion air, meets that rule. B is wrong because a louvered door still draws combustion air from the bedroom. C is wrong because a single attic opening does not supply the complete outdoor-air arrangement and the furnace remains open-combustion. D is wrong because a CO alarm is a warning device, not a combustion-air supply method.

questions.question: Plastic gas pipe is being installed underground between a meter and a garage heater. What must accompany the plastic pipe in the trench so the line can be located later?

answers.text: A layer of sand over the pipe, dyed yellow so future excavators recognize the trench as a gas line
An electrically continuous corrosion-resistant tracer wire run with the pipe for locating the line
A concrete cap poured over the pipe along the full length of the trench from meter to building
A second empty plastic sleeve beside the pipe, left open so a locating rod can be inserted later

questions.explanation: B is correct: Nonmetallic underground gas piping must be installed with an electrically continuous, corrosion-resistant tracer wire (or equivalent locating means) so the buried plastic line, which cannot be found with a metal detector, can be located. A is wrong because colored sand provides no locatable signal. C is wrong because a concrete cap is not the locating provision and complicates access. D is wrong because an empty sleeve is not a tracer and gives no surface locating signal.

questions.question: A condensate drain runs 12 feet horizontally from an air handler to its termination. The drain must slope at least 1/8 inch per foot in the direction of flow. What is the minimum total fall over the run?

answers.text: 12 inches of fall, figured at a full inch of slope for every foot of horizontal drain run from the unit
3 inches of fall, figured at one-quarter inch of slope for every foot of horizontal drain run from the unit
1.5 inches of fall, figured as 12 feet multiplied by 1/8 inch per foot in the direction of discharge flow
0.5 inch of fall, figured by dividing the run length in feet by the slope figure for the drain piping size

questions.explanation: C is correct: Total fall = length x slope = 12 ft x 1/8 in./ft = 1.5 inches, the minimum drop from the unit outlet to the termination. A is wrong because 1 inch per foot is eight times the required slope and is not the minimum figure. B is wrong because 1/4 inch per foot is the vent-connector slope figure, double the condensate minimum used here. D is wrong because fall is found by multiplying length by slope, not by dividing the two values.

questions.question: A single combustion air opening serves appliances totaling 60,000 Btu per hour. The vent connectors passing through the space have a combined cross-sectional area of 26 square inches. What minimum net free area must the single opening have?

answers.text: 20 square inches, since the ratio computation alone sets the size of a single combustion air opening in every arrangement
13 square inches, since a single opening is sized at one-half of the combined vent connector area
100 square inches, since every combustion air method carries the same flat minimum opening size
26 square inches, since the opening must be at least the larger of the ratio result and the vent connector area

questions.explanation: D is correct: The single-opening minimum is the larger of (1) 1 sq in. per 3,000 Btu/h = 60,000 / 3,000 = 20 sq in., and (2) the sum of the vent connector cross-sectional areas = 26 sq in. The larger figure, 26 sq in., governs. A is wrong because it stops at the ratio result and ignores the vent-connector prong. B is wrong because no one-half rule applies. C is wrong because the 100-square-inch floor belongs to the indoor-air and two-opening methods, not to the single-opening method.

questions.question: A licensed journeyman wants to advertise under a personal business name and sign a contract directly with a homeowner for a system change-out. What is the correct position?

answers.text: It is permitted, because a journeyman license carries the same right to advertise and contract as a master license holds
It is permitted if the journeyman carries the required insurance, because insurance alone confers contracting authority
It is permitted for jobs under a set dollar amount, because small residential change-outs fall outside the contracting rules

It is not permitted: a journeyman performs HVAC work under a master's supervision, direction, and responsibility, and only a licensed master may advertise and practice HVAC contracting and obtain the permits for the work

questions.explanation: D is correct: The journeyman license authorizes performing HVAC work under the supervision, direction, and responsibility of a master contractor; advertising and practicing HVAC contracting, including obtaining necessary permits, belongs to the master license, and using a title implying master status without that license is prohibited. A is wrong because the two licenses confer different authority. B is wrong because insurance is a practice condition, not a grant of contracting authority. C is wrong because no small-job dollar exception to the contracting rule exists.

questions.question: With the air handler running and a bedroom door closed, the bedroom measures noticeably positive to the hallway, the door is hard to latch against air pressure, and a tissue at the door undercut blows into the hall. The bedroom has supply air but no return. What is the correct fix?

answers.text: Seal the door undercut with a door sweep so the pressurized air cannot escape into the hallway at all
Close the bedroom supply register halfway so less air enters and the pressure difference slowly fades away
Provide a return path, a larger door undercut, a transfer grille, or a jumper duct, sized for the supply air delivered
Move the thermostat into the bedroom so the system satisfies that room first and ignores the pressure difference, as measured during the service visit described in the scenario above

questions.explanation: C is correct: A closed room with supply air and no return path pressurizes until air forces out through the undercut and envelope leaks; the fix is a deliberate return path (transfer grille, jumper duct, or adequate undercut) sized to the room's supply cfm. A is wrong because sealing the last escape path raises the room pressure further and starves system return air. B is wrong because throttling the register sacrifices the room's heating and cooling delivery instead of fixing the missing return path. D is wrong because thermostat location does not change the airflow imbalance causing the pressure.

questions.question: On a running split system, suction pressure converts to a 42-degree saturation temperature and the suction line measures 61 degrees, while liquid pressure converts to 112 degrees and the liquid line measures 99 degrees. Airflow is verified correct and the outdoor coil is clean. What fault do the paired readings indicate?

answers.text: An overcharge of refrigerant, shown by the low superheat and the low subcooling in this pair of readings
A low refrigerant charge, shown by low subcooling combined with the low suction pressure expected here
A dirty outdoor coil, shown by the clean-coil inspection together with a head pressure below the normal range
A liquid-line restriction, shown by high superheat of 19 degrees together with high subcooling of 13 degrees

questions.explanation: D is correct: Superheat = 61 - 42 = 19 degrees, which is high and starves the evaporator; subcooling = 112 - 99 = 13 degrees, which is high and shows refrigerant backing up ahead of a restriction such as a clogged filter drier or strainer. A is wrong because an overcharge drives superheat down and this superheat is high. B is wrong because a low charge gives low subcooling, not the 13 degrees measured. C is wrong because the coil was verified clean and a dirty coil raises head pressure rather than producing this starved-evaporator pattern.

questions.question: A furnace with a 5-inch draft hood outlet shows signs of flue-gas spillage at the hood on cold starts. The installed connector was necked down to 4 inches to fit an existing thimble. What is the most likely problem?

answers.text: The connector is smaller than the draft hood outlet, restricting flow where the vent system should never be reduced below that outlet size
The connector is larger than the flue, so flue gases slow down, cool off, and condense before they can reach the top of the chimney
The draft hood is oversized for the furnace input, so replacing the hood with a smaller one will restore proper draft at the burner
The thimble is the restriction the code intends, so spillage at the hood on a cold chimney is normal and needs no correction at all even on the coldest morning start of the heating season

questions.explanation: A is correct: A vent connector must not be smaller than the appliance draft hood outlet; reducing 5 inches to 4 inches restricts the vent and promotes spillage. B is wrong because the installed connector is smaller, not larger, than the outlet it serves. C is wrong because the draft hood is part of the listed appliance and is not field-resized to fix a connector restriction. D is wrong because spillage at the draft hood is a venting defect to correct, not an intended condition.

louisiana-hvac.quiz_title: Louisiana HVAC Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam

questions.question: A hermetic compressor's motor windings are cooled primarily by:
